5807742f0b56.text:
A critical flaw in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud let an attacker log in as a trusted client without holding that client's private key. To do it, the attacker had to reach their HTTPS API over the network and have the trusted client's public certificate.

Once in, the attacker would act as that client, with access to the cluster and its virtual machines. If the impersonated account is privileged, the attacker could gain "root access to the host machine," Canonical said.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-112816, carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, and Canonical has released fixed versions of both products.

How the Flaw Works

LXD and MicroCloud let remote clients access their APIs over mutual TLS, a setup in which the client presents a certificate to prove who it is. A client is trusted when its certificate is in the server's trust store, the list of identities the server will accept.

The flaw was in how the server checked that certificate. It compared every certificate the client sent against the trust store, but a TLS connection only proves the client owns the private key for the first certificate in the chain, the leaf. The rest of the chain is whatever the client chose to attach.

So an attacker could take a trusted client's public certificate, which is not secret, attach it to the chain behind their own, and the server would accept them as that client.

Who Is Affected

Using the flaw takes two things: network access to the HTTPS API, and the public certificate of a client the server already trusts.

A standalone LXD server does not expose that API by default. It listens only on a local socket unless an administrator turns on the network API with the core.https_address setting.

MicroCloud, which ties several machines running LXD into one cluster, has a specific weak point. Canonical said an attacker who can capture a member's public certificate as it joins the cluster can then log in as that member.

The CVE record lists LXD 4.0.14, 5.0.10, 5.21.8 and 6.9 as affected, each before the fixed release that follows. Canonical lists these fixed snap versions:

Product

Snap channel

Fixed version

LXD

6/stable

6.10.1

LXD

5.21/stable

5.21.9

LXD

5.0/stable

5.0.11

LXD

4.0/stable

4.0.15

MicroCloud

3/stable

3.4.1

MicroCloud

2/stable

2.1.5

The bug did not start at Canonical. The Incus project, which began as a community fork of LXD, reported it, and Canonical confirmed it affected LXD as well. Incus fixed the same flaw in version 7.6.0.

Ubuntu's own archive packages of LXD are listed as not affected or not shipped, so the fixed releases are the snaps.

There is no public sign the flaw has been used in an attack. The CVE record carries a U.S. CISA assessment, dated October 30, that the flaw is not known to have been exploited; it is not on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and no working exploit has been published.

What to Do

Update LXD and MicroCloud to the fixed versions. On a snap install, run sudo snap refresh lxd and sudo snap refresh microcloud.

Canonical said the fixed LXD point releases were still rolling out from the candidate channel to stable at the time of its advisory, so check the version you actually have after the refresh rather than assume the fix arrived.

Canonical's advisory gives no temporary workaround for LXD. Because the attack requires network access to the API, limiting who can reach it reduces risk until you update. The Incus project, reporting the same flaw, said there is no configuration fix and that the only step is to restrict network access to the listener.

Incus users should move to 7.6.0, which fixed this flaw along with 17 other security issues.

59dbc26176f9.text:
Malicious code on the website of prediction market Polymarket sold some signed-in traders' positions and moved their funds to the hackers on October 29. The code had replaced a page-speed script that the site loaded from an outside company.

Polymarket says it is refunding about $2.7 million to 726 affected wallets. Blockchain records show crypto worth about $2.64 million reached the hackers' wallet in under an hour.

The replaced script came from DebugBear, whose real user monitoring (RUM) tool measures how fast web pages load for real visitors.

Researchers at Hudson Rock downloaded the malicious file on October 29 from the address Polymarket's site used to load the DebugBear script. They also found a change in Polymarket's site code that removed the DebugBear script.

DebugBear's DNS records were compromised through its domain registrar, the company said on X. Its early findings indicate the attack targeted one customer's website. It has seen no sign of a break-in to its own systems, though it is still looking.

Researchers at Ohey found a different server answering for DebugBear's web addresses at 18:13 UTC, when the malicious file was still online. Earlier that day, the normal script had been served from Google Cloud Storage. Each DebugBear customer loads its own copy of the script, and the file that was swapped was Polymarket's.

How the Script Took the Money

The code reuses the access a signed-in trader already has in an open Polymarket page, Hudson Rock found after reviewing the file without running it. It reads account details that Polymarket keeps in the browser, including a set of trading API keys.

Those API keys alone cannot place an order on Polymarket, because orders also need a wallet signature. Hudson Rock found no part of the code that sends the keys, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to the server it reports to.

Instead, the code searches the page for the part of Polymarket's site that places orders, and for the signer that approves the account's transactions.

It then takes one of two paths. For accounts that sign in with their own crypto wallet, it moves the trader's positions straight to the hackers' wallet. For accounts that sign in via email, it sells positions at ever-worse prices and then moves the money out.

In both paths, the code asks the account's own signer to sign its requests and hands them to Polymarket's relayer, which submits them. Hudson Rock said a signing request alone does not prove a trader signed without seeing a prompt. The wallet provider may still ask the trader, refuse, or apply its own rules for the session.

The wallet written into the code received its first funds at 17:10 UTC and its last at 18:02 UTC, according to Ohey's blockchain trace. In that time, it collected 28.6 million POL tokens and positions from 33 wallets.

At 18:19 UTC, those 28.6 million POL were worth about $2.64 million at DefiLlama's price of $0.0922, DefiPrime calculated. The figure covers only the POL, not the positions.

The wallet sent all 28.6 million POL on to three other addresses between 18:28 and 18:38 UTC, its transaction history shows.

Polymarket's Response and Refunds

Polymarket posted its first status update about unauthorized activity in user wallets at 17:38 UTC. At 18:05 UTC, it said its exchange was in cancel-only mode, with relayer actions paused.

The company said it removed the script "within the hour." It also cleared every cache, reset all active login sessions and paused trading until the site was clean. It has referred the case to law enforcement.

By October 30, 689 of the 726 affected wallets had been refunded in full, and the remaining 37 were being paid as they were checked. Polymarket is also paying $1.19 million to about 5,500 wallets that lost money during the trading pause or had positions taken. In all, it is returning $3.9 million to traders.

Traders do not need to file a claim. Polymarket's status page links a form for anyone who thinks their amount is wrong or that they should have received a payment.

What Sites and Traders Can Do

DebugBear has told customers of its RUM product to remove its embed code from their websites. The address that served the malicious file, cdn.debugbear[.]com, had no DNS record when The Hacker News checked on November 1.

Polymarket said it is putting third-party scripts back in place with extra checks, such as a stronger Content Security Policy (CSP), pinned versions, and sandboxing.

Hudson Rock's advice for sites that load outside scripts:

Keep unneeded third-party code off pages where users trade or sign.

Where a file can be pinned, use Subresource Integrity (SRI), which lets the browser reject the file if its contents change. A security policy that simply allows a trusted CDN does not check the files that CDN serves.

Check what code on a signed-in page can ask the signer to do.

Hudson Rock's advice for traders is to reject any signing request they did not expect.

The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets to TraderTraitor, a North Korea-aligned elite hacking group also tracked as Jade Sleet, Pressure Chollima, PUKCHONG, Slow Pisces, and UNC4899.

The FBI, along with the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), said it observed the threat actor converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH).

"It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages," the FBI said in a statement.

The agency has also provided a list of wallet addresses that the attackers are said to be using to launder the stolen assets.

The development comes as Binance said it has resumed phase one of withdrawals starting today between 6 and 9 a.m. UTC after they were paused in the wake of the incident.

"Since the incident, our teams have taken precautionary measures to safeguard the platform, conducted security assessments, and worked to verify the readiness of affected services," Binance said in a statement.

"We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks. Deposit services remain open and are not affected by the incident."

The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin.

"This single incident almost doubles the total cryptoassets stolen by the regime," blockchain analysis firm Elliptic said. "Actors linked to North Korea, officially the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK), are believed to have stolen over $6.5 billion in cryptoassets in recent years."

Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism.

TraderTraitor is the name assigned to a North Korean group that has a history of orchestrating cryptocurrency thefts against the Web3.0 industry by tricking victims into downloading malware-laced applications. The cluster is known to be active since at least 2020.

In recent years, the adversary has been attributed to cryptocurrency heists targeting DMM Bitcoin, Bybit, KelpDAO, and Bitget.

Reports from SentinelOne, Zscaler ThreatLabz, and Microsoft have revealed that TraderTraitor is continuing to hone its tradecraft, using trojanized Terraform providers as a malware distribution vector and leveraging front companies to conduct job-themed targeting against individuals involved in cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, and talent recruitment companies.

The poisoned Terraform provider is used to deliver a Bash loader that selects and downloads malware tailored to the victim's operating system. This includes a cross-platform implant called FLATROOF, which siphons sensitive data from the victim using a Python-based information stealer before ultimately dropping the ROOFDECK backdoor to obtain complete remote control.

The activity once again demonstrates how North Korean threat actors continue to abuse trusted developer workflows through trojanized Terraform providers to deliver cross-platform malware across macOS, Linux, and Windows systems, and gain persistent access.

TraderTraitor's modus operandi, like other North Korea-linked campaigns such as Lazarus Group's Operation Dream Job and Famous Chollima's Contagious Interview, employs recruitment-themed lures as a pretext to convince victims to run malicious code. The social engineering phase is augmented by the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to craft convincing lures, create fake personas, and evade detection.

"The actor leveraged tailored domains, social media profiles, and industry-specific knowledge to pose as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company, using software engineer-themed opportunities to initiate contact and schedule interviews with individuals who engaged with the outreach," Microsoft said.

"Within this short time frame, Jade Sleet conducted similar job-themed targeting using two additional front companies, supported by comparable infrastructure and relevant domain knowledge."

690ba49167f4.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what has been described as a "highly sophisticated infection chain" targeting government organizations in Asia.

The activity, detailed by Kaspersky this week, targeted a custom Windows 10 build used exclusively by government entities in Asia and involves the deployment of a previously undocumented .NET assembly-loading framework codenamed NetamLoader.

The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Nor is it clear if the intrusion compromised more than one system and allowed the hackers to steal any sensitive information.

The Russian cybersecurity company said the artifact was detected in the first half of 2026, packaged inside a Windows cabinet archive (CAB) file placed in a directory that stores Windows operating system update packages.

It's suspected the operation involved a supply chain attack, in which bad actors compromised a trusted third-party vendor to gain access to downstream users who rely on its services or software.

The sample in question features a ".config" file that employs AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. AppDomainManager injection is an adversarial technique used to load arbitrary payloads by hijacking .NET Framework's AppDomainManager mechanism when a .NET application starts.

Put differently, the approach targets .NET Framework's application-domain initialization to achieve code execution. The end result is the same as DLL sideloading: to run malicious code inside a legitimate application's process so as to fly under the radar.

According to Kaspersky, the CAB archive containing the .config file was placed in the path: "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24," with its contents extracted and dropped into "C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\."

Infection chain: Stage 1

The exact delivery vehicle for the CAB archive remains unknown. Present in the archive are seven files, four of which are legitimate components of Patch My PC, an endpoint management software -

fabric.config

Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll

PatchMyPC-Enum.dll

PatchMyPC-Models.dll

PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe

PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config

Resources.resx

None of the files with the exception of "Resources.resx" embed malicious code. The infection chain plays out as a two-stage process as follows -

The execution of "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe" serves as the launchpad for several payloads. It abuses AppDomainManager injection to parse "PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config," resulting in the execution of "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll."

Once loaded, "Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll" finds "fabric.config" located in the same directory and parses its contents to load "Resources.resx."

"Resources.resx" contains "multiple layers" of encoded, compressed, or encrypted payloads, such as XAML files, .NET assemblies, and JSON data, which are decoded and loaded by the component before it.

Infection chain: Stage 2

A brief description of these payloads is listed below -

XAML-1, a loader for an embedded payload, XAML-2.

XAML‑2 initializes the second stage of the attack chain by loading two compressed and Base64‑encoded XAML files: XAML-2-1 and XAML-2-2. XAML-2-1 is used to bypass Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI).

XAML-2-2 contains two parts, a .NET module (aka .NET 1 Loader) and a JSON data payload (aka JSON-1).

JSON-1, the JSON payload that contains two components: JSON-1-c, which stores command-and-control (C2) server configuration, and JSON-1-p, which contains a Base64‑encoded file (.NET 2 Plugin) and a collection of compressed, encrypted XAML templates used to build XAML-3.

XAML-2-2 loads .NET 1 Loader, which then serves as a decrypting, assembling, and loading for XAML‑3, reports the status to the C2 server, and deletes malicious files extracted from the CAB archive, along with CLR usage logs and Windows system Prefetch cache files to cover up the tracks.

XAML-3, the XAML payload that runs within "dllhost.exe" and is designed to decode, decompress, and load .NET 2 Plugin.

.NET 2 Plugin, a .NET assembly that loads the C2 configuration, gathers system information from Windows Registry, checks if the current host process is "dllhost.exe," waits a random jitter delay of 20-40 minutes before issuing its first request to the C2 server ("openaigpt4v[.]com"), and enters into a periodic polling loop to fetch an XAML file and execute it in an isolated AppDomain.

"If a valid response is received from C2, the loop pauses for 5-6 minutes before the next request; otherwise, it pauses for 22-28 hours, checking every 10 minutes to determine whether the allotted time has elapsed," Kaspersky explained.

Telemetry data gathered by Kaspersky has identified a single victim in Asia, with NetamLoader designed to attack a Windows 10 build customized for government-only use. Although the targeted Asian country was not disclosed, signs are that it's likely China, as Microsoft offers a bespoke version called Windows 10 China Government Edition specifically for the Chinese government and state-owned entities.

Earlier this August, Bloomberg reported that China's Ministry of State Security had ordered some government agencies to stop using the "Government Edition" in favor of Chinese-made Linux distributions as part of an effort to reduce its dependence on foreign technology.

"Beijing's instruction stemmed from data security concerns," Bloomberg said, citing "people familiar with the matter." No additional details were disclosed at the time.

"In today's geopolitical climate, a growing number of countries are building their own core software platforms, including operating systems, databases, middleware, and cloud services, with operating systems often the top priority," Kaspersky concluded.

"The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own. Bringing the operation and maintenance of such a system to maturity is a lengthy process."

97e803b471d6.text:
SMS of Death lets attackers crash Android call services with a hidden, zero-click message, blocking phone calls, even emergency calls too.

A specially manipulated SMS message is enough to crash Android’s phone service, interrupt ongoing calls, and temporarily render the smartphone unusable. The attack requires no interaction from the victim and can even compromise the ability to contact emergency services.

The vulnerability, dubbed the SMS of Death, is bringing renewed attention to the security of the messaging system in Android smartphones. The issue, documented by independent researcher Mark Blaszczyk, allows a remote attacker to cause a disruption in phone service by sending a single, specially crafted WAP Push message.

WAP Push (Wireless Application Protocol Push) is a particular message transmitted over the mobile network, generally in the form of a binary SMS, which contains structured data and is processed automatically by the smartphone without requiring user intervention. Unlike a traditional SMS, it can carry notifications, links to Internet resources, and configurations for mobile services.

The most worrying aspect is the execution method. It’s a zero-click attack, in which the recipient doesn’t have to open the message, select a link, or authorize any action. The content is automatically processed by the operating system and can cause the process responsible for phone functionality to crash.

The vulnerability affects “WapPushOverSms“, an Android framework component located in the “frameworks/opt/telephony” path, responsible for interpreting and managing WAP Push messages received by the device.

The technical cause lies in the incorrect handling of a numeric value used during message interpretation. Specifically, the “decodeWapPdu()” function, the researcher explains, reads the length of the WSP header through a value encoded as “uintvar” , initially returned as a 64-bit number. The value is subsequently converted to a 32-bit integer without prior range checking. This operation can transform a seemingly valid number into a negative value, which is then used to determine the size of an array. The consequence of this is a “NegativeArraySizeException” exception, thrown when Android attempts to allocate a negative-sized array. The exception is not handled correctly in the processing path and causes the “com.android.phone” process, responsible for telephony functions, to terminate.

The researcher demonstrated that a five-byte WSP header can generate the value “-2147483648“, which is sufficient to trigger the issue. Therefore, it is not necessary to transmit particularly large amounts of content to cause the issue.

“A 5-byte uintvar of 88 80 80 80 00 decodes to 0x80000000. Cast to a signed 32-bit int, that is -2147483648. Allocating new byte[-2147483648] throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing com.android.phone:” reads the analysis.

An invisible attack that also interrupts emergency calls

The message is transmitted as a data SMS via the WAP Push channel on port 2948. Unlike a regular SMS, it isn’t displayed in the message inbox and doesn’t generate a user-recognizable notification. The sender’s number isn’t normally visible in the conversation, and when the device receives the message, Android automatically starts processing it. A crash in the phone process causes a temporary loss of connectivity and interrupts active voice calls, including those to emergency services.

According to the researcher’s published evidence, each message processing can cause a disruption in telephone service lasting about one to two seconds, during which the component is rebooted. However, the problem can become much more serious if the message is processed repeatedly.

One of the most significant aspects of SMS of Death is the ability to transform a simple crash into a persistent Denial of Service condition. The malicious message can remain in the incoming SMS queue and be reprocessed during subsequent delivery attempts. The telephone operator’s retransmission mechanism can also contribute to a repeat of the event, causing further service disruptions.

The researcher reports observing intermittent crashes for up to a week after receiving a single message. Sending around twenty specially crafted messages can render the device unusable for an extended period. In more severe cases, the phone process can continue to crash during system startup, triggering a condition similar to a boot loop. Recovery may require using the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) on a computer, directly intervening in the queue of messages waiting to be processed. For a typical user, this is far from a simple procedure.

A threat to communications availability

SMS of Death demonstrates how a cyberattack doesn’t necessarily have to involve information theft, code execution, or device control to have significant consequences. In this case, the target is phone service availability, a crucial feature especially when contacting emergency services. The ability to interrupt communications without any user interaction makes this vulnerability particularly sensitive. To reduce exposure, it’s important to check the Android security patch level installed and apply available updates, paying particular attention to devices no longer receiving manufacturer support.

Testing conducted by Mark Blah has shown that the issue is reproducible on several devices, including the Google Pixel 9 and Samsung smartphones from the Galaxy and Galaxy A families. The vulnerable code appears to be present on Android versions ranging from Android 12 to Android 17. However, the availability of the fix is ​​not uniform across all generations of the operating system.

According to documentation published by the researcher, Google has distributed a fix via the October 2026 security update for Android 14, 15, 16, and 17. Older devices, such as those running Android 12 and 13, may remain exposed if they do not receive corrective updates.

It's assigned CVE-2026-58882 and a Critical severity in the November 2026 Android Security Bulletin. We've had it listed as one of the patches included in our security preview releases since our 2026072901 release which you can see in the release notes:https://t.co/tBoWBpALw1

— GrapheneOS (@GrapheneOS) October 29, 2026

Northstar Security, a startup developing AI agents for security teams, has emerged from stealth mode with $7 million in seed funding.

Wing Venture Capital led the round. MVP, Outliers, and cybersecurity veterans Gerhard Eschelbeck, Renaud Deraison, and Justin Somaini also invested.

The company ingests data from existing security and IT tools to build what it calls a Security Context Graph. Updated in real time, the graph shows how identities, assets, applications, vulnerabilities, and business systems connect to one another.

Northstar aims to catch so-called toxic combinations. Issues such as a vulnerability, an unmanaged device, or an account with excessive privileges may seem under control on their own, but together they can expose critical business systems.

For instance, the platform could flag a laptop lacking endpoint protection whose owner is a privileged user able to reach a critical payroll system.

Analysts can investigate findings like this by asking questions in plain language. Northstar’s agents can then kick off fixes, such as installing endpoint protection, notifying the user, or limiting their access, and people can supervise those actions where appropriate.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Customers can also give external AI agents access to the graph through Model Context Protocol (MCP) and build their own security workflows. Northstar says it connects to more than 70 enterprise security and IT products, among them Okta, GitHub, Workday, Microsoft Defender and Entra, AWS, and Google Cloud.

“Security teams are drowning in data but starving for context,” said Amer Deeba, Northstar’s CEO and co-founder.

Deeba co-founded Normalyze, which Proofpoint later acquired, and was previously a senior executive at Qualys. His co-founder, CTO Ed Rowe, held the same role at Farmers Business Network and led engineering as an SVP at AppDynamics.

The startup will use the money to develop its platform, hire staff, and expand its go-to-market push.

Hackers attempted to exploit a critical GitLab vulnerability in Alpine Linux's development infrastructure on October 20–21, prompting the open-source project to rebuild its GitLab server and reset all passwords over concerns of a possible compromise.

The attacks targeted CVE-2026-97229, a maximum-severity remote code execution flaw, repeatedly crashing GitLab processes, with some attempts coming close to succeeding.

Although Alpine Linux found no evidence that attackers executed code or tampered with its software packages and releases, it could not rule out a successful compromise due to missing logs and a lack of outbound connection records.

"Because we cannot rule out code execution, and the evidence we would need to confirm it no longer exists, we took the harder route and rebuilt the GitLab instance from scratch," explained the Alpine Linux team.

Alpine Linux is a small, lightweight operating system widely used as the foundation for Docker container images that run applications and services.

Their GitLab instance hosts development repositories, code reviews, and CI jobs, including the "aports" build recipes used to produce Alpine’s software packages.

That makes it a valuable supply chain target, as tampering with their GitLab environment could affect downstream software.

CVE-2026-97229 is a maximum-severity integer overflow vulnerability in GitLab’s CI/CD regular expression compiler Onigmo, bundled in Ruby, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on the server.

GitLab disclosed the flaw and made fixes available on October 12, warning that attackers can trigger it under certain conditions by submitting a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD pipeline configuration.

Alpine initially installed GitLab 19.3.4 instead of the patched version, 19.3.5. A later upgrade to 19.3.6 also failed to close the flaw because the fix required a patch to Ruby, which GitLab bundled with its official packages but Alpine’s custom container image did not include.

On October 20-21, the attacker submitted malicious CI configurations targeting the flaw, causing eight worker crashes; four were partially successful, though none seemed to go all the way.

The Alpine Linux team found that the attackers downloaded its GitLab container image, suggesting they may have been preparing a supply-chain attack.

After investigating, Alpine found no tampering in the repository commits, packages, or releases up to October 27. Also, no signing keys could have been exposed, as those aren’t stored on the GitLab server.

If exploitation succeeded, potentially exposed information includes user details, password hashes, 2FA secrets, CI/CD secrets, integration credentials, and private project content, though no compromise of the above has been confirmed.

Alpine advises users to reset their GitLab passwords and pull the alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 image published on October 27, which contains Ruby 3.3.13 and addresses CVE-2026-97229.

Recently, I had to extract embedded files from a set of OneNote files (extension .one).

My onedump.py tool can extract individual files, so I would have to run this many times. To avoid this, I added a new feature to my onedump.py tool: producing JSON data. Several of my tools already have such a feature: they produce JSON data with the content of their analysis results.

onedump's option --jsonoutput produces JSON output with the content of each embedded file found inside the OneNote file. And it can do this for many .one files in one go:

onedump.py --jsonoutput *.one

To write these files to disk you can use my myjson-filter.py tool, like this:

onedump.py --jsonoutput *.one | myjson-filter.py -W hashvir

This will write all the embedded files to disk, their name will be the sha256 hash of their content plus extension .vir (hashvir).

Didier Stevens Senior handler blog.DidierStevens.com

Here’s an overview of some of last week’s most interesting news, articles, interviews and videos:

r/opensource bans AI projects, and solo devs go down with them Moderators of r/opensource, Reddit’s catch-all forum for open source software, have barred any project that “uses AI, is made by AI, or is intended for AI.” Moderator Wolvereness announced the rules in a post over the weekend.

AI slop is piling up highest on the biggest open-source projects The maintainers of large open source projects are taking the worst of the AI slop. In a Linux Foundation survey of 234 open source contributors and maintainers, people running projects with more than 50 contributors estimated that close to a third of the code changes landing in their queue are low quality or AI-generated. Those maintainers now worry more about burning out than about the code itself.

Microsoft Authenticator vulnerability let rogue Android apps steal work account access If you use Microsoft Authenticator on Android, update it. Researchers at Enclave found a flaw that let any app on your phone quietly take over your work account. The app didn’t need permissions, and you didn’t need to tap anything.

Several AI security market categories are headed for bigger platforms In this interview with Help Net Security, Jonathan Care, Lead Analyst and Practice Lead AI at KuppingerCole Analysts, compares AI security startups to the early fraud market he helped define at Gartner. He explains which categories will survive as products and which will become features inside bigger platforms.

Private repos still leak secrets to Gheist, a stolen GitHub token campaign Wiz Research has recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from 850+ compromised GitHub accounts, the work of a campaign it calls Gheist, after the user agent the tool sends with its GitHub API requests. The tool takes a stolen token, finds every repository that token can open, and plants a workflow in each one. The workflow prints the repository’s secrets into a log, and the attacker downloads it.

Bellini Capital CISO on AI security governance and the limits of patching faster In this Help Net Security interview, Brian Blakley, CISO at Bellini Capital and ConnectSecure, explains why AI makes finding vulnerabilities faster while fixing them still takes time. He argues that “patch faster” is not enough and that teams need to cut exposure while remediation is pending.

CISA updates ScubaGear and ScubaGoggles, and says Microsoft 365 checks get faster CISA released ScubaGear v2.0 and ScubaGoggles v1.1.0, new versions of the open-source tools it publishes to check Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace settings against its security baselines. The agency calls ScubaGear v2.0 the most comprehensive update to that tool since its 2022 launch. ScubaGoggles, which launched in 2023, gets a new baseline and enhanced Gemini controls.

GitHub’s npm package firewall can block brand-new versions before they install GitHub announced a package firewall that checks npm packages against an enterprise’s policy before they install. It blocks known malware, critical vulnerabilities, and brand-new versions, and any developer can turn it on by pointing npm at the firewall.

Stolen staff logins are spreading attacks between K-12 school districts Last school year, 808 K-12 school organizations got some unwelcome news. The Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) told them their staff accounts or credentials were circulating on underground and dark web marketplaces. That’s 808 of the center’s 6,116 K-12 members, and attackers are using those logins to get in the door and then reach the next district.

IT bosses are confident they’ve found the certificates they don’t know about Forty percent of 500 senior IT and security leaders surveyed for certificate authority Sectigo said they are very prepared for monthly TLS certificate renewals because automated systems are already in place. Their more specific answers point elsewhere. Only 4% said their certificate management is already automated, and 61% said their organization had a certificate-related outage or incident in the past 12 months.

Qualys CISO on what security teams can do as exploit campaigns grow In this Help Net Security interview, Nathan Smolenski, CISO at Qualys, talks about how security teams can handle the growing volume of AI-discovered vulnerabilities. He explains why CISOs should track the average window of exposure instead of standard MTTR, and why only a small share of disclosed flaws, under one percent in 2025, pose active risk.

Researchers broke the browsers built into VS Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex and Claude Desktop Forever Security found ways out of the built-in browsers in five AI coding assistants: Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI’s Codex, Microsoft’s VS Code and Anthropic’s Claude Desktop. In all five, a web page or a local file reached the computer behind the browser. Cursor ran attacker code, Copilot showed a fake address, and Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop let a single local file read the rest of the disk.

Fake IT help desk callers got by on little more than names and email addresses Attackers posing as IT help desk staff contacted employees by phone, email and Microsoft Teams in the third quarter of 2026 and talked them into opening remote access sessions, Cisco Talos Incident Response (Talos IR) found across several engagements. In one case, that access ended in ransomware.

Cyberattack disrupts University of New Mexico hospitals, extortion group claims attack University of New Mexico (UNM) Health Sciences Center (HSC), the academic medical arm of the University of New Mexico, has suffered a cyberattack that has temporarily disrupted the operation of its hospitals and may have resulted in a substantial data breach.

Brotli bug reaches far beyond Node.js (CVE-2026-111497) A vulnerability in Brotli, Google’s widely used open-source compression library, is putting a broad range of software at risk. Alternatively known as “Node2Shell”, “Broccoli2Shell” and “Brotli2Shell”, CVE-2026-111497 is a remotely exploitable out-of-bounds write flaw that gained widespread attention after Node.js publicly disclosed it on October 21, 2026.

Tailscale fixes SSH flaws allowing lateral movement within tailnets Tailscale, the company behind the popular software-defined mesh networking and connectivity platform of the same name, has shipped fixes for several vulnerabilities, including some in Tailscale SSH that could let an attacker who already had access to a device in the network gain more privileges on other machines that are part of it.

Compromised camera management software gives attackers a way into corporate networks Attackers have been breaking into business networks through camera management software, according to new research from security firm Huntress, which traced several incidents in September and October back to a compromised application.

Volt Typhoon targeted enterprise control planes via ever-changing “Silent Train” relay network Volt Typhoon, a Chinese state-sponsored APT group that’s focused on cyberespionage and United States’ critical infrastructure, has been using a covert, constantly rotating relay network to hide its most sensitive intrusions, Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs revealed on Wednesday.

Chinese hackers used VMware ESX zero-day; PHP2Shell and Fragnesia chained to root firewalls China-nexus threat actors have exploited a VMware ESX zero-day to hide their tracks and chained PHP2Shell flaws with the “Fragnesia” Linux kernel bug to root servers and firewalls, cybersecurity researchers claim. Cisco has also confirmed that attackers are crashing its firewalls with a newly disclosed vulnerability.

LLM agent security needs more than guardrails Madhu Shashanka, Chief Scientist at Concentric AI, explains why securing LLM tools and agents depends more on your data than on the model. Controls on model behavior, such as guardrails and injection detection, lower the rate of bad outcomes but never reach zero. Controls on what goes in are different, because you own the documents, systems, and credentials an agent can reach.

Product showcase: Stellar Cyber’s ISOC platform provides full-cycle architecture An AI SOC that starts with somebody else’s alert is already too late. Stellar Cyber collects and normalizes telemetry, detects suspicious activity, correlates evidence, builds cases, investigates incidents, triages findings, and drives response from the same security architecture. That gives people and AI access to the evidence behind the alert – not just the alert itself.

I underestimated how fast security teams would trust AI to act in the SOC For most of her career, Aqsa Taylor has watched enterprises adopt new security platforms slowly. She expected AI adoption in security operations centers (SOCs) to follow the same pattern, particularly given strict compliance requirements. Instead, adoption moved faster than she expected as AI helped attackers shorten the time between initial compromise and damage.

What exactly is ISOC? And what does it mean for you? Security teams often spend too much time moving between tools to piece together an incident. Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) solutions aim to reduce that work by bringing detection, investigation, and response together, while SIEM remains the system of record for security data. Stellar Cyber’s approach uses the same underlying data throughout this process, giving analysts and AI access to the evidence behind an alert.

Security pros reckon the biggest AI risk comes with an employee badge Employees pasting company data into AI tools worry security teams more than AI-powered attacks do. AI-generated phishing, the attack they run into most often, made the list of top concerns for only a quarter of the 209 security professionals O’Reilly surveyed in September.

DreamHost incident triggers password resets, locks customers out of email and FTP accounts DreamHost has brought its File Manager back online after an incident that disrupted several of its services, though some of its customers still can’t get into their email or FTP accounts until someone sets a new password for them.

Cyberattack on University of Copenhagen exposes data of 525,000 people The University of Copenhagen (UCPH) has ruled out a second cyberattack, saying the activity that led it to shut down several administrative systems on Monday is tied to the breach it disclosed last week, which exposed personal data belonging to some 525,000 people.

Hackers bury inboxes in spam then show up on Microsoft Teams posing as IT support Threat actors are flooding employees’ inboxes with spam and then contacting them on Microsoft Teams as IT support, offering to fix the problem they created, Arctic Wolf has found. The security company documented more than 400 incidents in which the external chat feature in Teams was abused.

Data breach at Sony-owned internet provider compromises 2.6 million customer records Attackers who broke into the So-net member database made off with personal information belonging to more than 2.58 million current and former customers, along with the email passwords of 54,401 users, Sony Network Communications has disclosed.

FBI seizes Virtualine, bulletproof hosting provider that promised to shield criminals from police The FBI has seized virtualine.net, the domain of a bulletproof hosting provider that laundered money for its criminal customers and kept a forum trading in child sexual abuse material online despite repeated warnings from police and child protection groups.

345,000 email addresses stolen in cyberattack on Germany’s far-right party AfD Over 345,000 unique email addresses were exposed in the September 2026 breach at German far-right political party Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). Breach notification service Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the data to its database on 27 October, listing email addresses and email messages as the compromised information.

Hacktivists leak 41,000 DHS staff records, revealing undercover ICE agents Names, offices, contact details and assignments of more than 41,000 U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees have been leaked by a hacktivist group calling itself the Department of Peace.

Exploitation attempts against recently patched Oracle EBS flaw have begun (CVE-2026-101767) Exploitation attempts have started against CVE-2026-101767, a recently patched Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS) flaw. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and affects the Application Object Library product in EBS versions 12.2.3 to 12.2.15. Oracle’s description in the NVD entry calls it an “easily exploitable vulnerability” open to an unauthenticated attacker over HTTP.

Yoba malware hides in fake desktop versions of ChatGPT and Claude Fake GitHub projects posing as desktop versions of ChatGPT and Claude have been used to spread a malware chain that ends with a cryptocurrency miner, Check Point has found. The researchers have been tracking the campaign, dubbed Yoba, for the past two months.

Binance hit by $6.3 billion theft in what could be the biggest crypto heist on record About $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency was stolen from Binance in what might be the biggest crypto hack in history. The company found no evidence of a wallet private key leak and plans to publish a technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete.

Claude Code extension poisoned with persistent SSH backdoor A tampered build of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension for VS Code-compatible editors planted an SSH backdoor on developers’ machines, researchers at macOS security firm Phorion have found.

Assad regime hacker who caused $136 billion market drop sentenced to 42 months A Syrian man who used a hijacked news agency Twitter account to post a fake report of explosions at the White House has been sentenced to 42 months in prison, the US Department of Justice has announced.

OpenSSL 4.1.0: What’s new, what’s removed, and what’s still broken The OpenSSL project released version 4.1.0, adding support for DTLS 1.3 and listing four known bugs in the DTLS code that ships with it. DTLS is the variant of TLS built for datagram transports such as UDP, and version 1.3 is defined in RFC 9147.

Google open-sources the Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin its engineers use to catch AI coding mistakes Google has open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin, an internal tool that makes an AI coding agent write and defend a design document before it touches any code. The plugin hands that document to fresh AI sessions that have never seen the design conversation and tells them to find what is wrong with it.

Synthetic identities leave US lenders with $2.4 billion in fraud exposure Criminals are exploiting established customer accounts and familiar brands to steal money and personal information, according to TransUnion’s Fraud in the Age of Continuous Trust report. Eighty-one percent of suspected digital fraud in its network during the first half of 2026 occurred during account logins and financial transactions, highlighting risks that persist throughout a customer relationship.

Forgotten AI agents may still access sensitive company data AI agents that have not run recently retain credentials and connections to company systems, according to Arrakis Security’s 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report. About 76% of enabled agents examined had not run in 60 days, leaving access available through inactive software.

Witness: Open-source framework for verifying how your software was built Witness is an open-source command-line tool that records how software gets built, signs that record, and checks it against a policy before the software ships. TestifySec built Witness and donated it to the in-toto ecosystem within the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, and an open community now maintains it.

Anthropic details what stops Claude Duet from going rogue Anthropic has outlined the security and privacy protections behind Claude Duet, its proactive AI agent that can monitor connected accounts and complete tasks while users are away. The safeguards include approval requirements, checks for sensitive information and infrastructure that keeps credentials outside the model’s reach.

Kali Linux 2026.3 ships kernel 7.1.5, brings wardriving to the TicWatch Pro 3 The Kali Linux team released version 2026.3 after overhauling the public build scripts it uses to produce every official image. The refreshed scripts share the same features, command-line arguments and, where possible, the same layout, so a pipeline written against an older script may need edits.

GPT-6.1 Terra meets OpenAI’s Critical cyber threshold, and it’s cheaper than GPT-5.6 Terra OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, a model that operates desktop software, to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, and to developers through its API as gpt-6.1-terra. API prices are 50 percent below those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol: $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens. Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes.

71% of vulnerability exploitation starts within a week of disclosure Attackers are exploiting newly disclosed security flaws within days, leaving organizations little time to respond, according to Rapid7’s Q3 2026 Quarterly Threat Landscape Report. The company reported an average of three days between public disclosure and exploitation of high-severity vulnerabilities, with 71% of tracked exploitation occurring within the first week.

Amutable Foundations is a Linux system with no SSH and no package manager Amutable opened signups for the private preview of Amutable Foundations, a Linux system in which each machine sends a signed report of the software and configuration it runs, drawing on local hardware to make the report easier to verify. The company says its engineers write and maintain code in the kernel, in systemd and in image-building tools.

CISA lays out plan to push cyber adversaries out of US critical infrastructure The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has released CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail, a strategy to strengthen national security and the resilience of critical infrastructure. It addresses intersecting cyber, physical, and geopolitical threats that can disrupt essential services.

Breach victims discover their data was held by companies they’ve never heard of Nearly seven in ten people affected by data breaches handled by Kroll were exposed through an outside supplier, according to its Data Breach Outlook 2026. Businesses rely on outside providers to store information, process transactions and operate software. A breach at one of those providers can expose customer records across multiple organizations, including people who have never heard of the company holding their data.

NIST starts the countdown to retire quantum-vulnerable encryption The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has released a roadmap for moving to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), with earlier deadlines for certain sensitive federal systems. The report, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (NIST IR 8547), explains which cryptographic methods need to be replaced, what organizations should consider and how the transition will unfold.

AbuseBox: Open-source monitor for blacklists, DNS, SSL and email records AbuseBox is a free, open-source tool that checks IP addresses and domains against 60 DNS blacklists, pulls reputation scores from AbuseIPDB, inspects DNS, SSL and email-authentication records, and sends an alert when something changes. A DNS blacklist, or DNSBL, is a list that mail servers and other services consult when deciding whether to trust an address.

Ukrainian ransomware hacker sentenced, $11 million reward offered for co-conspirator A Ukrainian national who participated in ransomware attacks targeting hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses was sentenced to five years and 10 months in prison. Artem Stryzhak, 36, pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.

Upwind secures $400 million to protect AI across endpoints, code, and cloud Upwind Security has raised $400 million in Series C funding to expand its cloud and AI security platform, bringing the company’s total funding to more than $800 million.

Shame and sleepless nights haunt scam victims long after the money is gone Scams and identity theft hurt people in different ways, and recovering involves much more than getting money back, according to ITRC’s 2026 Consumer Impact Report. Scam victims often struggle with shame and self-blame, while identity theft victims can spend weeks of personal effort trying to repair the damage.

Ubuntu Core Desktop returns as Canonical’s plan for an immutable default desktop Canonical has restarted work on Ubuntu Core Desktop, the immutable and attestable version of Ubuntu that the company says will over time become the default Ubuntu desktop. Jon Seager, Canonical’s VP of engineering, laid out the plan and admitted that the 2023 developer preview “fell short” of what the company had in mind.

Google says Gemini 4 Carbon beats its predecessors at finding and fixing security flaws Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is a frontier AI model designed for software engineering and cybersecurity tasks, with safeguards built on those of its predecessor, Argon. Google says its teams have seen Carbon spend days investigating and fixing bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. The model was also trained to handle complex tasks and high-pressure situations.

Smart TVs can harbor unpatched security flaws and track what you watch Smart TVs and connected plugs accounted for a large share of recorded security weaknesses in household devices, according to Bitdefender’s 2026 IoT Security Landscape Report. The analysis covered approximately 10.4 million protected home routers between January and September.

Scammers rebuild fake shopping sites within hours of a takedown One retail scam used more than 1,200 look-alike .shop domains sharing a single IP address. The sites reused HTML, JavaScript and payment-page designs intended to harvest card numbers, expiry dates and security codes, according Akamai’s Fraud and Abuse Report 2026.

Open-weight AI model GLM-5.3 cheated its way to correct answers Irregular evaluated Zhipu AI’s open-weight model GLM-5.3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench, the company’s framework for measuring an LLM’s ability to plan and execute multistage attacks under realistic constraints.

Cybersecurity jobs available right now: October 27, 2026 We’ve scoured the market to bring you a selection of roles that span various skill levels within the cybersecurity field. Check out this weekly selection of cybersecurity jobs available right now.

OpenAI has just confirmed that it's rolling out ChatGPT Work capabilities directly into regular Chat, while also combining usage allowances across ChatGPT and Codex.

In an email seen by BleepingComputer, OpenAI noted that it will test a combined experience for Chat and Work tabs in the coming weeks, initially with a small group of users.

If you're selected for the test, you'll be able to move from ordinary conversations to more complex tasks without switching modes.

"This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place," OpenAI explained.

"You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work."

The combined experience will initially be tested with a small group of users before OpenAI expands it to more people.

It is worth noting that Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app.

ChatGPT and Codex will share the same usage allowance

There's another significant change coming to Pro subscriptions. OpenAI is preparing to unify usage across ChatGPT and Codex, meaning both services will draw from the same allowance.

"Your use of ChatGPT and Codex will draw from the same allowance," OpenAI noted in the email.

However, not every conversation will consume that allowance. OpenAI says Unlimited Instant is included in the subscription and won't count towards the shared usage limit.

More advanced models and complex tasks will consume more of your allowance, depending on the work involved.

You'll also be able to check your combined remaining usage and reset times under Settings > Usage:

If you run out, you can wait for the allowance to reset, upgrade your subscription, or purchase credits for eligible features.

Separately, OpenAI has already doubled Work and Codex allowances for its Pro 100, Pro 200, and Pro 500 subscriptions, effective October 29.

The FBI has confirmed that North Korean state-sponsored hackers known as TraderTraitor were behind the $6.3 billion crypto-theft attack on Binance, making it the largest cryptocurrency heist on record.

In a security alert published Saturday, the agency attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group also tracked as Lazarus Group, Jade Sleet, and APT38, linked to numerous cryptocurrency thefts.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the FBI said.

This official attribution follows blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis, which had already linked the theft to TraderTraitor.

As previously reported, Binance linked the breach to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed the attackers to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

The attackers stole approximately $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency across ten blockchains, with most of the funds transferred in just 20 minutes.

The FBI says it has observed TraderTraitor converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH), which it expects will be further laundered through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant cryptocurrency swap services.

The FBI, U.S. Secret Service, and IRS Criminal Investigation are now asking cryptocurrency exchanges, blockchain operators, and other virtual asset service providers to block transactions linked to addresses the hackers used to launder stolen funds.

The agency also published a list of 628 cryptocurrency addresses associated with the theft, including 608 Ethereum addresses, 19 Bitcoin addresses, and one Solana address.

TraderTraitor has a long history of targeting cryptocurrency companies and their employees, with North Korean hackers linked to numerous crypto-theft attacks, including the $387.5 million Bitget theft in September 2026, the $280 million Drift hack in April 2026, $1.5 billion Bybit heist in February 2025, and the $308 million DMM Bitcoin theft in May 2024.

One tactic used by North Korean Lazarus hackers is a long-running campaign known as 'Operation DreamJob,' in which they impersonate recruiters and approach software developers and cryptocurrency employees with fake job offers to trick them into installing malware.

Both the DMM and Bybit attacks involved compromising computers belonging to employees or developers with access to cryptocurrency infrastructure.

In the DMM Bitcoin attack, hackers impersonated a recruiter on LinkedIn and tricked an employee at the cryptocurrency wallet company Ginco into running malicious Python code disguised as a pre-employment test.

The Bybit heist also stemmed from a compromised Safe{Wallet} developer's computer, which let hackers access the wallet platform and manipulate a legitimate transaction request by a DMM employee, redirecting $1.5 billion in cryptocurrency to wallets they controlled.

More recently, the April 2026 Drift attack involved a six-month social engineering operation in which individuals posing as representatives of a cryptocurrency trading firm met Drift contributors in person at multiple industry conferences.

The attackers spent months building relationships, and are believed to have compromised employees' devices through a malicious code repository or a TestFlight application.

In a statement shared with BleepingComputer today, Binance said it was preparing to resume the first phase of withdrawals on November 1 between 06:00 and 09:00 UTC, as it continues working to restore services and cover the stolen assets.

The exchange says it has now covered approximately 95% of the impacted amount, up from 90% in its previous update. The remaining 5% consists of less-liquid tokens that Binance is continuing to purchase through market and over-the-counter channels.

Binance also said that BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC balances are fully backed, and that deposit services remain unaffected by the incident.

"Our commitment remains unchanged: Binance will bear the financial impact of the stolen funds. These losses will not be passed on to users," Binance told BleepingComputer.

"Resuming withdrawals is a major milestone, but our work continues. We will continue strengthening our safeguards, completing the recovery process, and providing updates as progress continues."

Some attacks this week didn't need much of a trick. A fake support call, a trusted extension, a shared link, or a device with no password. Small things that people barely think about. Yet each was enough to cause serious trouble.

Then there were the bigger messes. Billions stolen, hidden networks of hacked devices, poisoned software, and attackers finding new ways to turn normal tools against their users. Even the places meant to keep money and systems safe ended up with problems of their own. The strange part is how often the damage started somewhere nobody was looking.

And that's before getting to the long list of fresh bugs, shady services, and scams making the rounds. Quite a bit to sort through. Here's what made the list.

⚡ Threat of the Week

N. Korea Sets New Record with Binance $6.43B Crypto Theft — The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially attributed the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance to a North Korean hacking group called TraderTraitor. The haul eclipses the $1.46 billion plundered from Bybit in February 2025, making it the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. The funds were stolen across 11 blockchains, 82% of which were on Ethereum and Bitcoin. Of the $6.43 billion stolen by TraderTraitor, $2.85 billion of the assets have been frozen on-chain by Tether, Circle, Ripple, Arbitrum, and Optimism.

Mythos: Map Attack Paths to Collapse Lateral Breach Routes

Access the Gartner® CTEM report to see how the Mythos platform continuously maps cross-domain attack paths and isolates key choke points to break active lateral movement to critical assets.

Get the full report ➝

🔔 Top News

Volt Typhoon Uses Covert Silent Train Network in 0-Day Attacks — Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon has been using a framework that relies on rotating chains of connected devices compromised on demand, including to facilitate zero-day attacks targeting high-value systems. It's codenamed Silent Train because the threat actor uses it against select targets, cleans it up after each operation to minimize detection and attribution, and refreshes it continuously. Silent Train is a relay infrastructure formed of compromised devices to hide the origin of its attacks. The findings highlight evidence of efforts to pre-position access within what it described as "strategic communications, critical infrastructure and other ecosystems that become essential during geopolitical tensions or crises." Silent Train is built around "rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices." The nature of these victims "indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region."

Polymarket Briefly Suspended Trading After Third-Party Hack — Prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily suspended trading after hackers compromised DebugBear, a third-party service, to distribute cryptocurrency-draining JavaScript that siphoned approximately $2.7 million in assets from 33 deposit wallets in under an hour. "Our DNS server records were compromised through our domain registrar. We are currently unable to receive emails sent to our domain," DebugBear said in an update shared on October 31, 2026. "Based on our initial investigation this attack targeted the website of a specific customer. We have not seen any indication of a compromise of our internal systems, though we will continue to investigate this." In June, Polymarket disclosed another third-party compromise that injected a malicious script into its frontend, leading to reported losses of around $3 million.

Shared ChatGPT Links Lead to Code Execution — Researchers from Parameter Labs disclosed a now-patched flaw in ChatGPT that turned an ordinary share link into an attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it. "An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," Parameter Labs said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session." Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation, and send data from that conversation to an external server.

Official Claude Code Extension on Cursor Marketplace with SSH Backdoor — Two versions of the Claude Code extension distributed through Cursor Marketplace were tampered with to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems. Cursor said the incident impacted up to 5,000 users. In response to the incident, Cursor said it rotated its keys, rebuilt the marketplace, and worked with the cloud provider to take the server offline so that the reverse shell is no longer functional. It also stressed that no other extensions were maliciously modified as part of the attack. However, several questions surrounding the supply chain attack remain unanswered, including how the threat actor managed to publish a malicious extension under Anthropic's name on Cursor's marketplace and what level of access they were able to obtain.

FBI Seizes bulletproof hosting provider Virtualine — The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) announced the seizure of a domain associated with a bulletproof hosting provider (BPH) named Virtualine. The DoJ said the service was being used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity, including "the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults and minors, and international money laundering designed to conceal and promote criminal conduct. However, the long-term impact of such crackdowns has been questioned. According to Intel 471, disruptions have driven customers to newer services operated by former resellers, fragmenting the market rather than eliminating demand. The disclosure comes as the Australian Signals Directorate said it gained backend access to Amadey's operations and severed its access to 180,000 computers across the globe.

Keystone to Destroy 18,835 Hardware Wallets — Keystone confirmed a security incident involving its official website where an attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party data monitoring tool to escalate privileges and obtain some customer information and a key used to verify the authenticity of our devices. This included 25,964 records containing names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order information, along with 12,873 checkout records containing names, contact details, and shipping information submitted by users. Besides stopping the use of the old key, Keystone plans to destroy 18,835 devices in existing inventory that contain the old key. "Shipping of all unshipped orders from our official website has been suspended," it said. "Sales will switch to a preorder model until production of devices using the new key is complete, after which shipping will resume." In a related development, another hardware cryptocurrency wallet maker Trezor said it received credible reports about a suspected hardware crypto-theft implant in a Trezor Safe 5 sold by its reseller CryptoBilis in Southeast Asia. "If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onwards and are using it to store funds, please move your funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed as soon as possible," it said.

uCreator Android Spyware Can Clone WeChat Accounts — A commercial Android spyware offering called uCreator is designed to target ordinary users of mobile wallets and messaging applications across China and Southeast Asia, including GCash (Philippines), WeChat, WeCom, QQ, Telegram, WhatsApp, LINE, Zalo, KakaoTalk, Viber, and MoMo. It can also be used to clone WeChat accounts. Victims install repackaged copies of legitimate applications disturbed through sideloading or social engineering flows. The attack leverages a variation of on-device virtualization techniques observed in malware like GodFather to conduct fraud. "GodFather spins the banking app up inside a virtual container and drops a fake overlay on top to phish credentials: the victim is really typing into the attacker's screen," security researcher Ovi Liber said. "uCreator shares the substrate but it draws no overlay. This is a case really of overlay-the-app versus instrument-the-app, with the second being quieter and also not being confined to a login screen. As an operator, it scales to any app the vendor writes a module for."

Gheist Turns GitHub Actions into a Secret Extraction Service — An automated campaign dubbed Gheist has been observed planting a secret-dumping workflow named "sync-check" in every repository that stolen GitHub tokens can reach. "The workflow seeks to print the repository's secrets into its own workflow log," Wiz said. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later." The Google-owned cloud security company said it recovered more than 13,500 planted branches from more than 850 compromised accounts. The campaign was first detected in mid-September 2026.
