📰 Around the Cyber World

A massive search-hijacking campaign called Searchjacked involving 319 Chrome extensions with a combined 13.4 million reported installations hijacked users' searches through tracking servers, captured queries, and collected referral payments from Microsoft Bing and Yahoo. The findings from Socket expand on the April 2025 discovery of 57 Chrome extensions with six million users, adding 264 newly identified add-ons with another 8.7 million users. Although they are hosted on the Chrome Web Store, they are unlisted and don't appear in users' searches on the extension store. Instead, the extensions are promoted through sketchy advertisements shown as pop overs or pop unders on websites. Socket also discovered a cluster of malicious Firefox extensions that mimic Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget wallets to steal recovery phrases and private keys. A third campaign, documented by Am I Being Pwned?, involves 60 Chrome extensions with 2.3 million installs across 4 publisher accounts. Called OffiDocs, the extensions masquerade as document programs and exfiltrate all URLs visited by users to be shared with business partners, and other third-parties, or redirect users to one of their pages on redcoolmedia.net or runapps.org

Microsoft revealed details of two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. "Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths," Microsoft said. "This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure."

Threat actors are increasingly turning to vulnerabilities as a means for breaking into corporate systems, as exfiltration and extortion-only attacks emerged as the fastest-growing category in the third quarter of 2026.

Check Point detailed three anti-detect browsers, Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin, that could enable a single operator to silently manage thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms, and evade detection systems that look for scams and coordinated inauthentic behavior. "Threat actors abuse these platforms, taking over accounts and using them for financial fraud, phishing and malware distribution," Check Point said. "These accounts can also be used to coordinate influence operations, which becomes an even greater concern ahead of elections. These tools already use AI integration, from built-in automation templates to offering a dedicated MCP server that pipes LLM-generated content directly into pre-warmed account profiles at machine speed. Running a large-scale social media operation now requires only a credit card instead of a technical team."

Russia and Ukraine both revealed their emergency alert systems were hit by cyber attacks. The attacks caused the two systems to send fake emergency alerts. Per BBC, Ukraine's air raid app sent false red-level air raid warnings nationwide. A few hours later, Russia said its alert app was also attacked, but said that it was only an "ancillary" service among sirens and other warnings. It’s not clear if the two incidents are connected.

A sophisticated Android malware campaign has been targeting the Indian banking sector since July 2025 using seven distinct trojan families that facilitate banking fraud through coordinated phishing, credential theft, and unauthorized cryptojacking. It is orchestrated by a financially motivated threat cluster codenamed CyberDakait that's operating in India since January 2025. The malware families are GhostBat, cyb3rx, godz, d-passive, d-shine, tenxen, and appkjl. Distributed via coordinated smishing and vishing campaigns, they are designed to harvest sensitive information, including bank mobile application credentials, credit card details, outstanding balances, through sophisticated overlay attacks. "The main goal of the campaign is the distribution of Android malware to conduct cryptojacking and elaborate banking fraud," Group-IB said. "The malicious applications are commonly hosted on GitHub repositories to maintain legitimacy and evade security controls, where the initial APK functions as a dropper that downloads and executes the main payload alongside a cryptocurrency mining module, enabling the threat actors to generate revenue through both direct financial theft and unauthorized cryptocurrency mining on infected devices." A total of at least 17,960 compromised devices have been identified, and about 7.6 million SMS messages were intercepted from victim devices.

A new phishing campaign has disguised credential theft as an invitation to a private AI event from Anthropic, and uses GoTo Webinar branding, a Zoom-style registration page, and convincing Google and Microsoft login pages to steal login credentials. "Risks to the organization from this campaign include threat actors compromising a sensitive account, accessing the account’s sensitive documents (e.g., proprietary marketing material), and using the compromised account as an initial vector to further infiltrate the organization," Cofense said.

A new campaign is using judicial-themed phishing emails targeting Colombian organizations to deliver XWorm via a multi-stage chain. The initial payloads resemble legitimate Colombian administrative or judicial correspondence, according to Arctic Wolf.

Multiple Russian-language traffer teams that have adapted affiliate-fraud models to capitalize on growing public interest in prediction markets such as PolyMarket and Kalshi. "The platforms offered by three such teams — AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team — provide websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment infrastructure, victim-management capabilities, technical support, and promotional guidance," Recorded Future said. "This model lowers barriers to entry for affiliates and enables campaigns to scale rapidly as new trends attract potential victims. The services combine convincing prediction-market interfaces with established fraud mechanisms designed to manipulate victims and prevent them from recovering deposited funds." Advertised compensation includes 70% to 80% of net profits for AtlasCore affiliates, a minimum 60% revenue share for PolyFucked affiliates, and a base 70% share of victim deposits for Magnetic Team affiliates.

Nozomi Networks detailed a new Go-based malware for Linux called Kairos that turns a compromised machine into a node in the operator's DDoS botnet. "On command, the bot opens hundreds to thousands of TCP connections to a target chosen by the operator and keeps them open for the requested duration, sending a single near-empty keepalive byte every few seconds," Nozomi Networks said. "Initial access came through Telnet, using the default credentials (user root, empty password). The operator then staged the payload with a short shell sequence that downloaded it over HTTP from the same server the bot later calls home."

A previously undocumented Microsoft device code phishing kit codenamed MadApe is using business-themed PDF lures, configurable redirects, and fake document-sharing pages to trick victims into completing Microsoft device code authentication. It was first observed by Group-IB on January 7, 2026.

Threat actors behind Aur0ra ransomware, aka Gold Ogre, are extensively using AI to develop tools and to orchestrate and execute ransomware operations, Sophos said. The AI-assisted post-exploitation framework is developed with Cursor AI assistance. "The threat actors used Cursor to escalate from credential access to domain administrator in preparation for data collection and ransomware deployment," Sophos said. "AI guardrails were bypassed by framing the intrusions as authorized red team activity or 'diagnostics testing.' Intrusions were orchestrated by Cursor's Composer agentic coding model as well as AI models provided by Anthropic, xAI, and Moonshot." Although the threat actors initially used Anthropic almost exclusively, they have since introduced other models.

Malicious model repositories on Hugging Face are being used to fuel a cryptomining and backdoor campaign. "The payloads were written for GPU hosts running self-hosted inference, especially Xinference and GPUStack, along with rented GPU machines, shared research notebooks, and CI jobs that pull small test models without anyone reading the code," Pluto Security said. Instead of using poisoned weights or pickle exploits, the campaign abuses a Hugging Face option, trust_remote_code, that lets a model ship its own Python code. When this option is set to true, that code is automatically executed on a victim's machine as soon as the model loads.

Bitdefender and NETGEAR found that Smart TVs and connected plugs accounted for a large share of recorded security weaknesses. Televisions represented 22.7% of vulnerability observations, followed by smart plugs at 22.4%. "Before buying connected equipment, the support period deserves attention alongside the price and features," the 2026 IoT Security Landscape Report said. For equipment already in the home, knowing whether updates are still available is part of knowing whether it should stay connected.

A tech-support scam is directing victims to install the commercially available remote access application UltraViewer. Infoblox, which broke down details of the campaign, said it found links to a long-running QuickBooks phishing campaign. "That campaign uses over 350 QuickBooks-lookalike domains and directs victims to call scammers who attempt to steal QuickBooks credentials," Infoblox said. The scam has been found directing users to trojanized UltraViewer and UltraMailer, installers that lead to the deployment of DarkKometa and njRAT, respectively.

In an analysis of The Com ecosystem, Flare said the loose-knit collective comprises three distinct intrusion clusters, Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and ShinyHunters, while SP1D3R HUNTERS (aka Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters) represents an amalgamation of all three. Security researcher Jon DiMaggio warned against attributing any activity post-2022 to LAPSUS, which ceased operating years ago. "LAPSUS$ operated at full capacity for roughly nine months, from its December 2021 attack against Brazil’s Ministry of Health through its concentrated campaign in early 2022, before a series of arrests in mid-to-late 2022 ended it as an organized entity," DiMaggio said. "Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$ overlapped by a few months at the start and by at least one individual across their lifespans, and they still ran different playbooks against different targets toward different ends."

Conclusion

That's about it for this week. Some attacks were carefully planned. Others worked because someone clicked the wrong thing, trusted the wrong tool, or left something exposed. Different methods, same result. And with so many systems connected to other systems, even a small mistake can travel further than expected.

The bigger concern is how normal some of these attacks have become. Nothing particularly clever is needed when the easy routes still work. Keep an eye on what has access, check what needs fixing, and don't assume familiar means safe. See you next week.

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign targeting Israel and the Kurdistan Region of Iraq by an Iran state-aligned threat actor between August and October 2026.

According to a report published by Dream Research Labs, the campaign has led to the compromise of a high-profile individual in Israel, along with additional compromises affecting a government cloud environment in the Kurdistan Region.

The activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as DarkBlinders, an Iran-nexus group assessed to be active since at least September 2024 and linked to attacks aimed at aviation infrastructure and telecommunications in the U.A.E. and Iraq. It exhibits no technical overlap with other known hacking groups.

Attacks mounted by the group are known to rely on spear-phishing as an initial access pathway to lure recipients into opening trojanized utilities or clicking on attacker-controlled websites that host similar tools as direct downloads.

Previous attack chains documented by Elastic Security Labs and Group-IB have led to the deployment of SHELBYLOADER (aka HOTAIR), which is launched via DLL sideloading to ultimately execute a backdoor called SHELBYC2 (aka AEROSTAT) that uses GitHub for command-and-control (C2), data exfiltration, and remote control. Elastic is tracking the threat cluster under the moniker REF8685.

Then early last month, Palo Alto Networks shed light on a campaign dubbed Blinder Tunnel in which the threat actor, which it calls CL-STA-1178, was observed masquerading as the Dubai Airports IT department to distribute malware-laced coding challenges to high-value targets.

The bogus recruitment scheme was first detected in late March 2026, although evidence indicates that the attackers were staging and testing attack infrastructure as far back as November 2025.

The social engineering campaign is assessed to have approached specific targets with lucrative job offers to trick them into executing a self-contained application that mimicked a career portal and instructed them to complete a questionnaire.

Submitting the questionnaire does not cause any data to be exfiltrated or initiate any response from an external domain. Instead, it's meant to serve as a harmless decoy and build credibility before delivering the next stage payload containing the malware in the form of a Microsoft Visual Studio project archive that's dressed up as a coding assessment.

The attack chain makes use of three techniques to establish persistent access: A malicious C# project ".csproj" file is used to trigger AppDomainManager injection, followed by DLL sideloading to deliver an updated version of SHELBYLOADER (aka ShelbyLoader V2), which then launches SHELBYC2. Also deployed via SHELBYC2 is a tunneling utility called Blackwood.

"The attackers behind the activity used tailored social engineering techniques to masquerade as Dubai Airports recruiters, using a trojanized Visual Studio coding challenge to target a high-value job seeker based in Iraq," Unit 42 said.

"The campaign is characterized by misuse of built-in developer tools and DLL sideloading. Attackers also used AppDomainManager hijacking to bypass security monitors like ETW [Event Tracing for Windows]."

The latest findings from Dream show that the threat actor continues to rely on social engineering, while combining both credential phishing and malware delivery. This involves the use of government, webmail, and cloud-service lookalike domains to collect credentials or present attacker-controlled file downloads. Some of the highlighted domains include -

gcc-sg[.]cloud/owa/auth/logon.aspx

mfakuwait[.]online/owa/auth/logon.aspx

moelcloud[.]online/drive/file/d/1JpH3ySmJpvX6TyGnF7C-S8qYiaoxyC5O

The threat actor has also been observed setting decoy brand domains for a fake videoconferencing application called StarkMeet (stark-meet[.]com, stark-meet[.]online, and stark-meet[.]website). Installing and launching the app leads to the execution of ShelbyLoader V2 and SHELBYC2.

The development is also a sign that the threat actor is trying out different methods for malware delivery, ranging from coding assessments to counterfeit software.

Dream said the DarkBlinders activity belongs to the same operational cluster as UNC5795 and Dust Specter, citing infrastructure and malware overlaps. Dust Specter, documented by Zscaler in March 2026, refers to a suspected Iran-nexus operation targeting government officials in Iraq by impersonating the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"Historical server fingerprints, overlapping victimology, and supporting attribution research lead us to assess with medium confidence that UNC5795 and UNC5187 may represent related sub-clusters within the broader APT34 group," it added.

"Their overlapping focus on Iraqi government entities adds context to this technical connection and suggests a shared intelligence collection interest. Combined with their respective APT34 associations, these findings support a medium-confidence assessment that the two clusters are operationally related and may belong to the same broader group."

Prince of Persia Hosts C2 in the U.S. for the First Time in a Decade

The disclosure comes as Prince of Persia (aka Infy), a lesser-known threat group sponsored by the Iranian government, has been observed running one of its C2 servers ("68.65.122[.]203") from the U.S. this year. The server was likely built in July 2026.

The infrastructure is a second-stage C2 server associated with Tornado, a Tonnerre variant that's dropped via one-day software vulnerabilities and uses both HTTPS and the Telegram API for C2. The emergence of new C2 servers in late May 2026 follows three months of inactivity, which has been described as the "longest downtime in nearly two decades of activity by the threat actor."

"We have been monitoring Prince of Persia's exfiltration activity for the past six months," Tomer Bar, associate vice president of security research at Semperis, said. "The number of victims remains low, which could indicate either targeted attacks or difficulties infecting new victims."

"The Iranian threat actor decided to host its new C2 server on U.S. soil — at the same time as the beginning of the recent hostilities between Iran and the United States. This is the last place we expected to find the threat actor hiding."

207c789db333.text: A coalition of private-sector security firms working with Japan’s National Police Agency has disrupted XCPE, a backdoor used to build a massive botnet comprising more than 1.3 million Android devices across more than 200 countries. Google, Lumen, Human Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI participated in the disruption. “We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology,” the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a Monday blog. Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates, allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge. The firmware’s pre-installed management agent purported to be a standard remote-management client, according to TrendAI. It pulled updates from a GitHub page, and connected to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) server that gave the operator full remote control of each box, allowing them to install and remove apps, change settings, and push updates to the infected devices. Between June 3 and October 1, TrendAI documented more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation. The coalition also disrupted the command-and-control domains used to manage the affiliate modules. “Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices,” according to GTIG. Google said it had since cut ties with Videostrong, and banned the OEM from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Videostrong did not immediately respond to The Register’s inquiries. This backdoor and botnet operation is part of the same ecosystem as BadBox 2.0, another notorious botnet that infected more than 10 million TV boxes and other devices before Human, Google, and TrendAI disrupted it in March 2025.®

Summary As we’ve written, AI is shrinking the time between “a fix is public” and “someone has a working exploit” to near-zero. JFrog products are not affected by Linux kernel CVE-2026-98432. Artifactory, Xray, and the rest of the JFrog Platform do not contain this flaw, as it lives in the Linux kernel itself. We are advising every self-managed JFrog customer to check their Linux hosts and update their kernels now to protect their environments, which may include hosted versions of JFrog products. Once your OS is updated, JFrog products are not at risk.

Our goal is always to protect your systems, and in some cases that may include advice on the protection of the environments your JFrog products operate in. JFrog Cloud customers are not affected by the Linux vulnerability, but if you self-manage JFrog, read on.

Your Linux kernel may be exposed, requiring you to patch it to protect your environment.

What happened

On October 15, the Linux kernel CVE team published CVE-2026-98432. It’s a use-after-free in the code that sets up new IPv4 TCP connections, caused by a race condition. The bug dates back to Linux 4.4. Upstream fixed it on October 5 following main line patching on September 17; upstream was fixed a full ten days before the CVE went public.

The kernel team scores this vulnerability a 9.8. Red Hat, Oracle, SUSE and Amazon score it lower, between 5.9 and 8.1.

Then, Anthropic published research on October 27 saying its Claude model wrote a working exploit. A remote attacker with no credentials gets a root shell on servers with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener. In Anthropic’s test, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes. Getting command execution took only five more. In this scenario, a lost race only kills that one connection, so the attacker just tries again.

Importantly, Anthropic did not publish the exploit code. As of November 2, there have been no reports of attacks in the wild. MPTCP is less exotic than it sounds: since Go 1.24, Go programs request it by default on the sockets they listen on. The Go Security Team also says the underlying bug isn’t specific to MPTCP. (Tip: JFrog deployments include several Go services within versions later than 1.24.)

As a JFrog customer…

In a self-managed deployment, you own the operating system that JFrog operates in. We are responsible for the security of our products, and you for the platform underneath (host, kernel, patching) in a shared responsibility model. A vulnerable kernel under a healthy JFrog install still puts that host, and everything on it, at risk.

As of October 30, neither Ubuntu nor RHEL had released a fixed kernel. Ubuntu 22.04 through 26.10 are marked work in progress, and older releases are plain vulnerable. RHEL 8, 9 and 10 are listed as affected, with no date. Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE and Amazon Linux have shipped fixes for at least some kernels. Check your exact release, because coverage varies within each distro.

What we’re advising you to do as soon as possible

Find out what you’re running. Version numbers lie, because distros backport fixes without bumping them. Check the changelog instead.

On Debian or Ubuntu:

apt changelog linux-image-$(uname -r) | grep CVE-2026-98432

On RHEL and its derivatives:

rpm -q --changelog kernel-$(uname -r) | grep CVE-2026-98432

If the command prints nothing, your running kernel doesn’t have the fix.

Patch where a fix exists, then reboot. A kernel update does nothing until the machine boots into it. If you build your own kernel, the fix is in 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. The kernel team recommends moving to the latest stable release rather than cherry-picking the one commit.

Where there’s no fix yet, be proactive about it. Red Hat says no available mitigation meets its bar. Switching off MPTCP program by program is fragile, and the Go team says so directly: one forgotten listener and you’re exposed again. Narrow who can reach those hosts at the network layer, watch your vendor’s advisory for CVE-2026-98432, and patch the day the package is available. Another mitigation option could be using an L7 load balancer or reverse proxy with TCP termination to reduce direct exposure of vulnerable hosts. Reducing exposure doesn’t repair the bug, but it does reduce the number of people who can try to exploit it.

Make the next one simpler. If you proxy your Debian or RPM repos through Artifactory, the fixed kernel arrives in the repo your hosts already pull from. Stage it, promote it, roll it out in waves, with the same process you use for everything else. A kernel package is an artifact like any other, and it should have a system of record.

JFrog Xray scans your supply chain artifacts and images. It won’t tell you what kernel your host is running, because the kernel isn’t in either one; step one is a command you must run yourself.

The window is big, but shrinking

In an approaching-zero window from fix to exploit, rapid patching is required. The fix for this vulnerability was made public on October 5. A working exploit story hit on October 27. On October 30, two of the most widely run enterprise distros still had no update.

Our advice to protect your systems is simple:

Run the changelog check on every host that runs JFrog today. Update and reboot where a fixed kernel exists. Where it doesn’t, restrict access and subscribe to your distro’s advisory for CVE-2026-98432 so the fix doesn’t sit in a queue that could get forgotten.

VOLTA is an AI-powered infostealer that steals personal data, then uses LLMs to assess victims’ value and rank targets for attackers.

Cisco Talos has analyzed a new Windows infostealer called VOLTA, which calls itself VOLTA-AUTODOXER. It steals the usual data, then hands the loot to a large language model that ranks what the victim is worth. Ryan Fetterman laid it out in a Talos report, after the malware turned up through the CAIRN research effort.

“There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.” reads the report published by Talos.

The malware deletes itself after running and does not use servers controlled by the attacker. Instead, it uses third-party systems to carry out its activities.

The malicious code supports data-stealing features are advanced. It collects browser passwords, cookies and saved payment card details from Chromium browsers, as well as data from Firefox, Thunderbird and Outlook. It also steals Slack workspace information and login sessions from Discord, Telegram, Steam, Battle.net and Roblox.

The malware also collects Microsoft OAuth tokens, SSH keys, cloud service credentials, screenshots and all saved Wi-Fi passwords. For crypto wallets, it tries to crack the wallet password directly on the infected device and saves the results in its report. To steal some browser tokens, it must bypass Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption.

But VOLTA goes further. It also builds a detailed profile of the victim. This includes their location and home address, employer and company domain, estimated year of birth, the last four digits of payment cards, Slack workspaces and information about who created documents. It also looks for signs of iPhone backups and checks the current value of the victim’s Roblox account.

“After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine.” states the report.

It uses the victim’s own logged-in sessions to fill the gaps. It searches Gmail for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart and PayPal to confirm a home address, pulls order histories from Uber Eats and DoorDash, and adds detail to the victim’s Discord profile. Even a takeout history can now count as evidence.

The bundle goes to OpenRouter, a routing service for AI models, with a system prompt that tells the model to act as a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment.

“The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY’RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim’s security posture and password hygiene.” states the report. “The model is the operator’s triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.”

It also needs a section called “THEIR OPSEC”, rating the victim’s security habits and password hygiene. In short, it’s a performance review for the person it just robbed.

The prompt asks for something agents do well: connecting scattered facts. It pushes the model to link names, addresses or universities to patterns in the victim’s passwords. The model isn’t hunting for new data, only stretching what the malware already took. The operator wants a short, blunt assessment with a trail of citations.

By default VOLTA calls Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. If the model refuses, which VOLTA spots by scanning replies for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able”, it moves on to Moonshot AI’s Kimi K2 and then Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. A low temperature setting of 0.2 keeps the output consistent.

The requests are hand-built JSON with no software kit, and the malware still runs without the AI stage if no API key is present.

Talos sees the fallback system as evidence that the malware’s author expected security protections and designed ways to bypass them.

The AI analysis runs directly on the victim’s computer, using their own internet connection, before any data is sent out. The malware creates a file called Identity_Report.txt, receives the AI’s response in AI_Analysis.txt, and sends both files together in a ZIP archive called volta_dox.zip.

The stolen data can be sent to the attacker in up to three stages. The first archive, volta_log.zip, contains the information collected by the malware. The second, volta_dox.zip, contains the AI analysis. A third archive, volta_doxnet.zip, is created if the malware finds additional network information. The attacker receives everything through a Telegram channel.

The malware also has six configurable fields that can be changed when it is built. This suggests that its author may offer a builder service, allowing customers to create their own customised versions.

The credentials stored in these fields are encrypted, but the encryption is weak because the key is stored inside the malware itself. Anyone who analyses the file can recover them.

If VOLTA is sold as a commercial product, its AI feature could allow even inexperienced criminals to identify valuable victims and receive detailed, ranked profiles directly through Telegram.

For defense, Talos suggests an application control policy that restricts which processes can launch Chrome with the –headless flag, which would block the App-Bound Encryption bypass. At minimum, alert when Chrome starts with –headless from any process outside a known developer set. Storing credentials in hardware-backed stores also helps.

If you’re compromised, the main program may have deleted itself, but try to keep %APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt. It’s a timestamped log of what was collected and whether the AI call worked. Revoke any exposed tokens and change passwords. If a wallet’s seed phrase sat in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and move the funds to a new wallet whose seed was generated on an air-gapped device.

“VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase.” concludes the post. “These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, malware)

836b38681bb5.text:
As the email administrator for your organization’s domain, you receive a Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) aggregate report showing email passing DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) verification as though it came from your domain, sent from IP addresses you don’t recognize to recipients you didn’t contact. To clear the issue, you rotate your DKIM key, confirm the new selector is live, and verify that your DMARC policy is already set to p=reject. Days later, you see that the same unfamiliar traffic is still authenticating as you.

In this post, you learn why rotation alone can’t stop a DKIM replay attack, how to confirm that you’re looking at a replay rather than a legitimate relay or ordinary spoofing, and the DNS cleanup step that most rotation guidance leaves out. You also learn how you can use Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to detect and respond to this activity faster.

How DKIM replay works

DKIM verifies one thing: that specific parts of a message didn’t change between the signer and the receiver. The signer signs the message with a private key, and receivers fetch the matching public key from your domain’s DNS to check the signature. A valid signature continues to validate wherever the message travels afterward. Mailing lists, .forward rules, and third-party relays all preserve it, which is the protocol working as designed.

A replay attack takes advantage of that durability. The attack works as follows:

Your ecommerce platform sends a customer a legitimate response email, signed with your DKIM key.

An attacker obtains one copy of that message. They might subscribe to your mailing list, compromise a mailbox, retrieve it from a list archive, or capture it through a forwarding rule.

The attacker resends that message, unchanged, from their own servers to thousands of new recipients.

Each receiving server fetches your public key from DNS and checks the signature. The signature passes, because the body wasn’t modified. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) fails, because the sending IP isn’t yours, but DMARC requires only one of SPF or DKIM to pass with alignment. Because DKIM passes, DMARC passes, and the message is delivered as authenticated email from your domain.

Understanding what an attacker can and can’t do matters, because the limits define the problem. An attacker can’t modify your message, add new content, or read your email. The signature is only valid while the message remains byte-for-byte identical.

What an attacker gains is your domain’s reputation, which they use to deliver your genuine message to an audience you didn’t intend. A receipt or invoice becomes a lure, and email that would normally be filtered is delivered because receivers trust your domain. This is abuse of reputation and reach, not content forgery, and the distinction matters when you explain the incident to your security team.

This also explains why an enforcing DMARC policy doesn’t stop an attack. DMARC passes when SPF or DKIM passes with alignment. During a replay, DKIM passes, so DMARC passes, and p=reject does not apply. A p=reject policy is designed to stop spoofing, where a forger has no valid signature and DKIM fails. It does nothing against a message that you signed. Determining which of the two was used is what tells you how to respond.

Is it replay, spoofing, or a legitimate relay?

Email from an unfamiliar IP address that passes DKIM has three common explanations, and each requires a different response. Confirm which you’re dealing with before you make any changes.

DMARC aggregate (rua) reports provide the source IP address, message volume, and SPF and DKIM results. This is enough to identify an anomaly, but not to prove a replay. A report row might read as follows:

source IP: 203.0.113.45 | count: 4,200 | SPF: fail | DKIM: pass (d=yourdomain.com)

You need to evaluate that row against the three possibilities:

The first possibility is a legitimate relay that you haven’t inventoried, such as a mailing list, a forwarder, or an email security gateway such as an inline cloud access security broker (CASB) that you route through. The signature validly survives the relay, and this is normal email flow. In the report, the source IP address usually resolves to a known provider, and the volume tracks your actual sending.

The second possibility is replay abuse, in which an attacker redistributes a message that you legitimately signed. In this case, the DKIM-passing volume comes from an IP address that has no business relationship with you, often well above the usual number of recipients that you send to, and frequently to recipient domains that you haven’t worked with.

The third possibility is ordinary spoofing, which is a forgery with no valid signature. That row shows DKIM: fail. DKIM that passes from an unknown IP address is therefore usually not ordinary spoofing.

Aggregate counts can’t prove a replay on their own. To confirm a replay, you need message-level evidence: a specific message that you sent matched to one that reached recipients you didn’t address. If you can’t make that match, treat the activity as an unconfirmed anomaly, and begin with the enforcement and monitoring steps that follow rather than removing keys.

Set up an enforcing DMARC policy first

Before you take any other action, confirm that you’re enforcing DMARC. Many domains that encounter this problem are still at p=none, which is monitoring only. This situation is common. Every DMARC deployment begins at p=none, and many organizations do not advance beyond it because nothing appears to be broken. At p=none, receivers take no action on failures, so no change you make affects delivery, and you can’t determine what enforcement would have caught.

The first step is therefore not key removal; it’s completing your sender inventory and reaching enforcement:

Inventory every legitimate sender and relay for your domain, including your email service providers, mailing lists, and any security gateways that send on your behalf.

Bring each sender into SPF and DKIM alignment so that legitimate email authenticates.

Advance the policy one stage at a time, from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. Review your rua reports at each stage before you advance, typically for a week or two per stage, and longer if you have many senders to work through. The pct tag lets you ramp up gradually, for example by quarantining 25% of failing email before you increase the percentage.

After you’re enforcing DMARC, receivers that honor DMARC drop unauthenticated spoofing on your behalf. Only after this baseline is in place, and only after you have confirmed a replay of genuinely signed email, does the next step apply.

Remove the old key from DNS: routine hygiene after rotation

Most rotation guidance omits this step. Rotating a key and removing the old key are two separate actions.

Rotation means that your provider begins signing new email with a new key and selector. Removal means deleting the old public key from DNS, so that previously signed messages, including the copies that an attacker captured, can no longer be verified. If you rotate but leave the old public key published, every message ever signed with that key remains replayable for as long as the record exists. Removing the old key is what closes that window and is the step that’s commonly overlooked.

Removal affects only messages that are still in transit and were signed with the old key. After email is delivered, the receiver no longer needs your key, so we recommend that you leave the old key published long enough for in-flight email to arrive and then remove it. How much of this process you manage yourself depends on your DKIM method, which the following section describes. During a confirmed active replay, closing this window is essential.

How you manage keys depends on the DKIM method that you use with Amazon SES. With Bring Your Own DKIM (BYODKIM), you generate the key pair and publish the public key as a TXT record that you control. You can rotate and remove keys whenever you want, including removing an old key on demand during an incident. As the BYODKIM documentation states, “you can rotate the DKIM keys for your domains as often as you want.”

With Easy DKIM, a feature where Amazon SES generates and manages the keys for you, you publish CNAME records that point to AWS-hosted keys. Because your DNS points to AWS-hosted keys through those CNAME records, Amazon SES manages the underlying key material for you, so you don’t publish or remove individual keys yourself. Unlike BYODKIM, Easy DKIM doesn’t provide an on-demand option to delete a specific key immediately.

If you’re an Easy DKIM sender during a confirmed replay, your defenses are early detection (described in the following section), the duplicate-message throttling that receivers already apply, and, over the longer term, the emerging DKIM2 effort, an IETF initiative to update the DKIM specification with built-in replay resistance, which is being designed to give receivers better signals to identify and act on replayed messages at the protocol level.

How Amazon SES helps you detect and respond

Your first response is detection, not DNS changes. The goal is to identify anomalous DKIM-passing volume early, while you build the message-level evidence that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay.

Begin by enabling logging. Create an Amazon SES configuration set with an event destination (see Monitor email sending using Amazon SES event publishing) that streams per-message events (Send, Delivery, Bounce, and Complaint) to Amazon Data Firehose or Amazon EventBridge (see Add an event destination), tagged with the From domain.

Separately, confirm that you’re receiving rua reports for your domain. You enable these reports by adding a rua= address to your domain’s DMARC TXT record, for example rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@yourdomain.com. For the record syntax and a phased p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject rollout, see Complying with DMARC authentication protocol in Amazon SES. Reports arrive as daily XML digests, and most teams process them with a DMARC analyzer rather than reading the raw XML.

With both sources in place, you can correlate them. Compare the email that your account emitted—based on your Amazon SES delivery events—against what DMARC reports show that receivers accepted as your domain. When DMARC shows DKIM-passing volume from IP addresses outside your SPF record that exceeds the delivery events that Amazon SES recorded for that From domain in the same window, that gap is your signal. It’s also how you build the message-level case that distinguishes a replay from a legitimate relay.

We recommend three additional controls. Amazon SES sending authorization restricts which AWS principals can send using your verified identity. It doesn’t stop an external replay, but it addresses the insider and third-party vector that SPF, DKIM, and DMARC don’t cover on their own, so use identity-level policies to limit sending to specific AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principals.

Use Amazon Route 53 to set short DNS time-to-live values (TTLs) (for example, 300 seconds) on your DKIM records so that changes propagate quickly; and enable DNS query logging with an Amazon CloudWatch Logs metric filter that watches for queries to a selector that you’ve rotated away from.

A spike in lookups for an old selector is a useful early indicator of a replay attempt using a retired selector. For a BYODKIM domain during a confirmed replay, Route 53 is also where you remove the old selector’s TXT record. You can automate that removal by using an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that starts an AWS Lambda function to call the Route 53 API and retire an old selector’s record.

Scope the function’s IAM role to only the specific Route 53 hosted zone and record that it needs to change, so that it follows least privilege. Because an incorrect DNS change can have a wide effect, gate any automation behind confirmed-replay criteria and test it against a non-production domain first. For most teams, alarm-to-human is safer than alarm-to-automatic-removal.

When your domain is the one being abused

Most guidance assumes that you’re either the provider preventing abuse or the receiver detecting it. In a replay, your domain is the one whose reputation is being consumed, and you aren’t on the recipient list. As a result, you don’t have the message that everyone asks for when you report the issue.

When you file an abuse report with the provider that hosts the source IP address, they ask for full message headers. The email went to people you didn’t contact, so you don’t have the message headers. You then provide DMARC aggregate reports that show the source IP address and volume, and the provider asks for headers again. At this point, you’re unable to proceed.

To break this cycle, go to the recipients. Review your rua reports for the top recipient domains—which are often .gov and .edu domains—contact those recipients directly and request a sample message with full headers. In addition to providing the headers, that sample lets you confirm a replay rather than a legitimate relay. Build your abuse report around the IP address and the DMARC evidence rather than the message content. If the source IP address belongs to Amazon Web Services (AWS), report it through the AWS abuse process and include your DMARC reports and SPF record as evidence.

Incident response: ordered actions

If your reports show suspicious DKIM-passing email from unfamiliar IP addresses, complete the following procedure.

To respond to a suspected DKIM replay

Confirm that it’s a replay. Match a message that you sent to one that reached recipients you didn’t address and rule out legitimate relays and gateways. Aggregate data alone isn’t proof.

Reach an enforcing DMARC policy. Inventory your legitimate senders, align them, and advance from p=none to p=quarantine to p=reject. This stops spoofing.

Harden SPF to -all rather than ~all, but only after your sender inventory is complete, since -all hard-fails any legitimate source you haven’t listed.

Check the DKIM-Signature header of a fresh message to confirm that your provider signs only with the current selector.

Report the source IP address to the hosting provider and include your DMARC evidence.

Investigate the capture point, such as a compromised mailbox, a mailing list, a forwarding rule, or a newsletter subscription.

Remove the old DKIM public key after in-flight email has cleared. For BYODKIM, delete the old selector’s TXT record. For Easy DKIM, rely on the managed Amazon SES rotation together with the monitoring and receiver-side defenses described earlier.

The following table summarizes what each action does and doesn’t do.

Action

What it does

What it doesn’t do

Confirm replay (message-level)

Separates a replay from a legitimate relay or spoofing

Can’t be done from aggregate DMARC data alone

DMARC enforcement (p=none to p=reject)

Drops unauthenticated spoofing

Does nothing against a replay because DKIM still passes

Key rotation

Signs new email with a new key

Doesn’t invalidate already signed messages

Remove old key (routine, post-rotation)

Invalidates old-key signatures, including captured ones

Doesn’t protect in-flight old-key email; on-demand removal available only with BYODKIM

Amazon SES sending authorization

Restricts which principals send as your identity

Doesn’t stop external replay of captured messages

Conclusion

DKIM replay succeeds because a valid signature keeps validating, and an enforcing DMARC policy doesn’t change that. To respond effectively, confirm that the activity is a replay with message-level evidence, reach an enforcing DMARC policy, and then remove the old key from DNS as routine post-rotation hygiene. Keep your primary defense on monitoring and DMARC enforcement rather than on emergency DNS changes. The durable fix for replay is receiver-side: duplicate-message counting today, and stronger protocol-level signals through DKIM2 in the future.

To get started, review your current DMARC policy and confirm that you’re receiving rua reports, enable Amazon SES event publishing, and document how you rotate and remove DKIM keys for each of your domains.

Learn more

Authenticating email with DKIM in Amazon SES

Complying with DMARC authentication protocol in Amazon SES

Using sending authorization with Amazon SES

Monitor email sending using Amazon SES event publishing

Michael is a Technical Account Manager at AWS Enterprise Support, where he works with customers on email security, DNS architecture, and incident response.

345b1e776b8c.text: If you're a customer of cloud-hosted AI workflow platform Trigger.dev, take heed, because your environment variables may have been exposed in a security incident disclosed on Sunday. Trigger offered little explanation in its Sunday security incident report, noting that its investigation had identified “exposure across a subset of organizations” and that an attacker had gained unauthorized access to environment variables belonging to those organizations. Whatever exploit was used to gain access has been blocked, the company added, and affected customers have been notified of steps they need to take to prevent further security problems. We likely don't have to tell The Reg readers how important environment variables are in SaaS and cloud services like Trigger. If compromised environment variables contain sensitive credentials, an attacker could basically end up with the keys to the kingdom, potentially gaining access to connected services and digital infrastructure. For those unfamiliar with Trigger.dev, it’s a platform for building AI agents and workflows in TypeScript, but here’s the kicker: Trigger advertises itself as a durable execution platform that handles pesky things like retries, scaling, and keeping long-running tasks going through crashes and redeployments, while providing tools to monitor what those tasks are doing. Trigger, the company’s site notes, can be used to “build durable AI agents that survive refreshes, redeploys, and crashes,” and is ideal for “long-running tasks with retries, queues, AI observability and elastic scaling.” In short, companies running their AI on Trigger probably want it to keep running, which makes stolen environment variables all the more dangerous. Elastic scaling, automated retries, and, as Trigger notes, the ability to run lots of concurrent operations without timeouts could compound the consequences of compromised API keys, depending on what those credentials allow an attacker to access. An attacker with stolen credentials could potentially interfere with a customer's connected services or workflows. Additionally, Trigger recently added webhooks to its offering, supporting services like Stripe, Supabase, and Slack, potentially expanding the range of integrations that could be affected if their credentials were exposed. This could be pretty bad for anyone affected. Trigger has some fairly high-profile customers, with companies like fashion brand Emporio Armani, Pentagon-supporting AI acquisitions platform GovSignals, SaaS calendar platform Cal.com, and others all listed on the company’s site. Trigger has not publicly identified which organizations were affected by the intrusion. We reached out to Trigger, which declined to provide any additional information on the incident. A company spokesperson instead told us to wait for a full incident report to learn more. Luckily for Trigger customers and those concerned about SaaS security now that AI is regularly coming up with new vulnerabilities in commonly used platforms, Trigger is open source and can be self-hosted, which might be a better alternative in this day and age than relying on a hosted service. ®

Two critical flaws in Langflow could let a remote attacker with no account bypass authentication or run arbitrary code, IBM said last week.

Langflow is an open-source tool for building AI agents and workflows, and its vulnerability reports go to IBM. Every release from 1.0.0 through 1.12.8 has the flaws, and the only fix is version 1.13.0.

Neither flaw is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, as of the catalog's October 30 update. Six other Langflow flaws are listed there, most recently CVE-2026-9198, which was added in August.

The four Langflow flaws in IBM's bulletin, first published on October 28 and updated the next day, are:

CVE

CVSS score (IBM)

Account needed

What IBM says it could allow

CVE-2026-93680

9.8 (Critical)

No

Bypassing security restrictions, because of improper authentication

CVE-2026-110186

9.8 (Critical)

No

Running arbitrary code, because of improper control of code generation

CVE-2026-110193

8.8 (High)

Yes, a low-privileged account

Making the Agentic Assistant generate or submit component code that runs operating system commands on the server

CVE-2026-110192

6.5 (Medium)

Yes

Getting sensitive information from insufficiently protected credentials

One of the flaws is "unauthenticated remote code execution exploitable through model context protocol tool enumeration," according to IBM. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Langflow can offer its flows as tools to AI apps that support MCP.

A module in the public Metasploit Framework already cites CVE-2026-93680, the authentication bypass. It connects to a Langflow server's MCP endpoint without credentials, starts a session, and lists the tools the server offers. It does not run code or commands on the server.

Its author lists Langflow 1.5.0 through 1.11.4 as affected, a narrower range than IBM's.

When automatic login is enabled, Langflow logs users in as superusers without prompting them to sign in. The setting LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN is enabled by default in Langflow 1.12.8. Its code description warns that it "bypasses authentication and should only be used in development environments."

The module was tested on Langflow 1.8.4 with automatic login turned on. Another of the four flaws is "an incomplete remediation of an auto-login security control," according to IBM. The bulletin does not say whether servers with automatic login turned off are vulnerable.

Upgrading to 1.13.0

Langflow 1.13.0 came out on October 22. Version 1.12.8, released the same day, still has the flaws, and PyPI lists no later 1.12 release as of November 2. IBM offers no workaround for servers that cannot upgrade yet.

Langflow 1.13 turns automatic login off by default. To upgrade:

Back up the database, the secret key and uploaded files.

If the server uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in, as Langflow's upgrade guidance describes.

Upgrade the Python package with pip install --upgrade "langflow==1.13.0". For Docker, move to the langflowai/langflow:1.13.0 image and keep the deployment's persistent data.

If you cannot sign in after upgrading, follow the recovery steps that the same guidance links to. Do not delete or reinstall Langflow to get access back, because Langflow's documentation warns this can permanently remove your flows.

On October 29, IBM also published CVE records for 29 other Langflow flaws and named versions 1.12.4 and 1.12.5 as their fixes. One of them, CVE-2026-104339, could also let an attacker with no account run arbitrary code, and IBM rates it 9.8. None of the 33 records, these four included, lists 1.13.0 as affected.

9b672881f5d2.text:
A new ransomware operation appeared in August 2026 with an ambitious pitch: sophisticated infrastructure, aggressive affiliate payouts, global ambitions, and what it calls the “first AI powered, quantum resistant ransomware.”

Within approximately six weeks, Storm had claimed over 50 victims across North America, Europe, and Oceania. Its targets span healthcare, finance, manufacturing, business services, government, transportation, and critical infrastructure.

Storm arrived with the structure of an established Ransomware as a Service operation. Its affiliate program offers revenue shares reaching 90%, while its leak site looks closer to a commercial software platform, complete with an interactive victim map, search functionality, sector filters, victim tracking, and document previews.

Then there is the AI claim.

Storm heavily promotes itself as AI powered. Check Point Exposure Management researchers found no evidence showing AI use in the group’s ransomware deployment, victim targeting, encryption routines, or extortion processes. The AI message appears closely tied to how Storm recruits affiliates, promotes automation, and builds its brand. Figure 1, Storm’s pinned darknet recruitment post advertising itself as AI powered and showing its affiliate offer

Key Takeaways

Storm scaled quickly. The group claimed over 50 victims within approximately six weeks of public activity across North America, Europe, and Oceania.

It launched as a structured affiliate operation. Storm advertises lockers for Windows, Linux, ESXi, and NAS, along with victim chat management, call center services, AV and EDR bypass support, DDoS capabilities, and media outreach.

Affiliates can receive up to 90% of revenue. Storm advertises a tiered model starting at 75%, rising to 80%, and reaching 90% for revenue above $750,000.

Healthcare featured heavily in its early activity. Six healthcare organizations appear among the early victim claims, alongside victims across finance, manufacturing, retail, automotive, and other sectors.

Its leak site is unusually polished. Storm built an interactive platform featuring a global victim map, industry filters, search, victim timelines, document previews, and a custom CAPTCHA.

The AI branding remains unverified. Researchers found no conclusive evidence that AI supports Storm’s intrusion, encryption, extortion, or affiliate workflows.

Storm Was Built to Recruit

Storm’s public emergence was closely tied to affiliate recruitment.

Before its first observed victim publication, known Initial Access Broker BigBro advertised the new operation on a darknet forum. Storm later published its own pinned recruitment post, formalizing its RaaS offering.

The offering resembles a service catalog. Affiliates gain access to ransomware lockers, technical support, victim communication capabilities, call center services, DDoS capabilities, and other resources. Storm also openly solicits Initial Access Brokers, data brokers, and network access providers.

Its revenue sharing model adds another recruitment incentive. Affiliates can retain up to 90% of revenue once earnings exceed $750,000.

50+ Victims Across Multiple Industries

Storm claimed over 50 victims during its first six weeks, with observed organizations in the United States, Germany, Canada, and Australia.

Business services accounted for 13 observed incidents, followed by finance with nine and manufacturing with seven. Retail and healthcare each accounted for six.

Figure 2, Storm sector targeting distribution

Healthcare stands out in Storm’s early activity. Victim claims included hospitals, health networks, treatment providers, radiology organizations, and hospice services. Researchers assess that the early concentration suggests deliberate targeting of organizations where disruption can create significant pressure to pay.

A Ransomware Leak Site Built Like a Platform

Storm’s leak site reinforces the group’s focus on presentation and scale.

The Tor based site includes an interactive global map displaying victim locations, industry filtering, searchable victim listings, timelines, document tree previews, and a custom graphical CAPTCHA.

Figure 3, Storm’s advanced data leak site and interactive victim map

The investment provides Storm with infrastructure for managing victims while supporting affiliate recruitment, media visibility, and brand recognition.

How AI Fits Into Storm’s Strategy

Storm repeatedly describes itself as the “first AI powered, quantum resistant ransomware.”

Researchers found no conclusive evidence supporting AI use in intrusion, encryption, extortion, or affiliate support workflows. Current evidence points toward three roles for the AI narrative: recruitment, automation signaling, and marketing.

AI gives Storm a way to stand out in a crowded ransomware ecosystem and present itself as technologically advanced. References to automated victim management and negotiations may also signal workflow automation, though the available evidence does not establish AI enhanced offensive capabilities.

Storm’s rapid growth shows how quickly a ransomware operation can establish scale through structured affiliate recruitment, polished infrastructure, and aggressive branding.

For the complete analysis of Storm’s emergence, victimology, affiliate model, leak site, and AI claims, read the full report: Storm: Ransomware in the Age of AI

Learn how Check Point Exposure Management helps organizations monitor ransomware groups across the dark web, track emerging threat actor activity, and identify potential risks to their organization.

7261286b4241.text:
Forty percent of security teams now use AI every day, and another 56% are testing it. Only 4% have no plans to adopt it, according to Prophet Security's State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey of more than 250 CISOs, SOC leaders and practitioners. For the teams still testing, the next decision is whether their own SOC is ready.

AI SOC readiness has two parts: whether a SOC has the problems AI SOC agents are built for, and whether it has the data access, context, written standards and oversight rules that AI agents need to investigate alerts accurately in its environment. A SOC does not need to be far along a maturity model to be ready. AI agents do their first work on the bottom layer, alert handling, and the analyst hours they return give a team room to work on the layers above it.

The next section describes those problems. Technical readiness covers four areas: access and context, an investigation standard with baseline metrics, rules for what the agent may do, and a plan for the time it gives back.

Which SOCs benefit the most from AI SOC agents

The SOCs that gain the most from AI SOC agents usually recognize several of the problems below, whether an outside provider works their alerts or their own analysts do.

If an MDR or MSSP works your alerts:

Your MDR flags threats too slowly. The provider works your alerts in a queue it shares with its other customers, so the escalation for a real intrusion can arrive hours after the activity started.

Your MDR hands alerts back for lack of context. An escalation arrives with a short summary and questions such as is this login expected, is this a production server, or is this user traveling? The provider often does not know your users, assets and business well enough to finish the investigation, so your analysts do the rest.

Your MDR closes alerts without showing its work. When the provider marks an alert benign, the note may not say what it checked and how it came to that conclusion, so your team either trusts the call or runs the investigation again.

Your MDR's coverage stops at the tools it supports. Many contracts cover the EDR and a set list of log sources, so alerts from everything else, such as a SaaS application or a second cloud platform, land on your team.

If your own analysts work the queue, including whatever the provider sends back:

"Are we impacted?" takes days to answer. When a critical vulnerability or a new campaign makes the news, leadership wants an answer the same day. Getting one means hunting across the environment by hand, usually by an analyst who is also working the queue.

Lower-severity alerts wait or get closed in bulk. A thorough investigation means pivoting across the SIEM, EDR, identity provider, cloud console and email tools, so the team keeps up with critical and high alerts and gets to the rest when it can. In the survey, 60% of respondents said an alert they had ignored or missed later turned into a serious issue, such as a breach or downtime.

Noisy detections get switched off. Tuning a rule that fires too often takes time the team does not have, so the rule gets disabled and the technique it watched goes uncovered.

Hunting and detection engineering wait for spare time. Proactive work happens when someone has a free afternoon, because the alert queue comes first.

A few senior analysts carry the hard cases. Only one or two people know how to work the most difficult investigations, so a single resignation can set the team back.

Nights and weekends are thinly covered. Staffing the queue around the clock takes more analysts than the budget covers, so alerts that fire after hours wait until morning or go to whoever is on call.

AI SOC agents are built for this work. They are designed to start on each alert as it arrives, whichever tool raised it and at whatever hour. They can pull the context an outside provider lacks from your own systems and record the evidence behind each conclusion, so your team can check it. Some can also run a hunt the day a new threat is disclosed, which turns "are we impacted?" into a set of queries with answers. The analyst hours they return can go to the detection and hunting work that waits today.

If several of these problems sound familiar, the need is there. The next question is whether your SOC can support a deployment.

Where AI agents fit on a SOC maturity model

Prophet Security's SOC maturity model, the SOC Hierarchy of Needs, has five levels: alert management, detection coverage, threat awareness, proactive hunting and posture improvements. Each level depends on the one below it. A team buried in alerts rarely gets to hunting, and a team that hunts without threat awareness has no clear idea what to look for.

Many SOCs have not yet stabilized the first level. In the State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey, respondents said 28% of their alerts are never investigated.

AI SOC agents usually start at that first level, investigating alerts as they arrive. Newer platforms also run hunts and propose detections, work that reaches into levels two and four. Either way, the analyst hours they return go to work above the first level, so readiness depends on what the first level needs.

An AI agent can only investigate what it can query

An AI agent investigates by running queries against your tools, so it cannot see anything it has no access to. If it can query the EDR but not the identity provider, it can describe what happened on the endpoint but not which account was behind it.

Readiness here has three parts:

API access to the sources an investigation needs. That usually means the SIEM, EDR, identity provider, cloud platforms, email and key SaaS applications.

Context the agent can read. An agent needs asset criticality, user roles, VIP lists, business units and known-benign activity, such as scheduled scans and admin scripts, to tell an attacker from a legitimate administrator.

Healthy data pipelines. A silent or delayed log source can make an investigation look complete when key evidence is missing, so the health of the pipelines that feed investigations needs monitoring.

A quick test: take five recent incidents and list every query a senior analyst ran to close them. Any query the agent could not run marks a gap to close before a pilot.

Data access also raises the most common objection. In our survey, 44% of teams cited data privacy and how AI models are trained, the most frequent roadblock respondents named. Ask each vendor whether your data trains their models and where your data is processed.

Define a finished investigation and record your baseline

A pilot needs a written standard to grade the agent against. In many SOCs, only senior analysts know that standard, and it is rarely written down.

The standard covers which evidence closes a phishing case, when an impossible-travel alert needs a call to the user's manager, and what counts as enough to call an alert benign. Writing it down for your highest-volume alert types also gives new analysts an onboarding document.

Also keep a list of the detections that were switched off. In our survey, up to 40% of organizations had turned off some detections because they lacked the people to check them. When an agent investigates every alert, some of those rules can come back, and the list tells you where to start.

Then record the numbers you will compare against: the share of alerts investigated, mean time to investigate, time from alert to first look, and how often closed alerts are reopened. The survey gives a reference point. A thorough investigation takes an average of 75 minutes, and alerts often wait close to an hour before anyone opens them.

You can download our guide on detection engineering to learn more about how an agentic SOC benefits detection engineering.

Decide what the agent may do, and who approves more

Investigation and action carry different risks, and most teams treat them differently. In the survey, 57% of teams require a human to review every AI decision before an alert is closed. On response, 44% have AI recommend actions that people carry out, 30% let it handle low-risk remediation on its own, and no respondent gives it full, unsupervised autonomy.

A ready SOC has these rules written down before a pilot starts:

Default approvals. A list of the actions that stay human-approved, such as isolating a host, disabling an account or blocking a domain.

How permissions widen. Who can grant the agent more autonomy for a category of action, and what track record they need to see first.

Where findings land. Agent findings should appear in the case management or ticketing tools analysts already use, so nobody has to watch another console.

Who owns feedback. A named person reviews the agent's mistakes and turns corrections into guidance it will use next time.

Starting with read-only access for investigations, then widening permissions as confidence grows, applies the same rules a SOC uses for a new human analyst. Prophet Security's framework for building trust in an AI SOC follows the same stepwise approach.

A readiness checklist mapped to the maturity model

Answer each question yes or no. Part 1 checks the need, and Part 2 checks technical readiness. The level in parentheses shows which layer of the SOC Hierarchy of Needs each item belongs to.

Part 1: Does your SOC need AI SOC agents?

Do escalations from your MDR or MSSP arrive hours after the activity started? (Level 1: alert management)

Does your provider hand alerts back because it lacked the context to finish them? (Level 3: threat awareness)

Does your provider close alerts without showing what it checked? (Level 1: alert management)

Do alerts from tools outside your provider's coverage land on your team? (Level 1: alert management)

Does it take more than a day to tell leadership whether you are impacted by a new vulnerability or campaign? (Level 4: proactive hunting)

Do low- and medium-severity alerts wait, or get closed in bulk without an investigation? (Level 1: alert management)

Have noisy detections been switched off because no one had time to tune them? (Level 2: detection coverage)

Do hunting and detection engineering wait until someone has spare time? (Level 4: proactive hunting)

Do only one or two senior analysts know how to work your hardest cases? (Level 1: alert management)

Do alerts that fire at night or on weekends wait until morning? (Level 1: alert management)

Each yes is a problem an AI SOC agent can take on, and the more yes answers, the stronger the case for a deployment.

Part 2: Is your SOC ready to deploy them?

Can a new tool query your SIEM, EDR, identity, cloud and email sources through an API? (Level 1: alert management)

Are asset criticality, user roles and known-benign activity recorded somewhere a system can read? (Level 3: threat awareness)

Is there a written standard for what a complete investigation includes, for the alert types that make up most of your volume? (Level 1: alert management)

Have you decided which actions stay human-approved, and who can widen the agent's permissions? (Level 1: alert management)

Do you monitor whether the log sources your investigations depend on are arriving? (Level 2: detection coverage)

Do you know your current share of alerts investigated and your mean time to investigate? (Level 1: alert management)

Do you keep a list of detections that were switched off for capacity reasons? (Level 2: detection coverage)

Is there a plan, with named owners, for the analyst hours an agent will return, such as scheduled hunts or detection work? (Level 4: proactive hunting)

A "no" on any of the first four is worth fixing before a production pilot. The other four can be worked on during it.

What to do if the answer is not yet

Most items on the Part 2 list are configuration and documentation work: issuing API credentials, exporting asset and user context, and writing down the investigation standard. A workable order:

Close the access gaps from the five-incident test first, since every later step depends on the agent seeing the data.

Write the investigation standards for your highest-volume alert types.

Run the agent in parallel with your analysts for a few weeks. Record the baseline before it starts, and treat every analyst override as data about where the agent needs more context.

Widen the agent's permissions one category of action at a time, as its record supports it.

Some teams that are not ready consider building their own agents instead. The survey suggests caution: 72% of AI users had tried building internal AI tools, and 46% of those projects were abandoned, never reached production, or were replaced by a commercial product.

Building a functioning prototype is only a small chunk of the work. Most of the work is engineering and maintenance of integrations that take weeks to build but break when a vendor changes an API; rate limits to work around; model deprecations every six to nine months that force a full round of evals, guardrails, and prompt injection testing; and audit trails explaining why each alert was closed.

How Prophet Security Works

Prophet Security is the leading AI SOC platforms for enterprise SOCs, recognized in Rising in Cyber 2026, an honor voted on by more than 150 CISOs and security leaders. Its platform, Prophet AI, works from the stack a team already runs. First-generation AI SOC tools stopped at alert triage. Prophet AI enables an agentic SOC, with specialist agents for investigation, threat hunting and detection engineering.

Prophet AI SOC Analyst investigates every alert at every severity, around the clock, with the depth of a senior analyst. It queries SIEM, EDR, identity, cloud and email tools directly and records every question, query and piece of evidence behind a determination, so an analyst can rerun any query and check the work. It takes response actions only within permissions the customer sets, with human approval as the default.

Prophet AI Threat Hunter is built to answer "are we impacted?" It keeps a profile of each organization's industry, technology stack and the threat actors that target it. When a severe new threat emerges, hunts for it run automatically in the background. Scheduled hunts, including hunts against coverage gaps and questions the team writes in plain language, run on the cadence the team sets. Suspicious leads go to the SOC Analyst for a full investigation.

Prophet AI Detection Engineer takes on the detection engineering work that waits for spare time. It keeps a live MITRE ATT&CK coverage map built from the organization's own investigations, showing which techniques are covered, which have gone quiet and which are dark. It builds and tunes detections from what investigations, hunts and coverage gaps reveal, writes them in the rule language of the SIEM or tool they run in, and backtests each one against the organization's own history. Each change arrives as a reviewable proposal with its rationale and backtest results, and by default nothing reaches production until the team approves it.

Each product's findings feed the others. Investigations show which detections are noisy and where coverage is thin, hunts look in those gaps, and what the hunts find becomes new detections. The team teaches Prophet AI in plain language, and that guidance shapes how investigations run, how hunts are scoped and how detections are written. Customer data never trains its models, and the data plane can run inside the customer's own VPC.

The full State of AI in Security Operations 2026 report, including the survey data cited here, is available to download.
