e46f03d1501a.text: Victim organizations are losing millions of dollars in token charges as criminals hijack their corporate LLM access to steal expensive computing resources and AI services. These fraudulent charges from resource consumption can exceed $100,000 a day, according to a Monday report by Google's Mandiant incident responders, who saw cumulative charges at some organizations hit $1 million before the victim companies revoked intruders' access. "Whenever possible, threat actors want to use this technology to gain a scale advantage over defenders. They achieve that with agentic tools and by stealing tokens from unwitting third parties,” John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told The Register. “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks.” This tactic of hijacking access to LLMs is called LLMJacking, and it’s been increasing steadily over the past two years. In one extreme case, documented in an August report from CrowdStrike, a token thief sent about 200,000 API requests in just two minutes. In one case detailed in the report, a group Google tracks as UNC6993 illicitly gained access to LLM API keys, then generated additional keys and enabled services within the victim’s cloud projects, racking up $100,000 in charges. The threat intel biz also documented a different token thief subscribing victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements to access advanced models on the victim company’s dime. The crook selected premium foundation models, launched high-volume inference streams, and used a “burn and rotate strategy” to bypass rate limits by creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the billing interface to monitor financial impact. In yet another incident, an intruder executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours using stolen third-party API keys to power a token routing service called Jet Night, according to a Monday report from Google. “Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably,” the report says. “For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month.” Jet Night has also admitted to multiple outages on its public Telegram channel, which the Google threat hunters note is “likely due to stolen keys being revoked as victims discover their respective compromises.” Specialized LLMjacking roles As more criminals join the LLMJacking ecosystem, Google says it has documented a division of labor between the criminals that establish initial access to compromised cloud and AI services, and those that manage downstream monetization infrastructure, called “LLM Mixers.” In one case that Mandiant responded to in mid-2026, UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used this access to grant further access to a model API. The crooks also spun up a session hijacking page purporting to be an application portal to join a group of LLM users. “This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls,” the report says. Google predicts miscreants will “increasingly prioritize LLMJacking” compared to other types of resource theft like cryptojacking. And to prevent cloud LLM service abuse, the security firm says defenders should prioritize identity and access management plus supply chain security, and use a centralized secrets management platform to rotate keys and secrets. Also apply least-access privileges to users and service accounts, ensuring that they only have permissions necessary to complete their roles and tasks. And automate secrets scanning within codebases to identify and then remove any API keys and secrets added to source code. ®

ddfa6531c269.text:
An underground activist group says it plans to start openly doxing billionaires as part of a phased campaign against what it calls the American oligarchy—beginning this month with a release that maps the homes of Elon Musk, his brother Kimbal, and Tesla’s board, alongside investors and suppliers that keep the corporation afloat.

Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people they consider their top lieutenants, using nearly every method available to a private investigator, and some that are not.

The pair say the group is international and includes grassroots activists, researchers, journalists, and artists, including some who received top honors in print, television, and digital media in their former careers. For security, many work in “silos” and do not know each other’s names. Through its connections, the group says it has raised more than $1.2 million from “a heartening number of wealthy class traitors” who share in the view that concentrations of extreme wealth and political power pose an “existential threat.”

In a press release Monday, the group says it intends to publish in coming releases more than 150 home addresses, most of them previously unreported. It also promises more than 3,500 records on people with a combined wealth of about $1.4 trillion, plus reporting on what the group alleges are “criminal exploits and security lapses.”

Members of the organization call themselves Capytistas, a play on Zapatistas, the Indigenous insurgents of southern Mexico.

The capybara, a placid rodent famous for getting along with almost any other animal, became the group’s avatar during the early days of Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, as a secret rival to the Shiba Inu—the Doge meme Musk used to brand the agency. (The meme has since been reclaimed by pro-Ukranian activists who post as cartoon dogs to mock Russian propaganda and raise money for the war.)

Americans have long used the term “oligarch” to refer almost exclusively to Russian tycoons who carved up state industries after the Soviet collapse. But it entered mainstream American politics decisively in January 2025, when President Joe Biden used his farewell address to warn that an “oligarchy is taking shape in America.” No one typifies the “extreme wealth, power, and influence” Biden described more than the trillionaire Musk, who held an unpaid job as a special government employee for much of 2025 and has thrown more than $700 million into federal elections since 2023; the equivalent of roughly 15 million typical donations online.

Doxing—the Capytistas’ chosen tactic—has meanwhile become a favored weapon of political guerrillas and self-appointed state informants: In March 2025, as protesters gathered outside Tesla dealerships, an anonymous site called DOGEQuest posted what it claims were the addresses of Tesla owners and DOGE staff. Months later, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement official testified that his unit drew more than three-quarters of its deportation referrals from Canary Mission—a site with similarly nebulous funding but radically different goals: building dossiers on pro-Palestinian students and professors.

b0496e2f02a0.text:
Attackers posing as IT support on Microsoft Teams talked employees into giving them remote control of their PCs. They then used insecure Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) settings to obtain login certificates for privileged accounts, including one for a domain controller.

Microsoft said in a report that it investigated two such intrusions, one of which resulted in company data being copied to an external server.

The attackers exploited no flaw in Teams itself. They relied on social engineering and on AD CS that had been set up insecurely, and Microsoft did not tie the activity to any known group.

How the Attacks Began

Both intrusions started the same way, Microsoft said. The attackers messaged and called employees on Teams while posing as the company's own IT or help desk, working from outside tenants with support-themed names so the contact looked familiar.

They talked each user into opening Quick Assist, a remote-help tool built into Windows, and reading the connection code back to them. That gave the attacker direct, hands-on control of the workstation.

From there, the attacker dropped an archive into the Downloads folder, unpacked it into a new folder named to resemble a Windows update, and ran its contents with a portable Python, Bun, or Java runtime. File names alone were a weak signal, because one copy was renamed while still carrying the real runtime's version details.

What a Certificate Buys an Attacker

AD CS is the Windows role that issues the certificates users and computers present when they log in. A certificate from a poorly configured template lets whoever holds it sign in as the account it names.

Microsoft said such a certificate continues to work even after the account's password is reset or the first machine is wiped, so neither step ends the attacker's access.

Case 1: Privileged Certificates, and a Gap in Containment

In the first intrusion, the attackers found a certificate template with a weakness known as ESC1. With that kind of template, the requester can name the account the certificate will represent, so a low-privileged user can request one that stands in for a privileged account.

The first wave of calls targeted three users and one workstation, producing certificates for three highly privileged accounts. Microsoft Defender's automatic attack disruption cut those identities off and dropped their active sessions. One privileged account, though, had been left out of the automatic response, so it stayed usable.

About 90 minutes later, a larger wave hit 16 users and a second workstation, producing certificates for 8 more privileged accounts. Microsoft said more than 1,000 later attempts to reach files over SMB or to log in were blocked.

Within seconds of obtaining a certificate, the attacker signed in to a domain controller and ran DCSync, a tool for copying password data from Active Directory. The operation had already begun when containment took hold, limiting how much could be replicated. Microsoft did not say how much credential data the attacker obtained.

The excluded account was the opening. The attacker kept using it, reached a file server, and ran a renamed copy of the file-copying tool Rclone to move data from a share to an outside SFTP server. Microsoft did not say how much data was taken.

The case shows, in Microsoft's words, that "partial identity containment can reduce attack activity while still leaving a viable privileged route."

Case 2: A Certificate for the Domain Controller

The second intrusion began the same way but took a different direction because that template weakness was not present. The attacker instead used a technique called PetitPotam to force a domain controller to authenticate to a machine the attacker controlled.

That NTLM login was relayed to the AD CS web enrollment page, an abuse known as ESC8, with no password needed. The attacker used the relayed login to request a certificate for the domain controller itself. With that certificate and Kerberos (PKINIT), the attacker obtained a ticket-granting ticket for the domain controller, turning a one-off relayed login into a lasting identity.

Here the response held. Defender raised ESC8 alerts, the customer isolated the workstation, and Microsoft said no further activity followed.

The difference between the two came down to containment. In the first, automatic disruption blocked most of the attack, but the one excluded account stayed open. In the second, isolating a single workstation stopped it.

What Defenders Can Do

There is no patch, because nothing here was a software flaw. Microsoft's advice is about configuration and response.

Have staff confirm any unexpected support request through a known internal channel before sharing a screen or handing over remote control. Limit which outside Teams tenants can reach employees, and allow only approved remote-support tools.

Review sign-in certificate templates for ones that let the requester name the account, or that too many users can enroll in, and remove enrollment rights that are not needed.

Require HTTPS and turn on Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on web enrollment endpoints, and turn off NTLM there where you can. Microsoft's KB5005413 covers this, and its Defender for Identity posture checks flag templates and endpoints exposed to ESC1 and ESC8.

Turn on certificate auditing. If a bad certificate was issued, revoke it, but remember that revocation does not cancel Kerberos tickets already issued; review active tickets separately.

Treat any account left out of automatic containment as a deliberate decision and assign a manual action in its place.

What Is and Isn't Known

Microsoft did not attribute the intrusions to any named group and did not give the dates on which they happened.

The methods are not new. Researchers named the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate weaknesses in 2021, and the PetitPotam coercion trick was disclosed the same year. Microsoft itself had documented the Teams help-desk-to-remote-access entry method earlier in 2026.

What this report adds is that the two techniques meet in real intrusions, along with the lesson about the excluded account.

Newer Windows is less exposed to the ESC8 step. Microsoft turned EPA on by default for AD CS in Windows Server 2025, whereas Server 2022 and 2019 require it to be enabled manually.

Indicators and Detections

Microsoft's report lists Defender alerts across Teams, endpoints, and identity signals, and four advanced hunting queries that it calls "starting points for investigation" rather than proof on their own. It also published three file hashes tied to the initial-access scripts:

SHA-256 85b6c424117494d3056e88689dbc94c75e9afdb187a339714043aec0da109f17 (JavaScript initial-access script)

SHA-256 f326201269f1ee2f803ae435317507263bb6e0dbfdeb70bd1bb5446e2e46f001 (Python initial-access script)

SHA-256 06c5c14f043aee3bcc5843b5f50909623d5c9a6239a7c1fba9cddad4111469e7 (Python initial-access script)

b52cfc79b385.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a cyber espionage campaign specifically targeting Linux infrastructure associated with government entities and state-affiliated infrastructure.

The activity, observed by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 between October 2025 and April 2026, has been tracked under the moniker CL-UNK-1211, where "CL" refers to cluster and "UNK" stands for unknown motivation.

A notable aspect of the campaign concerns the use of large language models (LLMs) and/or automated artificial intelligence (AI) agents to generate payloads and execute malicious code.

"The attackers behind this cluster of activity focused on Linux environments to conduct extensive reconnaissance and maintain persistent network access to support intelligence-gathering," researchers Roey Porat and Tom Fakterman said. "The attackers attempted to dump sensitive databases and exfiltrate government mailboxes to access social media accounts."

The campaign employs a "versatile operational playbook," leveraging a combination of open-source tools, custom cross-platform backdoors, and web shells to maintain access. Another hallmark involves attempts to disable endpoint protections, wipe system logs, and plant deceptive red-team markers so as to disguise the activity as a legitimate security assessment.

The threat actor has also been observed using malicious PHP and shell scripts, likely generated using AI, to maintain persistence, perform reconnaissance, and exfiltrate data.

"Rather than standard developer documentation, multiple scripts contained conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the code's logic to the operator who provided the initial instructions," the cybersecurity company said. "Their presence suggests that the code was either copied directly from an AI prompt output or deployed by an automated AI agent."

A mix of open-source and bespoke PHP web shells is used as a way to maintain a persistent backdoor into the host networks. The access is then abused to gather credentials from the targeted environment using three different methods -

Replacing the .bashrc file with a malicious version containing a command to steal passwords.

Injecting code into PHP login pages to harvest admin credentials.

Scanning for cleartext email, SMTP, and database passwords within configuration files and command history files.

Also deployed as part of the attacks is a custom, multi-platform remote access trojan written in Go that supports various persistence methods to maintain long-term access on Windows and Linux systems. Called SysGoRAT, it establishes a command-and-control (C2) connection over WebSocket to a hard-coded IP address ("104.194.158[.]65:443") and fetches seven types of commands -

command, to execute arbitrary commands via /bin/sh -c (Linux) or cmd /C (Windows)

control, to spawn via sub-commands an interactive shell (shell_start), screenshots (screenshot), exfiltrate files to the C2 server (download), and install persistence (persist)

list_dir, to list directory content

shell_input, to create an interactive shell session

proxy_connect, to establish a TCP connection to an arbitrary target

proxy_data, to relay data bidirectionally to an established proxy connection

proxy_close, to terminate and remove a proxy session

Furthermore, the attacks make use of in-memory reverse shells to avoid leaving forensic artifacts on disk, as well as enumerate "/var/qmail/mailnames/" directories to count the number of emails stored in specific folders.

"Next, the attackers searched for social media-related emails," Unit 42 explained. "They deployed a PHP script, named search_social.php, that searched for specific keywords in email headers and displayed the results in a user-friendly format."

"The script then parsed the response and displayed the exact file path, social media account email sender, recipient and subject."

The attackers have also been found attempting to generate a bash script named "zip_mails.sh" in a bid to compress emails of interest into ZIP archives and exfiltrate the information. However, syntax errors present in the script meant that the program failed upon execution.

"This campaign demonstrates how attackers are combining traditional post-exploitation techniques with AI-accelerated workflows to target governmental Linux server infrastructure," Unit 42 said. "By leveraging AI to rapidly generate, adapt and deploy operational scripts, the attackers behind CL-UNK-1211 maintained a fast pace of operation while minimizing manual developer overhead."

The development comes as Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, along with Microsoft, documented threat actors' abuse of open-source agentic penetration testing frameworks like ARTEX, PentAGI, Hexstrike, and CAIRN to carry out a "broad range of actions" across various stages of the attack life cycle at an unprecedented speed and scale.

Although ARTEX was taken down by its author after reports of widespread misuse emerged, it has spawned multiple versions, including a commercial offering dubbed ARTEX PRO and a localized variation called ScopeWeaver.

Some of the cases are listed below -

Use of ARTEX by Storm-0940 (aka UNC7228) to orchestrate data theft campaigns targeting entities in the U.S. and Europe across the enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor manufacturing and design, and telecommunications industry verticals.

Use of ARTEX by financially motivated threat actors to facilitate data theft extortion, including the targeting of the financial sector in Asia.

Use of ARTEX by North Korean state-sponsored hacking groups like Onyx Sleet (aka Andariel) and Pearl Sleet (aka Lawrencium) in operations.

Use of PentAGI for WHOIS asset mapping and systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against organizations in Asia.

"The emergence of ARTEX and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses," GTIG and Mandiant said.

"Frameworks such as ARTEX compress attack timelines to machine speed; however, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces, increasing the likelihood of detection and mitigation."

64ee5867692b.text:
CISA added two new Ivanti Connect Secure vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday, after Ivanti updated an earlier security advisory with details about the flaws.

Three flaws chained to gain a foothold

CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for a critical function vulnerability that allows a local authenticated attacker to escalate their privileges, and CVE-2026-118527, a “Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers Vulnerability” that makes remote authenticated file upload possible, have been exploited as zero-days in conjunction with a third flaw: CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass and RCE vulnerability.

According to Volexity researchers, who discovered the attack and reported it to Ivanti, the attackers were covertly turning the SSL VPN appliances into a foothold in the targeted organizations’ network.

“Because the operation was detected and disrupted, the threat actor’s ultimate objectives could not be determined. However, Volexity assesses with high confidence that UTA0576’s actions signaled preparation for lateral movement and a broader compromise of the victim network,” the researchers said.

The attackers engaged in credential theft and queried Active Directory for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, Rapid7 researchers noted.

Patch, then hunt

CISA has ordered US federal civilian agencies to address CVE-2026-111357 by November 2, 2026, and to engage in forensic triage and investigate for possible compromise. CVE-2026-118527 has a November 13 deadline.

All three flaws have been fixed by Ivanti, and customers using the Connect Secure SSL VPN appliance are advised to implement the provided updates.

Rapid7 recommended investigating for compromise after patching.

“Volexity reports that the observed activity evades Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool, so a clean result does not rule out compromise. Preserve memory and logs before rebooting or resetting where feasible. If compromise is suspected, follow Ivanti’s recovery steps and rotate potentially exposed credentials,” the company advised, and provided threat hunting guidance.

Volexity also shared a list of indicators of compromise related to this attack campaign, as well as helpful YARA rules.

eec582b1d11c.text:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 2nd November, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

Binance, a global cryptocurrency exchange, has suffered a cyberattack resulting in the theft of approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets. Attackers reportedly compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop and abused internal wallet infrastructure to authorize unauthorized withdrawals. The incident ranks among the largest cryptocurrency thefts ever recorded and is linked to North Korean group.

Polymarket, a US-based prediction market platform, has disclosed a cyberattack involving a compromised third-party service that distributed malicious JavaScript to its website. The script hijacked authenticated trading sessions and attempted unauthorized transactions. Approximately $2.7 million in cryptocurrency was traced to a suspected attacker-controlled wallet.

Japan Airlines, a major Japanese international airline, has disclosed a third-party data breach affecting approximately 92,000 passengers through the Amadeus reservation system. Exposed records included passenger names and flight information. Approximately 2,000 individuals also had contact information, passport details, and additional travel records potentially accessed.

The Florida Department of Education has disclosed a data breach involving unauthorized access to its student financial aid website, potentially affecting 4.9 million individuals. Compromised information reportedly includes names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, and contact details. The incident was identified on October 19.

AI THREATS

Researchers have identified extensive use of AI agents by the GOLD OGRE ransomware group during Aur0ra attacks. Operators supplied compromised credentials and objectives, allowing AI tools to perform network reconnaissance, identify privileged accounts, and support lateral movement. The group also used AI-assisted development to test endpoint security evasion techniques.

Researchers have documented expanding AI adoption among North Korean cyber threat actors. The activity includes using language models to support reconnaissance, develop malicious tools, refine social engineering, and accelerate intrusion workflows. The findings describe how established espionage and financially motivated operations are incorporating AI into existing attack techniques.

Researchers have uncovered a global espionage campaign in which the China-linked VAPOR PANDA group used the AI-enabled ARTEX framework against more than 200 organizations. Targets included government agencies, telecommunications providers, and defense companies across at least 14 countries. Confirmed intrusions involved credential theft and deployment of the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

Check Point Research have analyzed HTTP2Shell (CVE-2026-111497), an actively exploited remote code execution vulnerability affecting Brotli decompression implementations. Initially associated with Node.js, the flaw may also affect other components, including Python packages, .NET, and proxies. Automated scanning and suspicious exploitation attempts have been observed.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (Node.js Brotli Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-111497)))

A critical Linux kernel vulnerability, CVE-2026-98432, has been disclosed with a CVSS score of 9.8. The memory management flaw affects TCP networking and can enable unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on systems exposing Multipath TCP listeners.

Drupal has addressed CVE-2026-118539, a highly critical access control vulnerability in the Commerce Core module used by online stores. Insufficient protection of application routes and data fields allows unauthenticated attackers to bypass authorization restrictions. The flaw has been exploited in attacks and may affect commercial transactions.

Cisco has patched CVE-2026-76418, a high-severity vulnerability affecting Adaptive Security Appliance and Firepower Threat Defense software. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely crash devices configured with SSL VPN functionality. Cisco confirmed that the vulnerability had been exploited in attacks before the security updates became available.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point Research has uncovered the Yoba malware campaign, which distributes malicious installers disguised as ChatGPT and Claude desktop applications through fraudulent GitHub projects. Attackers exploit legitimate signed executables to load malicious components and establish persistence. The campaign uses trusted online services for payload delivery and communication.

Check Point researchers have analyzed unexpected network activity generated by Alibaba’s Qwen model during a security-related task. Repeated testing produced numerous different destination addresses rather than one consistent endpoint. The findings suggest unstable model behavior is a more plausible explanation than a deliberately embedded data-exfiltration mechanism.

Researchers have identified UAT-11473, an advanced threat actor exploiting a Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN authentication bypass to deploy the KeyDrift malware framework. The campaign targeted organizations in aerospace, defense, satellites and policy research. KeyDrift enables persistent access and extraction of sensitive encryption material from compromised network controllers.

Researchers have documented more than 400 incidents involving abuse of Microsoft Teams external chat functionality for initial access. Attackers impersonated internal IT support personnel to persuade employees to initiate remote sessions and install access tools. Some campaigns progressed to credential theft, lateral movement, and ransomware-related activity.

The post 2nd November – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

1e53c1d98fd7.text: Cyberattacks on both Russia’s and Ukraine’s emergency alert apps resulted in fake messages about missile and nuclear strikes broadcast to the public. Officials from both countries confirmed the attacks, which occurred at similar times, on Sunday evening. According to public statements and messages sent via social media, Ukraine’s alert app was hit first, with the country’s Air Force quick to dispel nuclear fears. "The Air Alert app has likely been compromised," it said via Telegram at around 2100 UTC. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel!" At around 0030 UTC on Monday, Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations confirmed the country’s app had also been abused, with fake messages sent to citizens' devices. "Attention! The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public," it said, also via Telegram. "Work is currently underway to patch the vulnerability and restore normal operation." The ministry issued an update around 90 minutes later, saying the app was once again functioning normally, and pointing out that an attack on the app was not the same as a compromise of the state’s national alert system. "Citizens are alerted through primary channels: regional and municipal alert systems (sirens, loudspeakers), communication networks (SMS messaging), and television and radio broadcasts. The mobile app is merely an additional, supporting information service," it stated. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Affairs also issued a public announcement reminding citizens about how to receive emergency warnings while its “Alarm!” app was down. These include enabling iOS and Android emergency alerts, state-controlled sirens, and other official sources, such as the official social media accounts of Ukraine's government. According to the messages sent to devices after the compromise of Ukraine's alert app, the fake warnings pertained to various threats, such as street fights in Kyiv, chemical attacks, and radiation hazards. Alerts about the threat of nuclear fallout from official government warning systems would normally lead to panic, however, one of the earliest messages sent to citizens was written in Russian and referenced the "Oreshnik" missile, which was an immediate signal that the message may not be genuine. Equivalent alerts sent to Russian citizens also warned of impending nuclear strikes "at all regions of Russia," referencing "P1-Sun," the name of a Ukrainian attack drone. Oleksander Merezhko, who chairs the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee and noted the suspicious Russian-language alert, told the BBC the attack was almost certainly part of Russia's cyber war. "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that," he said. "It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities." Russia has not explicitly blamed Ukraine for the attack on its app, and official sources say the app is running as normal. Ukraine's announcement of the alert app cyberattack came almost simultaneously with the official conclusion of a six-day ceasefire in Kherson. Russia agreed to the rare temporary suspension of conflict to allow hundreds of Ukrainians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Olehsky. Russia did not agree to a proposed extension of the ceasefire, which officially ended at around 2100 UTC – around the same time Ukrainians began receiving fake warning messages. ®

SecurityWeek tracked 37 cybersecurity merger and acquisition (M&A) deals announced in October 2026.

For a look at last year’s activity, see SecurityWeek’s 2025 Cybersecurity M&A Report, which covers more than 420 deals.

Here are some of the most important cybersecurity M&A deals announced in October 2026:

Absolute Security acquires FirmGuard

Endpoint security and cyber resilience firm Absolute Security has acquired FirmGuard, the UEFI BIOS firmware security and management business of Phoenix Technologies. Absolute will integrate FirmGuard with its firmware-embedded Absolute Persistence technology, adding below-the-OS management, continuous firmware integrity monitoring and patching, and compliance enforcement.

Aikido Security acquires OutKept and Cyberly

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Belgian application security unicorn Aikido Security has acquired OutKept and Cyberly and used the two startups to launch Noon, a workforce security business. OutKept is based in Belgium and provides phishing simulations and security awareness training. Poland’s Cyberly develops AI-powered attack simulations and tools for tracking employee AI usage. Both deals closed in September but weren’t made public until October.

Anthropic to acquire Opaque Systems

AI company Anthropic has agreed to acquire Opaque Systems, a confidential AI company that grew out of research at UC Berkeley. Anthropic has described the deal as licensing Opaque’s technology and hiring some of its engineers, reportedly including CEO Aaron Fulkerson and CTO Rishabh Poddar. Financial terms weren’t disclosed.

Cohere to acquire AISLE

Canadian AI developer Cohere has signed a letter of intent to acquire AISLE, a startup whose autonomous AI systems find and help patch vulnerabilities in critical software. AISLE’s roughly 50 employees will join Cohere, which is setting up a cybersecurity unit called Cohere Cyber. AISLE CEO Ondřej Vlček, the former CEO of Avast, will become its senior vice president.

Hex-Rays to acquire HexAI

Hex-Rays, the Belgian company behind the IDA Pro reverse engineering tool, has agreed to acquire HexAI, an Israeli startup founded in 2025. HexAI’s AI agents analyze source code and binaries to uncover vulnerabilities, malware and backdoors. The deal is reportedly worth $30 million to $35 million. Hex-Rays plans to grow HexAI’s Israeli operations and build new AI-powered research tools.

IonQ has to acquire Elisity

Quantum computing company IonQ has agreed to acquire zero trust security firm Elisity in an all-stock deal worth up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in performance-based earnouts. IonQ will combine its post-quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution technology with Elisity’s IdentityGraph platform, which enforces least-privilege access for users, devices, workloads and AI agents. The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Proofpoint to acquire Varonis

Thoma Bravo-owned Proofpoint has agreed to acquire data security company Varonis for roughly $6.3 billion in cash. Together, the companies want to offer a single platform for discovering and protecting sensitive data, controlling access to it, and preventing data loss as organizations adopt AI.

dfa3660e5bb3.text:
Last week, an often-ignored TCP option, introduced in 2020, made the news due to a new vulnerability in Linux's implementation (RFC 8684, CVE-2026-98432)

Instead of looking at the vulnerability, I am using this diary to talk a bit about multipath TCP (MPTCP) and how you may see it used in your network.

What is MPTCP?

Traditionally, TCP is a connection-oriented protocol. Connections are established between a client and server, and host IP addresses are not expected to change for a specific connection. This restriction to a specific path does not always match modern system architecture. For example, mobile devices may switch from a local WIFI network to a cellular network at any time. Having to re-establish TCP connections may break applications. At the same time, servers often have a hard time "filling" high-bandwidth links using a single TCP connection due to limits on Window Size and the sequence number range [RFC 6182]. MPTCP is supposed to solve these problems by allowing connections to be split and handed over between different IP addresses.

The only widely used implementation I have observed is iOS/iPadOS. In this case, IPv4 connections to Apple (17.0.0.0/8) often utilize MPTCP [Apple]. MPTCP was initially used for Siri, and later for other services like Apple Music.

Two versions of MPTCP are currently defined and used: v0 and v1. At first,

MPTCP Options

The MPTCP Option (0x1e, 30) is followed by a byte containing 4 bits indicating the subtype and 4 bits indicating the version (0 or 1).

+----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+ | TCP Option | Option Length|Subtype| Version| Flags | +----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+ | 30 | variable | | 0 or 1 | | +----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+

MP_CAPABLE (subtype 0): Indicates MPTCP support. Both sides must include it in the TCP handshake for MPTCP support to be enabled. Each MP_CAPABLE option also carries an 8-byte key that will later be used to identify and authenticate the different sub-sessions.

MP_JOIN (subtype 1): A second TCP connection may join an initial connection using the MP_JOIN option. This connection will typically be initiated by the client, but may originate from a different IP address. The RFC does specifically allow the server to initiate the second (or additional) connection. The RFC states: "It is permissible for either host in a connection to initiate the creation of a new subflow, but it is expected that this will normally be the original connection initiator." Ports should be the same, but do not have to be. Of course, this also accounts for common firewall rules. The web server will likely listen only on port 443, and the client's firewall will reject inbound SYN packets.

DSS (Data Sequence Signal, subtype 2): Each TCP connection which is part of MPTCP maintains its own sequence numbers, and acts just like any other "normal" TCP connection. To stitch the content of multiple connections together, the DSS option is used. It maps the respective's TCP sequence numbers to the sequence numbers of the combined connection.

ADD_ADDR/REMOVE_ADDR (subtypes 3, 4): these options are somewhat similar to MP_JOIN, but instead of actually setting up an additional connection, they advertise (or remove) additional addresses or ports that can be used.

MPTCP Detection

The best way to detect MPTCP is to look for TCP Option 30. Here are a few ways to do so:

Wireshark/tshark: Wireshark has a "mptcp" display filter keyword. As so often, Wireshark does make it easy.

tcpdump: There is no great way to match TCP options in tcpdump. But MPTCP packets, particularly SYN packets, tend to have large TCP headers, so a quick match on TCP header length can help. For example: 'tcp[12]>0xd0'

Suricata: Use the "tcp.hdr" keyword to inspect TCP options. The tricky part is that the option length isn't always the same. But there should be at least one MP_CAPABLE message that includes both the sender and receiver key, making this option 20 bytes long. The first three bytes are |1e 14 00| for version 0 or |1e 14 01| for version 1.

Snort: Snort does not have a keyword to inspect TCP options, and as far as I know, no way to filter for multipath TCP. The snort_decoder "experimental TCP option" alert only triggers on specific option types reserved for experimental use.

Zeek: By default, zeek does not log options, but it does offer the tcp_option and tcp_options events that can easily be used to log MPTCP. For example:

event tcp_option(c: connection, is_orig: bool, opt: count, optlen: count) { if ( opt == 30 ) { print(fmt("MPTCP between %s and %s", c$id$orig_h, c$id$resp_h)); } }

[Apple] https://support.apple.com/en-us/101905 [RFC8694] https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8684 [CVE-2026-98432] https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/10/30/1

-- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter|

eb024e820a81.text:
A new Windows infostealer sends the data it steals to an AI model and asks it to rank the victim’s assets by how much money they could bring in, Cisco Talos has found.

“There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics,” said Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco.

The malware calls itself VOLTA-AUTODOXER and turned up through Talos’ CAIRN research effort, which tracks malware that uses AI. It deletes itself after running, and every endpoint it talks to belongs to a third party, so there is no attacker-owned infrastructure to go after.

At first, VOLTA behaves like any other infostealer. It grabs browser passwords, cookies and saved payment cards, cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases, Microsoft OAuth tokens, SSH and cloud provider keys, screenshots, and sessions for Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox. It also dumps the password of every Wi-Fi network saved on the computer in plaintext and runs a built-in cracker against cryptocurrency wallet vaults.

“VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine,” Fetterman noted. “This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation.”

“It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim’s Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token,” Fetterman added.

A target assessment on demand

The finished bundle is sent to the OpenRouter API with instructions telling the model to play a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment of the victim.

The model has to rank the victim’s valuables by how easily they can be turned into money, tag each one low, medium or high, and then judge the victim’s security habits and password hygiene. The instructions also tell it to look for links between scattered details, such as a person’s name, address or university, and the passwords they pick.

The model’s job, Fetterman explained, is to stretch the stolen data and draw inferences that add to its value.

“After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called ‘Identity_Report.txt’. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as ‘AI_Analysis.txt’. Both files exfil together in ‘volta_dox.zip’,” he wrote.

By default, VOLTA sends its request to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. Each reply is checked for wording that signals a refusal, and if the model declines, the job passes to Moonshot AI’s Kimi K2 and then to Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash.

“This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models,” he observed.

Built for buyers

The malware’s settings, including its Telegram channel and API keys, go into six slots in a template that is filled in when the binary is built.

“This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way,” Fetterman stated.

If VOLTA is sold this way, buyers with any level of skill can aim it at victims and get ranked target assessments delivered to their Telegram inbox.

Handing the legwork to AI

Researchers describe VOLTA as a mature stealer with an AI layer added to take the analysis work off the operator’s hands. Talos saw the same approach in the CLOSEDQUORUM implant, applied to a different phase of an attack, where the step that demands the most human attention is also handed to a model.

“These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next,” Fetterman concluded.

2b111ea38155.text:
Some 88% of the critical and high-severity weaknesses found in live attack tests on enterprise environments this year would not have been identified through vendor advisories or other outside sources, new data has suggested.

The figure comes from a report published on November 2 by Armadin, the offensive security startup launched by Mandiant founder Kevin Mandia, based on AI-driven attacks against its clients' live systems.

The clients span nearly a dozen industries, but Armadin did not disclose how many organizations or findings the data covers.

Read more on exposure management: AI Threats and Alert Fatigue Challenge Cybersecurity Teams

Most Severe Findings Sat Beyond Advisories and Logins

Defects in software the clients had written themselves made up 67% of the critical findings and 78% of the high findings that advisories could not cover. Vendor products deployed in ways no advisory describes, such as administrative consoles exposed to the internet, accounted for 24% and 22%.

The remaining 9% of critical findings, and under 1% of high ones, were zero-days Armadin found itself, including one in an identity governance platform whose vendor took almost four months to issue an advisory.

Nearly 70% of critical and high findings sat on the unauthenticated attack surface. Of the documented attack chains, 82% began without credentials, and 56% of those went on without a password or key ever being presented.

In more than 70% of client environments, Armadin said it reached a critical outcome in three steps or fewer without valid credentials.

Exposed Service Accounts Created Further Attack Paths

Just under half of the chains that started without authentication relied on an exposed credential, 71% of which belonged to applications or service accounts rather than people. Nearly 90% were reachable without extraction, often in repositories, configuration files, backups, logs or cloud settings.

In one engagement, Armadin started from an unprivileged domain account and used a flaw in backup software to read the credentials it held. That led to a hypervisor management server and, via a domain controller backup, to domain administrator hashes.

Fixing the severe findings meant shipping application code in 51% of cases, changing a setting, permission or policy in 43% and rotating an exposed credential in 32%, with many needing more than one step.

Armadin's recommendations included policies for provisioning, storing and rotating service account credentials, and checks of pipelines and code repositories for exposed secrets.

By its count, 93% of severe findings needed no third party to act, leaving the fix in each organization's own hands.

2f3577c7a3fb.text:
The Florida Department of Education (FLDOE) says hackers breached its student financial aid website, potentially exposing the personal information of roughly 4.9 million people.

The department discovered the intrusion on October 19. It says it launched its incident response procedures after detecting the threat and has since contained the breach.

“At this time, we believe the incident was limited to the Florida Student Financial Aid website (FloridaStudentFinancialAidSG.org) and may have impacted approximately 4.9 million individuals,” the department said.

The website is the online hub for Florida’s state-funded scholarship and grant programs. FLDOE warns that anyone who has applied for financial aid in the state in the past could be among those affected.

Names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, home addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and gender codes are among the data types the attackers may have accessed.

“Not all individuals were necessarily affected, and the specific information involved may vary by person,” FLDOE noted.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The department has not disclosed how the attackers got in or who is responsible, and no threat group appears to have publicly claimed the attack. The Florida Digital Service and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement are assisting with the response.

The department has cautioned that some of its websites and online services may be disrupted for a time as remediation continues.

According to FLDOE, students’ existing aid is safe. The breach will not delay the disbursements and tuition payments it handles, nor will it change eligibility for its scholarships, grants, and student loans.

The breach follows a September incident at the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV). That agency confirmed hackers had accessed its driver database after the ShinyHunters extortion group claimed to have stolen more than 200,000 driver records.

FLHSMV traced the intrusion to compromised credentials belonging to a local police department user but did not name ShinyHunters.

Related: Revolve Data Breach Impacts at Least 180,000 People

Related: Chainalysis Discloses Data Breach Following AI-Driven Cyberattack

7591307f2633.text:
Recently, our team exposed sophisticated scam kits designed to steal sensitive data and trick consumers. But underground marketplaces are not just for malware and stolen passwords. They also offer services designed to manipulate your opinion of the products and services you buy every day.

In our latest research, we examined cybercrime forums where sellers advertise illicit “reputation management” services. For the right price, these underground operators offer to flood a product with glowing, five-star ratings or remove negative reviews. This shadowy industry works both ways—artificially boosting reputations and deliberately hiding legitimate complaints.

A major shift we are seeing in this space is the adoption of new technology. We also found that cybercriminals are using AI to automate these fake review campaigns. This could allow them to quickly generate realistic, human-sounding feedback in large volumes without much manual effort.

5 stars as a service

In the first example, discovered on a major English-language underground forum, a seller operating under the handle “aqenova” advertises both five-star review generation and negative review removal services.

The seller’s operations span widely used platforms, including Google, Trustpilot, Yelp, and various mobile app stores. By simply asking prospective buyers, “Just tell me which platform reviews you need?” the seller presents reputation manipulation as something buyers can just order on demand.

Five-star reviews and removal services

Decoding the seller’s FAQ

Analyzing another seller’s (TrustForge) “Frequently Asked Questions” section revealed some surprising details about how these operations reportedly run behind the scenes.

First, the seller emphasizes that real people manually post these reviews, offering a guarantee for both successful delivery and “non-drop”—meaning the platform won’t flag and remove the feedback later.

Remember, a real person posting a review doesn’t mean they’re a real customer. The important question is whether they actually used the product or service and are describing an honest experience.

Second, it appears this is a well-coordinated team effort rather than a solo operation, as the seller charges an extra fee if a buyer wants the main operator to write the review text personally.

However, what caught our attention most was their confidence in beating platform checks. The seller guarantees their fake reviews will stay active, claiming they rely on a closely guarded “private method.” According to TrustForge’s own statements, this method has allowed them to post more than 10,000 fake reviews.

Reputation management FAQ

The clean-up crew: Making bad reviews disappear

A single negative review is often all it takes to create a bad first impression of a product or service. When those negative comments start to pile up, they can completely ruin a business’s reputation and bottom line.

Recognizing how desperate businesses can be to protect their image, our research team discovered underground services specifically offering to remove “fake” or “unfair” reviews from major platforms like Google and Trustpilot.

Of course, the boundary between what is genuinely fake and what a business simply considers “unfair” can be blurry. Businesses can legitimately challenge fabricated reviews, but these services raise concerns about whether genuine customer complaints could also be targeted.

If legitimate customer complaints disappear, consumers lose information that could help them decide where to spend their money.

An offer to remove “fake” or “unfair” Google reviewsAn offer to remove ”fake” or “unfair” review Google reviews

On average, having a single review removed through these underground services costs between $100 and $200. However, the pricing jumps dramatically depending on the platform.

For instance, one seller advertised Airbnb review removal for around $1,100 per review.

When you check a business’s reviews, you’re looking for patterns in other customers’ experiences. If genuine complaints disappear, you could miss repeated problems with refunds, product quality, or customer service.

$1,100 to remove a “fake” or “unfair” Airbnb review

Artificial intelligence, artificial reviews

During the last few months, our research team spotted an interesting thread on an underground forum where two users discussed using AI to mimic human E-E-A-T.

E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. It is a quality evaluation framework outlined in Google’s Search Quality Rater Guidelines, which human evaluators use to assess content quality. E-E-A-T itself is not a direct ranking factor.

In the discussion we observed, one user asked the community if it was possible to use AI to effectively fake these qualities when writing product reviews and artificially boost website rankings. The answer was a resounding yes.

Another user claimed they had never experienced problems getting Google to index their completely AI-generated reviews.

AI vs. E-E-A-T

Behind the scenes: The IP addresses for fake reviews

To keep fake reviews from being flagged and deleted, scammers need to look like everyday consumers. To help do this, they can use something called “residential and mobile proxies,” which route their traffic through other internet connections to disguise where it comes from.

Think of an IP address as your computer’s caller ID. When scammers use bulk IP addresses from giant data centers, platforms may spot and block that traffic as coming from commercially hosted infrastructure. Residential proxies, on the other hand, route traffic through real, physical home internet connections—just like the Wi-Fi you use in your living room. Mobile proxies work the same way, but use real cellular networks.

Our team recently discovered a seller on an underground forum acting as a direct supplier of these residential and mobile connections. The seller explicitly advertises them as perfect for running fake review campaigns.

Residential and mobile proxies advertised for fake review campaigns

How to avoid being misled by fake reviews

The main goal of this research isn’t to make you panic or stop trusting every online review you read. We want to raise awareness about what happens behind the scenes, so you can make more informed buying decisions.

If a product or offer seems too good to be true, but is backed by a mountain of perfect five-star reviews, take a moment to pause. Scammers often use these artificially boosted ratings to make a bad deal look reassuring.

Read recent reviews and some of the middle-rated ones, rather than relying on the overall score. Look for recurring details about the things that matter to you, such as durability, delivery, or getting your money back.

Look for repeated wording or sudden bursts of glowing feedback. These signs don’t prove a review is fake, but they’re reasons to take a closer look. Check the seller’s contact details and return policy, too.

47a9fe98564e.text:
Applebee’s has fixed a security flaw that exposed customers’ personal information after a researcher discovered a database password embedded in the restaurant chain’s Android app.

The researcher, Robert Wiggins, found the password with help from AI. It gave him access to an internal Applebee’s customer database. A password written directly into an app’s code or configuration is known as a hardcoded credential. Anyone who extracts it may be able to use it to access the system.

The exposed database contained:

Names, email addresses, and email-verification status

Dates of birth, phone numbers, and ZIP codes

Veteran status

Account-creation dates and login counts

IP addresses from customers’ most recent logins, which can indicate their approximate location

TechCrunch independently checked Wiggins’ findings. It created an Applebee’s account with dummy information, which Wiggins successfully retrieved from the database.

According to TechCrunch, Wiggins could not find a suitable way to report the issue to Applebee’s or its parent company, Dine Brands, so he asked the publication to help contact them. TechCrunch held its story until the fix was confirmed. Applebee’s confirmed on October 29 that it had addressed the issue.

It’s unclear how many customers’ records were in the database. Dine Brands says it has not found evidence of unauthorized access, but its investigation is ongoing.

How to stay safe

The database fields described by TechCrunch did not include payment card details or account passwords. That does not tell us whether anyone accessed the database before the fix, so customers should watch for targeted scams.

Names, email addresses, phone numbers, and other personal details could help scammers make messages look relevant and convincing.

Be wary of unexpected Applebee’s-themed emails, texts, or calls. Be especially skeptical of messages offering refunds or compensation, warning that your account will be closed, or asking you to “verify” payment details.

Check security notices through a route you trust. Open the app directly or visit Applebee’s website yourself rather than following a link in an unexpected message. If necessary, contact the company using details you find independently.

Unsure whether a message is a scam? Check it with Malwarebytes’ Scam Guard for an assessment and advice on what to do next.

When sharing personal information, consider why the company needs it and whether you trust it to keep the information safe.

Unsure where a link goes? We’ll check it.

Check now

4b2ed981d263.text: The cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers in Europe continue, as a slew of grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden report widespread food wastage as a result of miscreants raising the temperatures to highs of 50ºC (122°F). In Belgium, around 40 Delhaize stores were affected after the attackers reportedly switched fridges and freezers into defrost mode overnight, between Sunday and Monday, resulting in stock issues. Diego Louwers, a Proxy Delhaize store manager in Overijse, near Brussels, told RTL Info that the consequences of the cyberattacks were "catastrophic," forcing the store to throw out the entirety of its fresh and frozen products. "We can't have anything worse in our line of work," he said. "We have to throw away all of our merchandise, and it's both heartbreaking and very complicated operationally." A Delhaize spokesperson said it took steps to ensure stores remain stocked, although fresh and frozen products are "temporarily somewhat limited." "On Monday, 2 November, we identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen of our stores," they said. "We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational and ensure that our customers can continue to do their shopping as usual. "In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centres are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores. "We are, of course, continuing to ensure that our products are stored and presented under optimal conditions, so that we can provide our customers with the quality and freshness they have come to expect from us." Around 15 Carrefour stores are also reportedly affected, as are sites operated by Intermarché, Spar, and Shop & Go stores located at Q8 service stations. Belgium’s De Laet & Van Haver chain of butcher shops reported temperature rises in its appliances too, but followed up with a statement on Monday saying there was no impact on its produce, and all stores remain open. Simultaneously, similar issues have affected Swedish grocery chain ICA, which confirmed attacks on a "small number of stores." "We can confirm that we have been informed of an incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network," a company spokesperson said. "The incident impacted the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation." ICA did not respond to questions about the scale of food wastage nor when normal operations are expected to continue. One store, ICA Nära in Böda on Öland, said via social media that it is open today but has no fresh or frozen produce to sell. "Unfortunately, we are one of the stores whose refrigerators and freezers have been hacked," it said. "We are open as usual, but unfortunately we have no refrigerators and freezers to sell. "We have no status on when the refrigerators and freezers are expected to be up and running again." The store manager, Mats Olsson, told SVT that he arrived to work on Monday morning and was greeted by a puddle of water and freezers set to 55 degrees C – a tale echoed by other managers across the country. Coop stores are affected by similar attacks too, with six locations in central Sweden experiencing fridge-freezer issues, according to a company spokesperson. Likewise, at least 13 SuperValue stores in Ireland are also affected, with fresh and frozen food being thrown out, according to parent company Musgrave speaking to RTE. The news comes less than a month after various grocery chains in France resorted to discarding bucketfuls of produce after their appliances were remotely defrosted by cybercrooks. Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others were hit with cyberattacks in mid-October, and hundreds of stores across the chains were reportedly impacted. At least some of the affected stores were running outdated firmware on their Danfoss refrigeration controllers, and shortly after the attacks were confirmed, CERT-FR published an alert pertaining to numerous Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controller compromises. Other retailers, such as Coopérative U, confirmed they were not Danfoss customers. It remains unclear if the latest attacks across Europe used the same methods as those used for the disruption in France last month. None of the companies that spoke to The Register on Monday responded to questions about who was behind the intrusions. ®

d8203545bb89.text:
Financial technology company Abrigo has restored its Sageworks risk management application, except for borrower-facing capabilities, following an outage triggered by "irregular activity" in its environment.

On October 30, the company began emergency maintenance and took the Sageworks application offline to investigate suspicious activity detected earlier that day, with the outage continuing through the weekend.

Abrigo provides cloud-based software and analytics solutions for community banks and credit unions across the United States. According to the company, it serves more than 2,400 entities.

Its Sageworks product is a software platform that helps lenders process loan applications, analyze borrowers’ finances, assess creditworthiness, and monitor loan portfolios.

Due to its nature, Sageworks handles sensitive information, including banking customer details.

"We identified irregular activity in our environment, and, out of abundance of caution, we disabled the Sageworks application at approximately 11:25 am ET," the company said on Friday.

In status updates over the weekend, Abrigo said its investigation was ongoing but did not disclose details about the nature of the incident.

The incident impacted the following services: Online Portal Now, Sageworks Analyst, and Sageworks API.

In its latest update today, the company said that most of the Sageworks functionality had been restored, with the exception of borrower-facing features.

BleepingComputer reached out to Abrigo for more details, but we have not received a response by publication time. Until the nature of the incident is disclosed, it is unclear if the outage was caused by a breach or a technical issue.

Earlier this year, someone allegedly part of the ShinyHunters extortion group claimed an attack on Abrigo, saying that they stole 1.7 million Salesforce records containing personally identifiable information and various internal corporate data.

The threat actor said at the time that they exfiltrated full names, email addresses, phone numbers, employee and account data.

Although a data breach has not been confirmed, some cybersecurity researchers advised banks and credit unions using Abrigo's solutions to rotate the API keys for the Sageworks platform.

A new report from TransUnion has found that 81% of digital fraud attacks target existing customer relationships, with more than half of U.S. businesses reporting increased scam and fraud activity over the past year.

“Identity-based fraud attacks often arise before organizations have sufficient information to establish trust in new customers,” the report says. “While account creation is a critical trust-establishing event, most fraud exposure occurs after the customer relationship has already been established. Different risk patterns appear across account creation, login, and financial transaction activities, especially for AI-enabled fraud. For instance, AI can help fraudsters rapidly generate or modify identities, credentials and interactions to target the weakest controls across the customer lifecycle.”

Most respondents cited synthetic identity fraud, which uses exposed consumer information and AI to craft phony personas, as their top concern over the next two years.

“Forty-three percent of U.S. business leaders said the growing scale and sophistication of fraud is placing significant or severe pressure on their organizations,” TransUnion says. “Synthetic identity fraud is a key concern, with 67% expecting it to increase over the next two years and 53% citing it as the threat they are least prepared to address. In the U.S., 51% of business leaders reported increased scam and authorized fraud activity over the past year. U.S. lenders face an estimated $2.4 billion in exposure tied to synthetic identities as of June 30, 2026.”

The increase is partly due to adversarial use of AI tools, which allow attackers to drastically improve the scale and sophistication of social engineering attacks.

“AI has fundamentally changed the economics of fraud by automating activities that once required significant human effort, including creating identities, generating content, and targeting victims,” TransUnion says. “This allows fraudsters to accelerate and scale their attacks faster than organizations can adapt their detection capabilities and mitigation strategies.

TransUnion has the story: https://newsroom.transunion.com/81-of-suspected-digital-fraud-attacks-target-existing-customer-relationships-transunion-finds/

A suspected South Asian cyber-espionage group has been observed pairing native Windows tools with a custom remote access trojan (RAT) dubbed PapRAT to maintain access to targeted organizations.

Cara Lin of Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs detailed the campaign in research published on November 2, attributing it with high confidence to Bitter, also tracked as TA397, based on lure filenames, command-and-control (C2) patterns, file metadata and malware analysis.

FortiGuard Labs tracked the campaign over several months and it described the targets as South Asian organizations, though its telemetry maps also show activity in Southeast Asia and South Korea. Lure files referred to a bilateral meeting request, an ambassador's letter about the 11th Belt and Road Summit and a 2026 gala dinner invitation.

Read more on Bitter: Middle East Hack-for-Hire Operation Traced to South Asian Cyber Espionage Group

Three Infection Chains, One Without a Malware Binary

The first chain took a living-off-the-land approach: a malicious Windows shortcut (LNK) file abused the built-in ftp.exe utility to run scripts and create scheduled tasks.

Those tasks used curl to fetch fresh commands from attacker servers, and the chain deployed no traditional malware executable. FortiGuard Labs said operators could change their instructions on the server without pushing a new binary.

"When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on," said Shane Barney, CISO at Keeper Security. He argued for least-privilege access, tighter limits on native scripting engines and the removal of standing administrative rights.

The other two chains delivered PapRAT through Windows Installer (MSI) packages, one hidden with a decoy spreadsheet in a virtual hard disk (VHDX) image and the other fetched via an internet shortcut in a RAR archive.

PapRAT Shifts to Rust and Pulls In WmRAT

The C++ build of PapRAT posed as a Microsoft component, beaconed over plaintext HTTP and supported eight commands, including remote shell access, file transfers and screenshots. A Rust variant obtained more recently switched to HTTPS and added three more, for PowerShell execution, pausing and exiting.

In the third chain, PapRAT downloaded WmRAT, a C++ RAT previously documented by other researchers, which FortiGuard Labs cited as a further indicator linking the campaign to Bitter.

Jason Soroko, senior fellow at certificate lifecycle management firm Sectigo, said the Windows-tools route meant "a search for PapRAT alone could miss part of the campaign." He warned that deleting the first implant found might not remove the attacker.

FortiGuard's recommendations included handling unexpected LNK files, internet shortcuts, disk images and MSI installers with care.

In the first chain, though, FortiGuard found no PapRAT at all, only a shortcut file, Windows tools, scripts and scheduled tasks.

771582dac28b.text:
Conclusion

This campaign illustrates how BITTER combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems. The first infection chain uses ftp.exe, curl, scripts, and scheduled tasks without deploying a traditional malware executable, potentially reducing visibility for endpoint controls focused on executable files. The other two chains deliver PapRAT through LNK files and MSI installers, enabling system reconnaissance, file manipulation, secondary payload delivery, screenshot capture, and remote command execution.

PapRAT’s C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in BITTER’s toolset. The Rust variant expands the implant’s command set from eight to eleven, adding PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean exit command. These changes underscore the importance of monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures.

Organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages. Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware.
