Most SOC teams start investigating when a threat alert fires. Analysts triage the alert, piece together context, and begin an investigation, all after something has already happened. That model was built for a world where attackers moved at human speed and relied mostly on known exploits.

That's no longer the case. Two shifts are happening at the same time, and both are changing the day-to-day for the SOC:

• Organizations are shipping more custom code than ever: AI-assisted development means teams are building custom AI applications at unprecedented speed. These apps can contain logic-driven vulnerabilities, such as broken authorization and authentication bypasses, that are impossible to detect with signature-based scanners.

• Attackers are using AI to move faster: Adversaries are using frontier AI models to scan perimeters, find exposed applications, and weaponize vulnerabilities in hours instead of months. AI also lowers the barrier to entry, so more attackers can probe custom applications for weaknesses, at greater scale than ever.

For the SOC, that means the first sign of a logic flaw is often the breach itself. By the time a detection fires, the attacker has already chained their way in.

Human-speed defense can't keep up with AI-powered offense. The only way to keep pace is to use AI to fight AI: find the open door before an attacker walks through it, and investigate at AI speed when someone does. This is critical for incident response in the AI era, and ensuring that the SOC can action at the speed required to defend the enterprise.

Proactive security belongs in the SOC

Gartner® makes the priority clear:

Proactive, continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) with offensive testing will dominate SOC operations, as reactive detection yields an exponential increase in diminishing returns.

Gartner Report, The Security Operations Roadmap to 2030, By Kevin Schmidt, Alex Tytarenko, etc., October 2026. Gartner is a trademark of Gartner, Inc. and/or its affiliates

For the SOC, this means treating validated, exploitable exposures as what they are: attack paths that are proven exploitable. They deserve the same urgency as an active threat, because in the AI era, it's only a matter of time before attackers find them.

That is the job of two Wiz agents working together:

• The Red Agent, our AI-powered attacker that continuously finds and validates exploitable risk across your attack surface, and delivers it as pre-breach, SOC-level alerts.

• The Blue Agent, our AI investigator that works alongside analysts to investigate active threats with full cloud, code, and runtime context, and reach a confident verdict fast.

Red Agent: Pre-breach alerts your SOC can trust

The Red Agent is an AI-powered pentester that enables teams to uncover complex, validated exploitable risks and remove them before attackers find them, at machine speed. It works alongside Wiz ASM to cover all types of risks- from known risks, such as CVEs and misconfigurations, to the unknown, logic-based risks in custom-built applications, like authorization bypasses that signature-based scanners miss.

Every validated exploitable risk Red Agent finds is a ticking time bomb. Red Agent has already proven the exploit works, so the only open question is who gets there next: your team or an attacker. That calls for pre-breach urgency, not a place in the vulnerability backlog.

Each finding arrives with proof of exploitability, reproduction steps, blast radius context from the Security Graph, and a clear owner and remediation guidance from the Green Agent. Instead of waiting for a detection, teams can shut down the attack path first and respond to fewer incidents.

What is most amazing about Red Agent is the way that we can track and get alerting or visibility on endpoints that can be attacked or manipulated from the outside. It tells me: 'You have an endpoint here, you are missing authentication, you have an exposure.' All of those insights are really, really helping me to close gaps fast.

Roy Weiss, Principal DevSecOps, Fireblocks

What a pre-breach SOC alert looks like

In one finding from our Red Agent POV series, Red Agent found a way into a financial services company's production cloud API without authentication, exposing live cloud credentials and the application's full source code.

Without Red Agent, the SOC might first learn about this risk when those credentials are used from an unfamiliar location, and only then start investigating what the attacker touched. With Red Agent, the SOC can act before an attacker finds it, and close the door on what would have been a breach before it can begin.

The pre-breach playbook

When Red Agent finds a validated exploitable risk, here's a playbook the SOC can follow. The steps will feel familiar from incident response, but they happen before a breach instead of after one. Here's how it works for this example:

1. Triage: already done. Red Agent proved the path is exploitable and provides reproduction steps. There's no "is this real?" debate.

2. Scope: has anyone already used this path? Threat hunters check whether a real attacker got there first. Here, that means assuming and looking for any use of the exposed credentials from unexpected sources.

3. Contain: put a stopgap in place. Rotate the credentials and restrict the endpoint. That buys time before the permanent fix.

4. Hand off: Green Agent routes the fix. The Green Agent identifies who owns the affected application and sends them specific fix guidance, so nobody has to hunt for the owner.

5. Verify: Confirm the path is closed. Once the owner ships the fix, Red Agent retests the same exploitable risk to confirm it no longer works.

Blue Agent: AI investigation for active threats

Proactive alerts shrink the attack surface, but no SOC can close every door instantly. When a threat is active, the Blue Agent takes on the manual investigation steps that usually eat an analyst's day: Is this activity legitimate, a security test, or an attack? What is the blast radius? Have our containment actions worked?

The Blue Agent goes beyond surface-level triage. It pulls together context from the Security Graph, code-to-cloud visibility, and runtime signals, and investigates the way a trained incident responder would. Specialized sub-agents answer the questions analysts would otherwise answer manually. For example, the Forensics sub-agent analyzes forensic evidence captured at detection time by the Wiz Sensor to uncover the root cause of suspicious activity and analyze what actually ran on a machine.

The Blue Agent shows its work: the questions it asked, the data it retrieved, and how each signal shaped the verdict. This ensures analysts can stay in control and trust the delivered verdict. With Wiz Workflows, teams can turn verdicts into action, automatically escalating incidents, notifying response teams, or triggering containment playbooks based on verdict and confidence level.

Agentic security for the SOC: proactive first, defensive always

Detection still matters, but it shouldn't be the first time you hear about a critical, validated, exploitable risk. With Red Agent and Blue Agent, your SOC has AI on both sides of the fight.

A Trezor Safe 5 sold by CryptoBilis, the reseller linked to the recent Ledger wallet drains, may contain a hidden implant that steals the owner’s recovery phrase, Trezor has warned.

Trezor is a Czech company and part of SatoshiLabs Group. It has made hardware wallets since 2014, and its current models are the Safe 3, Safe 5 and Safe 7.

“If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onwards and are using it to store funds, please move your funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed as soon as possible,” the company advised.

“If you don’t have a secure hardware wallet available, we recommend temporarily migrating your funds to a software wallet or an exchange you are familiar with. Before sending any funds, carefully check the full receiving address to avoid any mistakes,” it added.

The warning comes at a bad time for crypto holders, a day after Binance disclosed that about $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency had been stolen from its wallets in what analysts believe could be the biggest crypto theft on record.

A customer in Indonesia reported the implant to Trezor on October 28, through the company’s responsible disclosure program. He bought the Safe 5 in August from CryptoBilis’ store on Tokopedia.

At the time of writing, Trezor has still not received the device, but based on the customer’s description and a video interview, it is treating the report as credible and has decided to warn buyers as a precaution.

“Waiting for lab confirmation would leave CryptoBilis buyers exposed in the meantime,” the company explained.

Extra board behind the screen

The customer found an extra circuit board between the wallet’s main board and the screen, with a cellular module and an antenna on it. He told Trezor the board reads what the screen shows, including the wallet backup, and sends that data out over a mobile network whenever the wallet is plugged in.

According to Trezor, the implant appears to work like the ones found in Ledger wallets, though the company won’t compare the two cases further and doesn’t know who is behind the attack.

A Trezor community specialist told users on the r/TREZOR subreddit that the company is still researching the matter and “we are going to tighten security checks on our resellers.”

The Indonesian customer had moved his funds off the wallet before he found the implant, and no other CryptoBilis buyer has reported stolen crypto to Trezor.

The earlier Ledger thefts

Ledger owners in Southeast Asia started reporting drained wallets on October 9. Ledger, which is based in Paris, later said all confirmed cases involved devices bought from CryptoBilis, and that one of them had an unauthorized hardware implant inside. On-chain researchers put the losses at more than $93 million.

Former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès bought a tampered Ledger in Malaysia and found a similar board under its screen. “The implant just monitors what’s shown on the screen, will take note of the seed as it’s shown to you, then transmit it,” he said at the time.

CryptoBilis sold Trezor wallets in the region too. Trezor dropped it as a reseller on October 9 and has since cut down the number of sellers it works with.

Advice for Trezor buyers

Trezor’s guidance covers every model bought from CryptoBilis, whether directly, on Tokopedia or in another store it supplied. “If you’re not sure where your device came from, check the seller name on your receipt or contact Support,” the company suggests.

Restoring the old backup on another device won’t help, Trezor noted, and anyone whose wallet is still unused should not set it up.

Buyers can get a new device or a voucher from the company, and should keep the CryptoBilis unit. Trezor also tells owners not to weigh or open their wallets to check for tampering. The Indonesian customer did spot a weight difference, but small differences can have other causes, and there is no dependable way for users to inspect a device on their own.

“Scammers will likely use this incident to target crypto holders with phishing attacks, such as fake emails, physical letters and phone calls,” Trezor cautioned.

“NEVER share your wallet backup (recovery phrase) with anyone. Trezor Support will never ask for it,” the company concluded.

56ea450d5606.text: The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, pointing the finger at the notorious Lazarus Group as the exchange scrambles to replace stolen funds and reassure customers. In an alert published Saturday, the agency attributed the October 29 attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus, which has made a lucrative career out of relieving crypto exchanges of their digital assets. Pyongyang was already in the frame before the FBI weighed in. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Elliptic had linked the theft to North Korea, with TRM reporting that most of the $6.36 billion haul disappeared in about 20 minutes. Elliptic, which puts the total closer to $6.43 billion, says it has verified that $2.85 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen or seized. According to the FBI, the hackers have started swapping their loot for Ethereum, with investigators expecting them to move the funds through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to make the money harder to trace. The agency has published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the theft and is urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, and other virtual asset providers to block transactions involving the stolen funds. The FBI's attribution comes days after Binance admitted that hackers had made off with roughly $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. According to the exchange, the trouble started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the intruders access to a service container and allowed them to authorize withdrawals they had no business making. Binance has since resumed customer withdrawals, which it suspended after the attack, and says it has now replenished about 95 percent of the stolen assets. The remaining tokens are proving harder to replace because of their limited liquidity. The exchange has committed billions of dollars from its own reserves and emergency funds to cover the losses, with co-CEO Richard Teng promising that customers won't be left footing the bill. That hasn't stopped users from heading for the exits. Binance recorded approximately $3.64 billion in net outflows after withdrawals resumed, although the company said this represented only around 2.1 percent of its reported assets. Replacing the stolen cryptocurrency is one thing. Getting it back from North Korea is another, and investigators face the considerable task of tracking billions of dollars as the hackers attempt to move it beyond their reach. TraderTraitor has form when it comes to raiding crypto exchanges. The North Korean crew has previously been linked to a string of cryptocurrency thefts, including the $308 million attack on Japan's DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024. The group has previously used fake job offers and recruitment exercises to trick employees into handing over access to their employers' systems. As we reported here on Friday, crypto exchange Bitget has now confirmed that the cyberattack where hackers drained $387.5 million worth of digital assets from the exchange’s wallets also has all the hallmarks of a North Korean operation. Its CEO did not go into too much detail, but did say that “IP behavioral patterns and on-chain signatures” suggest it was Kim’s cronies at work. This isn’t Binance's first expensive encounter with hackers, either. Back in 2022, attackers exploited its BNB blockchain bridge and made off with roughly $566 million in tokens. Four years later, the sums have grown considerably. Binance may have the reserves to make its customers whole, but the attackers responsible for the latest raid still have billions of dollars to launder. ®

9fcf57b02726.text:
Cryptocurrency Exchange Binance blamed a compromised DevOps laptop for the loss of $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency last week, adding that it will now cover any losses faced by its customers.

“Binance will cover all losses from the Secure Assets Fund for Users (SAFU) and the company’s funds,” the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an update on Friday, adding that user funds are safe and that it had found no evidence of wallet private-key leakage during its investigation of the incident. It had frozen approximately $3 billion in assets on-chain, temporarily suspending withdrawals while security checks were completed, and revoking the affected address authorization.

Withdrawals are now being restored in phases, initially reopening services across 15 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and XRP. Binance says it has replenished approximately 95% of the affected assets using company funds, while the remaining 5%, comprising less-liquid tokens, could take longer to source.

The exchange said its preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised employee device that enabled access to a service container involved in withdrawals.

“This attack, reportedly on a development engineer, highlights that security is a critical element of every operational stage and personnel level,” said Tim Rawlins, senior advisor and director of security at NCC Group. “When security failures in trusted identities and administrative access can be targeted, attackers can exploit more than just the underlying technical vulnerabilities.”

The FBI has since attributed the attack to North Korean threat actors, identifying the TraderTraitor hacking group as responsible for the theft.

“Given what we know about the activities of countries like North Korea in targeting cryptocurrency, it’s unsurprising that attackers are prepared to invest considerable efforts in targeting individuals who have access to the building blocks of the exchanges,” Rawlins said.

A compromised laptop reaches the withdrawal pipeline

Binance’s preliminary findings suggest that attackers compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop before gaining access to a service container and submitting unauthorized withdrawals. The exchange has yet to publish technical details of the attack, leaving important questions about the precise intrusion path and how the attackers navigated its internal systems.

“A platform holding digital assets should have multiple layers of security to prevent a single compromise, such as an employee’s laptop being hacked, from being sufficient to authorize a transfer,” said Mario Rivas, blockchain and digital assets security lead at NCC Group.

The reported attack is similar to the February 2025 Bybit breach, in which attackers compromised a developer’s machine at Safe{Wallet} and manipulated the interface presented to transaction signers. However, the Binance incident involved a different mechanism.

F6’s Threat Intelligence Department (TID) said the Binance attack reportedly targeted an automated withdrawal process rather than directly deceiving authorized signers. Evgeniy Yanov, Head of Audit and Consulting Department at F6, cited Crypto security platform Blockaid, highlighting a batch of 50 EIP-7702 authorizations within a single transaction, alongside delegation to a malicious “sweeper” contract, as an unusual feature of the reported attack.

“This specific mechanism has not been seen before in large-scale breaches of this size,” Yanov said.

FBI points to North Korea’s TraderTraitor operation

The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit considered part of the broader Lazarus infrastructure.

The agency, working with the US Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, said it had observed the attackers converting stolen assets privately into Ethereum. It warned that the funds could subsequently be laundered through decentralized finance platforms and instant-swap services.

F6’s TID said the attribution was based on a combination of on-chain and off-chain intelligence. “The group’s signature matches previous thefts: small Tornado Cash withdrawals used to fund the operator’s wallet, extensive preparation well before the actual heist, and pre-signed transactions executed in a single burst,” it added.

TID researchers noted similarities with previous North Korean-linked cryptocurrency thefts, including the Bybit and KelpDAO incidents. However, they cautioned that Binance has not independently named the perpetrators and that the full attribution evidence has not been published.

Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

NCC Group’s Rawlins noted that the growing use of AI could help attackers chain vulnerabilities and operational weaknesses together, while organizations increasingly face adversaries willing to invest considerable effort when the potential financial return is substantial. “Good cyber hygiene and effective security fundamentals are key to defending against attacks that many organizations are still missing,” he said.

A new wave of fridge cyberattacks hit supermarket refrigeration systems across five European countries, raising temperatures and causing food losses.

A new wave of fridge cyberattacks has affected supermarket refrigeration systems in several European countries. Fridges and freezers suddenly rose in temperature overnight, with some incidents suspected to be caused by hackers. On Monday, November 2, Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt reported an IT incident affecting dozens of stores in Belgium and Luxembourg. Swedish supermarket chains ICA and Coop also reported similar problems.

“Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt said on Monday that an IT ​incident overnight hit fridges and freezers in dozens of stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish grocers ‌ICA and Coop reported similar temperature spikes, with one store blaming a cyberattack.” Reuters states.

BREAKING: Swedish grocery giant ICA, one of Sweden's largest supermarket chains, says several of its stores have been hit by a cyberattack overnight, causing refrigerators and freezers to be remotely set to 50°C.The incident has likely resulted in large quantities of food… pic.twitter.com/wrcmGHw1qV

— GeoInsider (@InsiderGeo) November 2, 2026

“Problems were discovered at several grocery stores in Sweden overnight Monday.” reported Sweden Herald.

“We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight that affected their refrigeration and freezer systems. Ica is providing support in handling the incident, Ica Group press officer Gustaf Nilsson tells TT.”

The latest incidents follow a similar wave of fridge cyberattacks in France last month. In mid-October, a large cyberattack hit the refrigeration systems of hundreds of French supermarkets, BFMTV revealed. The attackers targeted equipment from the Danish maker Danfoss that many French stores use to regulate their cold. Fresh and frozen stock was destroyed, and the Paris prosecutor says there were also fires.

The method is simple and nasty. Refrigeration systems have a forced defrost function that clears ice buildup, and the attackers appear to have triggered it remotely in a continuous mode, with a temperature setting of 50 degrees. The equipment heated for several hours instead of keeping goods cold, and when staff opened the fridges and freezers in the morning, a sector source told BFM, “a wave of heat” came out.

The attack caused fires and food losses. However, cybersecurity consultant Emil Olofsson of Integrity 360 told Swedish news agency TT that temperatures reached 80°C in some cases and several units caught fire. This figure differs from the one reported by police.

ICA Kvantum in Sjöbo said on Facebook that a cyberattack caused the refrigeration problems. ICA Hägerstensåsen in Stockholm was also reportedly affected. According to the Sjöbo store, the temperature inside its fridges and freezers rose to 50°C.

In Belgium, Delhaize detected unusual temperature increases in its refrigeration systems on Monday. Spokesperson Sarah De Meester said the company is investigating the incident.

Stephan Moelans, CEO of Sabcobel, the company that manages Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told news agency Belga that hackers had switched the units’ evaporators to defrost mode. His office declined to comment to Reuters. Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium through a franchise system, said five stores had suffered attacks on their refrigeration systems. Meanwhile, Belgian newspaper Le Soir reported that dozens of Delhaize and Carrefour stores were affected.

UPDATE: REFRIGERATION DISRUPTIONS SPREAD ACROSS EUROPE – SWEDEN AND BELGIUM AFFECTEDIN SWEDEN:• At least 6 ICA supermarkets affected by suspected refrigeration system hacks.• Coop has now CONFIRMED that 6 of its stores in central Sweden are also affected.• Freezer… https://t.co/a3oGMrGdmz pic.twitter.com/8Q3CFDDLhT

— Coffe Report (@CoffeReport) November 2, 2026

It follows a similar attack in France last month. Police said hackers seized control of the cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets and raised temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit), which caused fires and food losses. Cybersecurity consultant Emil Olofsson of Integrity 360 told TT, Sweden’s news agency, that temperatures there reached 80 degrees and some units caught fire, a figure that differs from the police number.

In Belgium, Delhaize noticed temperature increases in its cooling systems on Monday, spokesperson Sarah De Meester said, and the company is investigating. Stephan Moelans, CEO of the refrigeration firm Sabcobel, which runs Delhaize’s systems, told the news agency Belga it was a cyberattack that switched the units’ evaporators to defrost mode. His office declined to comment to Reuters. Colruyt Group, which runs Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops had their fridge systems attacked, and Le Soir reported that dozens of Delhaize and Carrefour stores were affected.

Ahold also reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month, after it detected suspicious activity in its infrastructure. Nothing in the reporting ties that report to Monday’s incident.

Fridges and freezers at dozens of supermarkets in Belgium and Sweden overheated overnight in a suspected cyberattack, similar to the one that hit French stores three weeks ago. Delhaize calls it an "IT incident."Delhaize said about 40 of its Belgian stores were affected… pic.twitter.com/qzw6uDybWb

— The Informant (@theinformant_x) November 2, 2026

In Sweden, John Billow, head of the national cybersecurity centre, told Reuters his team was working on several incidents involving refrigeration systems in grocery stores around the country. An ICA Kvantum store in Sjöbo said on Facebook that a cyberattack caused its problems, and an ICA store told its followers that its temperatures had been “hacked” overnight and set to 50 degrees. Fifty degrees is fine for a beach and poor for ice cream. That store later said it had opened.

At ICA Baronen in Stockholm, a notice said all the freezers were broken because of a cyberattack. The sales manager said the attack came at 2 a.m. and staff noticed it at 5:30 a.m. ICA Hägerstensåsen in Stockholm was reportedly hit too.

ICA said only a limited number of stores were affected and that it is helping them deal with the incident. However, press officer Gustaf Nilsson did not say how many stores were involved.

Coop told Swedish news agencies Aftonbladet and TT that six stores in central Sweden had similar problems. Press manager Carlos Cancino said it was still unclear whether any food would need to be thrown away or whether the refrigeration units had simply stopped working or had switched to heating mode. He also did not rule out further incidents affecting other stores.

An Estonian supermarket chain was also affected. Its refrigeration systems were reportedly set to 50°C, technology provider Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR. CEO Jann Mutso did not reveal the name of the supermarket chain, saying: “This is very recent. It happened this morning.”

How did the attackers get in? In France, Olofsson says they obtained login details for the control systems, which were exposed directly to the internet. He says the attack targeted a product that controls the cooling systems and that the hack isn’t very complicated, so amateurs may have carried it out.

Billow says Swedish authorities have noticed in recent weeks that quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices exist in Sweden, and they’ve been clear that these must be updated or patched.

Refrigerators and heating systems, security cameras and alarm networks were once largely mechanical, and now they can be monitored and controlled remotely. That gives cybercriminals new openings. Authorities haven’t said who was behind last month’s incidents, and nobody has claimed responsibility.

The Sweden Herald reported that the cause of the attacks on Swedish supermarkets remains unknown.

Update 20:00 Rome Time

The company at the center of the European supermarket refrigeration cyberattacks is Danfoss the same company whose refrigeration systems were targeted during the cyberattacks in France a few weeks ago.Danfoss says the incidents are primarily exploiting vulnerabilities in… pic.twitter.com/3tDNVMOyhn

— GeoInsider (@InsiderGeo) November 2, 2026

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, fridge cyberattacks)

Clive Robinson • November 2, 2026 11:45 AM

@ Jeff, ALL,

With regards,

“More bugs aren’t necessarily being found because there’s more of them being created than before, the more likely explanation is that the bugs were already there and now we’re closing them at the fastest pace in history! “

Actually both points are true…

Yes we are finding “new instances of bugs from known classes of bugs” at a much higher rate.

But that does not mean we are finding “new classes of bugs” (ie black swans).

But also “vibe coding” by AI is certainly generating “new instances of bugs” at a more alarming rate.

It’s why quite a few employers are now seeing “laying off humans with AI” as being not just horrifically unprofitable, but extremely dangerous to the business.

Yes, AI has niche advantages, but those niches are invariably not general in nature.

Even China is begining to see the dangers of even low cost AI.

None of this was unpredictable and quite a few have called it that way. However when you’ve handed over everything for a few tulip bulbs you had better be sure not only are they going to grow but that people are going to by the result sufficient to pay a “Return on Investment”(ROI).

Right now the ROI in “General AI” is not a certainty or even a likely hood based on the current economy…

Then there is “clearing up the mess of harms” the rush for AI has created… How many billions if not trillions that is going to cost companies that are already by normal forecasting methods “bankrupt”…

9a7af66c50a2.text:
Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis has suffered a cybersecurity incident that led to a data breach.

According to the company’s Friday announcement, the incident is unrelated to the recent Binance hack.

What was accessed?

In October, the company detected external attackers using “offensive agentic techniques” to gain access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools.

“Based on the evidence available to date, we have found no indication that these incidents resulted in the unauthorized access of investigation content (such as graphs, notes, or cases), transaction or query results, passwords in clear text, MFA secrets, or user session tokens,” Chainalysis stated.

However, the attackers managed to access some customer (user) IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on the company’s platform.

Chainalysis did not elaborate further on the offensive agentic techniques used by the attackers.

A key player in crypto crime investigations

Because blockchains like Bitcoin record every transaction publicly (but pseudonymously), Chainalysis clusters addresses, links them to real-world entities such as exchanges, darknet markets, or sanctioned groups, and flags risky flows.

The company has been involved in investigating the money flows following the massive Binance hack last week, which has been attributed to the North Korean cybercrime group TraderTraitor.

“Our investigators are observing never-seen-before laundering patterns with the stolen funds from the Binance exploit,” Chainalysis shared.

“Thousands of transactions in a short period suggest that the attackers are using automation to obscure the trail of funds. Rather than simply moving funds onward, they repeatedly circulate them among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses involved earlier in the sequence.”

Chainalysis’ response

Chainalysis sent out an email alert to impacted customers, urging them to be on the lookout for unexpected password reset requests or authentication prompts. The company also advised them to enable two-factor authentication on their accounts (if they haven’t already).

Among its customers are crypto exchanges and banks, as well as law enforcement and government agencies around the world. Unauthorized access to customers’ names and contact information puts them at heightened risk of social engineering attacks.

Third-party cybersecurity experts have been called in to help with the investigation and to review the security of Chainalysis’ platform, discover vulnerabilities and, in general, strengthen the company’s defenses.

“We are in the process of determining the records for your organization that were accessed and will provide a detailed breakdown as soon as that analysis is complete,” it told affected customers.

3cf9f4b6ad79.text:
A malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension distributed through the Cursor marketplace attempted to install a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor on developers’ machines, potentially giving attackers remote access to systems holding source code, credentials and other sensitive information.

“Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace,” Cursor said in a security notice.

Cursor removed the compromised versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, after discovering they had been available in its VS Code extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29.

The company said the malicious code attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable local SSH access, and establish a reverse tunnel to an attacker-controlled server.

“These malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic,” Cursor added in the notice. The affected versions were available for Windows and macOS.

Anthropic subsequently clarified how the tampered extension had been distributed. In a post on X, Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic’s technical staff, said the incident did not involve a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor had used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish the modified extension, he said.

“The versions on our official channels are not affected, and this only impacts Cursor users,” Rieseberg wrote. Anthropic said it was working with Cursor on the incident.

Cursor and Anthropic had not responded to requests for comment by publication time.

Malware ran without user interaction

Security company Phorion, which analysed the compromised extension, found that malicious code had been inserted at the beginning of its JavaScript file. It ran as soon as the extension loaded, before its normal activation code.

“The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire,” Phorion said.

The malware attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to the user’s authorized_keys file and establish a connection to a remote server. It also created scripts and startup entries intended to keep the connection available after a system restart, the company added.

Phorion identified a flaw in the macOS code. The malware tried to check whether Remote Login was disabled using a system command that required administrator privileges. When run without those privileges, the command returned an access error rather than the expected status. The malware consequently skipped the attempt to enable SSH.

Phorion also found an error in the Windows code that could prevent its SSH service setup command from running correctly.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate analysis, detailed the information the malware collected, including machine names, usernames, operating systems, working directories, and Git email addresses.

“It also looks for environment-variable names containing terms such as KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP, keeping up to forty matches,” Microsoft wrote in the analysis. It said the code collected matching variable names, not their values.

Removing the extension may not be enough

Cursor said enabling the local SSH service would generally fail without administrator privileges on affected Windows and macOS machines. However, the extension could still add the attacker’s SSH key, install persistence mechanisms, and send host information to the attacker.

The company warned that uninstalling the extension alone might not remove these components because the malware placed scripts outside the extension’s installation directory.

Steve Povolny, vice president of AI strategy and security research at Exabeam, said the planted SSH key made cleanup particularly important. “Removing the extension only sends the visitor away while the spare key stays on the hook,” he said.

Povolny recommended checking authorised SSH keys on machines accessible to affected developers, rotating potentially exposed credentials, and reviewing logs for logins using unfamiliar keys. Developers often have access to source code, cloud accounts, and production systems, he said, making a compromised workstation a potential route to other enterprise resources.

Phorion also advised checking the SSH key’s fingerprint rather than relying only on the comment svc-telemetry attached to it.

Questions raised about extension security

Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said enterprises should treat extension marketplaces as part of the software supply chain.

“An extension marketplace is effectively another software supply chain,” Kadakia said. “When malicious code can reach developers through what appears to be a legitimate, routine update, the traditional assumption that software from a trusted marketplace is safe starts to break down.”

He recommended stronger publisher verification, checks on package integrity, and controls over which extensions and versions developers can install.

Kadakia also called for extension allowlisting, controlled updates, endpoint monitoring, and restrictions on outbound connections. He said short-lived credentials, segregated development environments, and limited access to sensitive infrastructure could reduce the impact of a compromised developer machine. Cursor said it removed the malicious versions, temporarily shut down its marketplace, audited access, rotated keys, and rebuilt the marketplace before restoring the service.

d8170e4cf140.text:
They’re meant for a family member who I’ll call John, for privacy reasons. John lives in California and has made small donations to Democrats. I live in New York and have made no political donations at all. We have different names, phone numbers, and bank accounts—a distinction that has apparently proven difficult for a substantial portion of the American political fundraising industry.

For years, I diligently opted out. I’ve replied “STOP” 49 times since 2021, by my phone’s count. Sometimes “Stop2End,” when that was the magic word. In November 2025, I told Jon Ossoff’s campaign some version of “stop.” It did not stop. Since then, I’ve received 13 more texts boosting his campaign, from nine different numbers.

When the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee texted to inform me that Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden were calling me personally to action, I replied “eat shit.” That didn’t work either.

Exhausted, I decided this month to figure out what the hell was going on. Why did so many campaigns have my number? Why did they think it belonged to someone else? And why wouldn’t they fucking stop?

For starters, I downloaded my Messages history and pulled out the political texts I’ve received in recent years. Since March 2022, I’ve gotten 1,735, from 812 different phone numbers. By any measure, this is simply too many texts—nearly none of which were meant for me.

James Carville had written 27 times, soliciting money for at least a dozen political organizations. Ken Burns wanted help electing Jacky Rosen, then Roy Cooper, then Sherrod Brown. On April 2, 2025, the day after Cory Booker finished his 25-hour Senate floor speech, I received the same first-person appeal from “Cory” three times in less than two hours, sent by three different fundraising operations.

The thing is that John—the person these campaigns had me confused with—isn’t a particularly big donor. Federal Election Commission records show roughly 160 contributions since 2017, totaling about $1,700. The median gift was $6. This year, John donated six times, for a total of $51.

In the same period, my phone received 725 fundraising texts literally begging for his money.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee alone sent 60 of them—22 in the first 20 days of October—from 28 different numbers. My relative had given it $5, once, in 2020. The DCCC sent another 41 messages; it had received $8. House Majority PAC, which has never received a dime from John that I could find, kept offering to multiply contributions by as much as 900 percent.

I understand the logic of these messages on some level. They are cheap, and the strategy isn’t all that different from how a lot of scams work—spray out messages and pray someone will bite. You don’t need many people to respond for it to pay off. What I couldn’t understand, though, was how I’d gotten wrapped up in all of this. I didn’t have to look far for the answer.

Almost every text contained a link that, after a few redirects, led to ActBlue, the platform Democrats use to process donations. Helpfully, many of those links carried tracking codes—strings of letters and numbers identifying the fundraising appeal, the message being sent, and sometimes where the campaign got the recipient’s contact information.

An October DCCC link, for instance, contained acq_sms.p2p_fr_2026.10.13_b1_dccc_rent_4mtch_st. Squint a little and you can make out abbreviations for acquisition (“acq”), peer-to-peer fundraising (“p2p_fr”), and a rented list (“dccc_rent”). But one word kept appearing in these strings across messages from otherwise unrelated campaigns: Sterling.

Sterling Data Company is a relatively small firm that uses AI to help Democrats find people likely to give them money. In 2022, Forbes reported that Sterling had assembled a database of roughly 30 million political donors, with hundreds of details about some of them, including what cars they drove and what they watched on Netflix. Sterling says it uses that information to predict who might donate to a particular candidate.

Sterling appears to get much of its information from other data brokers, combining details about people’s age, location, politics, and donation histories into voter profiles that campaigns can buy or rent.

Of the 725 texts I’d received this year, nearly half contained tracking codes that appeared to reference Sterling. They came from dozens of PACs and campaigns, including the DCCC, DSCC, James Talarico, and Mark Kelly.

FEC records show that a Biden joint fundraising committee paid Sterling about $1.87 million for donor lists over four months beginning in November 2023. Around the same time, a text from the committee reached my phone with a code containing strl2b.

The DSCC’s first reported payment to Sterling came on November 22, 2023—the very day I received one of its texts tagged STL2. According to FEC data, the committee has continued paying Sterling, including roughly $250,000 this summer, which preceded another wave of Sterling-tagged texts.

Those recent texts all appeared to link back to a common platform. Dozens of campaigns had their own web addresses, but I could see that they used nearly identical software and tracking codes, often ending in tier1. Sterling’s own website advertises something it calls “Tier 1 contact data intelligence,” though I couldn’t establish whether the two were connected or who ran the system. Still, the breadcrumbs were leading me to suspect that, at some point, a Sterling database mixup had lumped John together with my phone number.

“High-frequency solicitation is a necessary evil,” Martin Kurucz, Sterling’s CEO, tells me when I ask about all of this. “Few people give, so every campaign chases the same donors, and texting at scale works too well to skip.”

Kurucz declined to discuss Sterling’s proprietary data but confirmed that the company handles the texting itself and can rent the same record to multiple campaigns. Sterling limits how often individuals can be contacted, he said, though he didn’t specify what those limits are.

“No contact database is perfect,” Kurucz says. Even matches made with moderate confidence are generally accurate enough to be worth using, he says. Wrong numbers tend to drop out of circulation because the recipients don’t engage.

Kurucz wouldn’t confirm that Sterling has caused the deluge of misdirected text messages my way, but he also didn’t deny it. Instead he offered some advice for making them stop: Don’t respond at all.

I found that there’s another way out: lawsuits. At least two people have successfully gotten a settlement out of Democratic organizations over apparently misdirected campaign texts, which presumably included never being contacted again.

That seems like a lot of work, though. Meanwhile neither of those lawsuits established how the wrong names got attached to their numbers. I still don’t know for sure how mine got mixed up with John’s. But the outcome is the same: The DSCC now texts me more often than my mother. Replying “eat shit” another hundred times won’t change that.

Blockchain analytics company Chainalysis has announced falling victim to an AI-driven cyberattack that resulted in a data breach.

“This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools,” the company said.

The incident, it pointed out, is not related to the recent $6.36 billion Binance heist that was blamed on North Korean hackers.

According to Chainalysis, the attack did not result in the compromise of investigation content, transaction or query results, passwords in clear text, or other credentials and secrets.

“Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users,” Chainalysis said.

The company continues to investigate the full scope of the data breach and has not disclosed how many individuals were potentially affected.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“Our teams have been working around the clock to investigate unauthorized activity, patch vulnerabilities, and harden our systems,” it said.

Chainalysis noted that it has observed an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyberattacks, as many other tech platforms have been hit in recent weeks.

The company has been working with external cybersecurity experts and LLMs to review its security posture and strengthen it against these evolving threats.

Because names and email addresses were compromised, it recommends that users watch for unexpected authentication prompts and password reset requests, and make sure they have MFA enabled.

Hackers reportedly hit Ukraine ‘s and Russia ‘s emergency alert apps, sending fake nuclear and attack warnings and raising concerns over public safety.

Ukraine and Russia both said on Sunday night that hackers had compromised their emergency alert apps and used them to send fake warnings about air raids and other attacks, including nuclear threats. The BBC reported the incident, but neither side’s claims have been independently confirmed.

Shortly before 11 p.m. local time (9 p.m. GMT), Ukraine’s widely used Air Alarm app sent the highest-level air raid warnings across the country. Some people, including residents of Kyiv, also received alerts about possible radiation, chemical attacks and street fighting. A message posted on Telegram said the app had likely been targeted by a cyberattack, confirmed there was no radiation threat and urged people to remain calm.

“Shortly before 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT), Ukraine’s widely usedair raid app sent red-level air raid warnings nation-wide, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.” reports BBC.

“The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.” an alert on Telegram read.

The false alerts started at about 22:47 with a message that a radiation threat had been declared in Kyiv. At 22:48 came a message in Russian saying a nuclear alert would cover all of Ukraine and not to worry because “it’s Oreshnik flying”. Oreshnik is a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile that can carry nuclear or conventional warheads, and Russia has the world’s biggest nuclear arsenal, with President Vladimir Putin repeatedly hinting he’s open to using every weapon available.

Two more alerts arrived at 22:49. One, in Ukrainian, warned of a chemical attack on Kyiv and told people not to go outside, and the other said street fighting was taking place in the city. Red, orange and green messages reached phones, and at 23:53 users got all-clear messages, each declaring one of the Kyiv threats over.

A Ukrainian intelligence body, which the BBC calls the Central Intelligence Agency, said there had been a failure in the app and urged people to use other sources of information. It added that the alerts triggered a radiation hazard signal on loudspeakers in the Lviv region, with no real threat.

“The Air Alert app is supported by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, and informs users instantly about the beginning and end of defence alerts. The ministry said it temporarily disabled the app for maintenance after it had “apparently been compromised”. states BBC.

“While the false alerts were quickly contained, cybersecurity experts suggested it was a new line in apparent Russian cyberattacks.”

The temporary shutdown of the Air Alert app also carries significant risks, even if it lasts only a short time. During an outage, users may not receive timely warnings about incoming attacks, leaving them with less time to reach shelters or take protective measures. This is particularly dangerous in a country where missile and drone attacks can happen with little warning.

The incident also highlights a difficult security trade-off: disabling a compromised alert system may prevent attackers from spreading false warnings, but it can temporarily remove a critical channel for delivering real emergency information. Any shutdown therefore needs reliable backup channels, such as sirens, official messaging services and other emergency communication systems.

Regional leaders tried to calm people. Svitlana Onyshchuk, head of the Ivano-Frankivsk region, said everything was calm, even though the app had shown a red-level alert for her region from 22:50 to 23:57. Natalya Zabolotna, her counterpart in Vinnytsia, confirmed a cyberattack on the app and warned people not to click the link in the message, which could be phishing.

Ukraine’s Centre for Countering Disinformation has advice for when the app isn’t working: turn on smartphone notifications, pay attention to sirens, and read only official sources. Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament and a member of President Zelensky’s Servant of the People party, said the attack caused no panic. Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, are used to practically non-stop alerts, he told the BBC, and the message in Russian aroused suspicion at once. The attackers picked a language that gave them away.

A few hours later, Russia’s ministry of emergency situations said its own app had suffered “a massive cyberattack” that sent fake information to the public. Ukrainian outlet UNN reported that the hack sent fake nuclear threat alerts inside Russia, citing Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating in Russian-held territory. A screenshot Atesh shared on Telegram, described as purported, claimed nuclear warheads mounted on Ukrainian P1-Sun attack drones had been launched at all regions of Russia, opened with a “risk of getting lively” warning and told residents to stock up on three weeks of food and hide. The alert also had profanities.

Russia said it was still restoring the app but claimed the hack had not affected its wider alert system. It said people could still receive warnings through sirens, loudspeakers, text messages, TV and radio. The false alerts appeared minutes before a local ceasefire in Ukraine’s Kherson region ended on Sunday night. The truce had allowed civilians to leave Russian-occupied Oleshky. Although the fake warnings were quickly stopped, experts see the attack as a worrying escalation.

“I think it’s the first time it’s happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won’t be the last,” Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service’s Newsday programme.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Ukraine)

6689b7a4ef6d.text:
The disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 placed immediate pressure on organizations running PHP. Both vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated remote code execution, including in products and appliances where PHP is embedded, and updates depend on third-party vendors [1].

Early guidance focused on patching internet-facing systems and monitoring for behavior associated with successful exploitation, including unexpected command execution, Webroot changes and outbound connections from PHP servers.

Darktrace observed widespread scanning across monitored environments involving hundreds of distinct source IP addresses that public reporting has associated with activity targeting the PHP vulnerabilities. The volume of scanning was significantly greater than the evidence available for successful exploitation. For analysts, that distinction is important. Scanning demonstrates interest in exposed infrastructure; establishing compromise requires evidence of subsequent behavior on the targeted system, including command execution, file modification or unexpected outbound communication.

PHP is not an isolated example. Imperva subsequently demonstrated remote code execution against a vulnerable Node.js build through malicious Brotli data, reproducing execution through compressed HTTP responses and configured request parsers. The same inputs were rejected by the patched runtime. Imperva linked its Node2Shell and PHP2Shell research to the increasing speed of vulnerability discovery and exploit development. [2]

While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent with zero-day exploitation activity, representing a 64% increase compared to historic data. This increase has not been confirmed as related to the PHP vulnerabilities. Darktrace’s behavioral approach is designed to detect anomalous activity without relying solely on rules written for a specific exploit. Comparable increases were observed around the Log4j disclosure and other globally significant vulnerability disclosures.

AI-assisted vulnerability research

The PHP disclosure arrives as AI systems have become more capable at vulnerability research [3]. OpenAI launched Daybreak in June 2026, combining GPT-5.5-Cyber, Codex Security and partnerships with security researchers and software maintainers. OpenAI says its models have been applied to discovering and generating patches for vulnerabilities in browsers, network infrastructure, FreeBSD and the Linux kernel. Darktrace joined the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program in June to explore how OpenAI's cyber capabilities could be integrated within Darktrace products and services [4][10].

OpenAI reported in August that Codex Security Cloud had analyzed more than 30 million commits across more than 30,000 codebases. According to OpenAI, Cloudflare uses models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code and combines findings with live traffic and security signals to assess whether affected routes are active or receiving suspicious traffic, with proposed mitigations and patches remaining subject to customer review [5][6].

Faster discovery still leaves defenders with the work of locating affected software, testing fixes and completing remediation. The PHP case shows that gap clearly, particularly when vulnerable runtimes are embedded inside other products.

Enterprise agents as an attack surface

Darktrace Signal Labs has also examined how a trusted enterprise agent could be abused after an attacker has already obtained access to an environment. In a controlled simulation, researchers demonstrated that, in that post-compromise scenario, the Claude platform’s memory stores feature could be abused to establish a live C2 channel between an external operator and internal Claude Code agents. The external operator was able to dynamically assign network discovery, credential access, and data exfiltration tasks to the agents via this C2 channel. Detection of the agents’ activities relied on the correlation of process creation and network traffic activity from agent harness processes, alongside behavioral analysis to identify deviations from expected behavior. Darktrace has not claimed it observed this memory-store command-and-control technique in operational attacks [7].

AI-assisted attacks in Japan

Evidence from Japan indicates AI being used for vulnerability scanning and attacks outside controlled research. On 21 October, JPCERT/CC published findings from an investigation into recent unauthorized access incidents affecting organizations in Japan. JPCERT/CC states that it confirmed attackers had used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and conduct attacks through APIs. According to JPCERT/CC, its examination of attack infrastructure found evidence of Android application analysis, API discovery and testing for weaknesses including server-side request forgery, and the infrastructure also targeted services intended for users outside Japan [8].

JPCERT/CC does not identify ARTEX by name in that publication. The named ARTEX attribution comes from separate investigations, including Microsoft's analysis of Storm-0940.

AI in offensive operations

Microsoft describes ARTEX as an open-source, multi-agent penetration-testing system capable of automating activity with limited human interaction. Microsoft reported that Storm-0940, which it assesses to be a China state-aligned actor active since 2021, used ARTEX against hundreds of organizations, and Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise [9].

Microsoft observed ARTEX accelerating scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse. Several ARTEX-driven operations reached privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting. Following the ConnectWise compromise, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate to more than 2,250 tenants at rates of up to 2,900 attempts per minute [9].

Darktrace Threat Research found activity in its own telemetry involving infrastructure later associated with the campaign. On 13 October, Darktrace recorded failed authentication activity involving 144.172.64[.]128, one of the addresses Microsoft later identified as performing sign-ins and Microsoft Graph activity in ConnectWise customer environments. Darktrace analysis identified 65 failed authentication attempts in around 20 minutes.

The telemetry establishes repeated failed authentication from infrastructure later associated with the campaign. It does not establish ARTEX execution or successful compromise. At the time of observation, Microsoft's later attribution was unavailable. Analysts therefore had the behavior itself: repeated failed authentication from the same source over a short period, together with any related identity, application or network activity inside the environment.

Microsoft documented a wider password-spray campaign against 327 accounts across eight organizations between 10 and 14 October. It recorded more than 151,000 failed logons, including more than 111,000 on 11 October, but no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call or directory change from that campaign. Microsoft also reported that most Storm-0940 targeting was unsuccessful [9].

Where the actor progressed beyond authentication, Microsoft observed service-principal sign-ins followed by Graph and directory operations. Activity included reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to modify privileges. Microsoft recommends correlating service-principal sign-ins with Graph activity, directory changes and resource access [9].

Behavior before attribution

The PHP and ARTEX cases begin with different information. PHP defenders knew which software required urgent remediation but initially had limited information about exploitation. Process execution, file modification and outbound communication could still provide evidence of compromise.

The PHP and ARTEX observations also illustrate the difference between volume and impact. Darktrace observed broad scanning around the PHP disclosure, while the ARTEX-associated infrastructure produced concentrated authentication activity. Neither observation independently demonstrates compromise and in each case examining the behavior that follows the initial interaction is the investigative clue.

The Darktrace ARTEX-related observation began with authentication behavior. Microsoft publicly attributed the source infrastructure eight days later. That attribution added context, but it did not change what had originally been recorded in the environment.

AI is now present at several points in this cycle. Daybreak applies models to vulnerability discovery and remediation. Darktrace Signal Labs demonstrated how a trusted enterprise agent could be co-opted in a controlled environment. JPCERT/CC confirmed AI-assisted vulnerability scanning and API attacks in recent incidents. Microsoft documented ARTEX being used by Storm-0940 in active operations [4][7][8][9].

Microsoft's findings also show why scale and impact must be assessed separately. One ARTEX-associated campaign produced more than 151,000 failed logons without successful access, while other operations reached privileged cloud access in less than three hours. Security teams have to distinguish high-volume attempts from activity that progresses through authentication, privilege changes and resource access.

The evidence required to assess these cases remains familiar: authentication records, process execution, application and directory changes, file activity and network communication. AI can increase the rate at which those behaviors occur. Defenders still need to establish their sequence and impact.

Credit to Emma Foulger, Sam Lister, Dylan Evans, Moishe Tajtelbaum

References

[1] NCSC-NL, php2shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), 21 October 2026. https://github.com/NCSC-NL/php2shell

[2] Imperva, https://www.imperva.com/blog/node2shell-from-brotli-data-to-remote-code-execution/

[3] Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2026-151/

[4] OpenAI, Daybreak: Tools for securing every organization in the world, 22 June 2026. https://openai.com/index/daybreak-securing-the-world/

[5] OpenAI Developers, Scaling cyber defenders with Daybreak, 21 August 2026. https://developers.openai.com/blog/scaling-cyber-defenders-with-daybreak

[6] OpenAI, Cloudflare links vulnerability discovery to defense with OpenAI, 21 October 2026. https://openai.com/index/cloudflare-cyber/

[7] Darktrace Signal Labs, Shared Memories as a Covert C2 Channel, draft research supplied for review.

[8] JPCERT/CC, Recent AI-Assisted Cyber Attacks in Japan: Investigating Attack Infrastructure and Techniques, 21 October 2026. https://blogs.jpcert.or.jp/en/2026/10/web_api_attacks.html

[9] Microsoft Security Research and Microsoft Threat Intelligence, AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise, 21 October 2026. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/10/21/storm-0940-uses-artex-agentic-ai-connectwise-supply-chain-compromise/

[10] Darktrace, Advancing the Use of Frontier AI in Cybersecurity: Darktrace Joins the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program to Explore Defensive AI Integrations, 22 June 2026. https://www.darktrace.com/blog/advancing-the-use-of-frontier-ai-in-cybersecurity-darktrace-joins-the-openai-daybreak-cyber-partner-program-to-explore-defensive-ai-integrations

The maintainer of BTCPay Server, an open-source cryptocurrency payment processor, has urged users to install the latest version as hackers have been draining “hot wallets” on instances running older versions.

Operators were initially advised to shut down their servers pending a full investigation into the unauthorized Bitcoin and Litecoin payments.

The BTCPay Server project provides businesses with a self-hosted payment processing solution that allows them to accept Bitcoin and other digital assets directly into their own wallets, eliminating payment intermediaries or paying platform processing fees.

It handles checkout invoices and payment verification, including payments over the Lightning Network.

Early Monday, the maintainer said it had “identified an attack vector targeting instances running version 2.4.1 (July 23, 2026) or earlier” and strongly urged users to update to version 2.4.7.

BTCPay founder Nicolas Dorier said the attacks did not target public servers. The investigation focused on determining how the threat actor was able to log in as an administrator to instances running versions older than 2.4.2.

On October 29, the company disclosed a critical vulnerability discovered via Anthropic’s Frontier OSS scanner, which prompted the release of version 2.4.7 as an emergency security update.

However, Dorier said that there were clues that the attacker used vulnerabilities in BTCPay Server versions earlier than 2.4.2, released on August 7, which the project later confirmed.

“Our incident response investigation identified an attack vector targeting instances running versions 2.4.1 (Jul 23, 2026) or older,” BTCPay Server says.

“We have no credible reports of hot wallet drains for users running the latest 2.4.7 release. We again urge everyone to keep their BTCPay Server updated.”

The BTCPay project began receiving reports of theft yesterday evening (UTC) and responded by asking VPS hosting providers to take affected server instances offline as a precaution to protect customers.

In a security alert today, the project maintainer said that it is currently responding to affected users and continues to receive incident reports. Users who lost funds as a result of the recent attacks are asked to send details to security@btcpayserver.org, and to report the losses to local authorities.

Impacted users should update to version 2.4.7 through Server Settings → Maintenance → Update.

For Docker installations, administrators can update BTCPay Server by logging in over SSH, running sudo su -, changing to the deployment directory with cd btcpayserver-docker, and executing ./btcpay-update.sh.

If running 2.4.1 or older, it is recommended to take the instance offline as soon as possible.

Update [10:23 EST]: Article update with information from the security incident report BTCPay Server published earlier today.

In 2024, AT&T lost sensitive communication logs of 109 million customers in a massive data breach. Call logs can reveal a lot about you, like your closest relationships, where you live and work, and your daily routine.

109 million people (nearly a third of Americans) suffered a massive data breach in April 2024 that exposed their AT&T communication logs.

AT&T lost sensitive information including phone numbers, call and text counts, call durations, and location data from May to October 2022, and January 2023, meaning the data was approximately two years old at the time of the breach, impacting both current and former customers.

AT&T said the records didn’t contain call content, customer names, or Social Security numbers. That’s less reassuring than it sounds, because even on their own, call logs reveal a lot about you.

What are call logs?

Every call, text, and data session generates records inside your carrier’s network. The two kinds that matter here are:

SIP messages. Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) manages calls and texts, both within a carrier and between networks. One message starts a session and another ends it. Carriers use them mainly to troubleshoot dropped calls and failed texts.

Call Detail Records (CDRs). CDRs summarize each call, text, and data session: who was involved, when, for how long, and often which cell site your phone used. Carriers use them for billing and for settling charges with roaming partners.

Anyone with access to your call logs can identify your closest relationships, locate your home and workplace, and reconstruct your daily routine in more detail than you could yourself. If you called an oncologist a few years ago, there’s likely a record of it, how long you talked, and where you were. If you texted an old friend afterwards, there’s a log of that too.

Call metadata can even be correlated with publicly available information to derive identities.

Malte Spitz showed how far this goes. In 2011 he sued his telecom for the data it held on him, received roughly 35,000 records, and reconstructed a strikingly specific replay of several years of his activities.

Why call logs are easy to get

Three things make them an easy target.

They’re kept for a long time. Most carriers don’t say how long. Privacy policies typically promise to retain data for “as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes” of the policy. In 2022, responding to a request from the FCC chair, carriers disclosed that they kept geolocation data for as long as five years, far longer than phone service requires. One reason is to monetize it.

They sit in a few big targets. Carrier data is frequently breached. AT&T was one of many Snowflake customers hit by credential-based thefts, alongside Ticketmaster and Neiman Marcus. Salt Typhoon, the China-linked campaign, reportedly compromised every major US carrier, which could put call metadata for any American within reach.

They have other buyers. Retained logs are used to build detailed behavioral profiles that are sold to ad networks and data brokers and, in some cases, handed to the government.

The AT&T breach is the predictable result. The records were available to steal because they existed.

Protect yourself with private cell service.

Most carriers track everything: where you go, who you call, what you do. Cape collects the minimum amount of information required to provide you with service, deletes call and text metadata after 24 hours, rotates your network ID to prevent tracking, defends against SIM- and network-based attacks, and more.

Learn More →

Cape is built to forget

Cape deletes call and text metadata in days instead of years. Unlike other MVNOs, Cape runs their own mobile core and produces their own logs, meaning they can control when logs are deleted.

Its Disappearing Call Logs feature sets a short retention window for each record type:

When a Cape subscriber makes a call, the signaling goes to the nearest radio tower and to Cape’s partner network operator, which passes it to Cape’s mobile core. The core forwards it to the recipient’s carrier.

Cape keeps SIP messages for 14 days to debug network issues, converts them into internal CDRs, and deletes those after one day. Daily totals (counts of calls, SMS, MMS, and data used per subscriber) are kept up to 60 days for billing and spam prevention.

CDRs sent by partner networks as billing evidence are held for 30 days, long enough to dispute a bill.

Cape’s partners and the tower operators generate logs too. For that reason Cape rotates the identifiers the towers see, which weakens their ability to tie those logs to you.

The audit

A retention claim is only worth what you can verify. Cape hired Trail of Bits to audit the feature in May and July 2026 and published the attestation.

During the audit, Trail of Bits found no evidence of violation of the two given claims:

CDR files are being deleted within the retention policy.

Cape does not extract or retain data from CDRs about individual consumer customers, except daily totals. Daily totals are the number of calls, number of SMS, number of MMS, and amount of data a subscriber used in a day. This data is retained for no more than 60 days and then deleted.

You can read the full audit write-up or 404 Media’s coverage.

You can’t un-breach a database, but you can shrink it

Better carrier security matters, but the more reliable control is to hold less. Records deleted days after a call can’t be stolen two years later.
