2d31b429935d.text:
At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator. Using digital coins sold in the app—around $4 will buy 130 coins—pet photos can be turned into an “anthropomorphic portrait,” with the critter dressed in “human clothing” and inserted into bizarre scenes. Think a hamster wearing beach shorts, sunglasses, and lounging in a swimming pool or a Hawaiian shirt-wearing cat, drinking from a coconut.

All of this is cover for what appears to be the app’s true purpose: creating sexually abusive deepfake images.

A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps that, like Viefur, often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

The network was discovered hiding in plain sight, by multiple researchers, after they investigated links from thousands of video ads containing explicit deepfake content that were published on Meta’s Facebook and Instagram. As WIRED has reported in recent months, hundreds of these ads contained AI generated child sexual abuse material, including images of real children and a member of a European royal family. The ads reached tens of thousands of people and have prompted investigations from regulators around the world.

In each case, the ads linked out to the deceptive apps in Apple and Google’s app stores—allowing people to generate explicit images and make payments using Apple and Google Pay. The network behind the nudify apps appears to have been publishing them for around a year, at times publishing dozens per week. This is despite Google, Apple, and Meta saying they enforce their policies that do not allow harmful deepfake content on their platforms.

The apps and domains investigated by WIRED appear to be run by Chinese developers and a Hong Kong registered entity called KeLing Technology Limited, according to a review of web domains and how the services operate. Email addresses linked to the entity, apps, and related services, did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED, but after being contacted, they appeared to erase public connections between KeLing Technology Limited and the deepfake tools.

“This is an organized, commercially run operation: One operator behind hundreds of disposable apps and domains, cloaked to pass App Store review and pushed through tens of thousands of Meta ads under fake payer names,” says Paul Bouchaud, a lead researcher at the nonprofit AI Forensics, who investigated the network. “They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.”

Hidden Behavior

Download one of the apps in the deepfake network and you may see exactly what was advertised—such as an app to create AI pet pictures. But behind the scenes, researchers found, the apps are quietly making determinations about whether to show the benign content or load a web interface showing explicit deepfakes.

“Each time the application is downloaded, there is a call to the server with some information, such as where the user is coming from, the language, some unique identifier, and then the server replies whether or not to show the explicit or the non-explicit version of it,” explains Bouchaud, who reverse engineered the apps’ and associated websites’ code. They say there’s no clear list of reasons why one user may be shown the explicit version of an app, but one trigger appears to be downloading it after clicking an associated ad on Meta’s platforms.

0a5cce5088da.text:
“Yesterday’s price is not today’s price,” a phrase Fat Joe popularized in 2021, reminds us that what worked yesterday may not deliver the same value today.

In cybersecurity, this matters when we continue to assess employees against familiar phishing techniques while attackers use AI to craft more convincing, personalized messages. Having conducted multiple phishing simulations and one in October, 2026, I believe we need to ask a harder question: are we preparing people for the phishing attacks they are likely to face today, or testing their ability to recognize or remember the warning signs we have taught them to expect? What happens when those warning signs don’t apply or they face novel attacks?

AI -enabled “phishing landscape”

The traditional tell-tale signs of phishing which we used to train employees for are becoming less dependable. Generative AI can help attackers produce convincing messages, personalize lures and improve the quality of their communication. This does not mean every phishing campaign uses AI in reality, but it raises the bar for what employees may encounter.

A 2025 report by SC Media covering Egress research found that 75% of the phishing kits examined on dark-web markets advertised AI capabilities, while 82% offered deepfake features. These figures relate to the kits analyzed, rather than all phishing activity, but they show that AI-enabled features are appearing in tools available to criminals. Add this to the spike in recent phishing attacks with AI prompt injections and you realize quickly the landscape has morphed.

This matters for awareness programs. If employees are mainly taught to look for spelling mistakes, generic greetings or suspicious formatting, they may be less prepared for a message that uses familiar names, relevant business context and professional language when attackers use AI to craft them. Training needs to emphasize verification in addition to simply recognition and unexpected requests should be checked through a trusted channel, even when the message appears legitimate.

Click rates are not everything

Phishing simulations often produce a straightforward headline and statistics: the percentage of recipients who clicked a link, entered credentials and deleted or reported the message. They are easy metrics to communicate, compare and track over time and also to present to Senior Management in meetings but it provides only one part of the picture.

Imagine two groups with the same click rate. In one, employees who suspect a message report it quickly, allowing the security team to investigate, detect other people who may have received it and warn other recipients. In the other, people delete the message or ignore it without reporting it. The click rates may look identical, but the organization’s ability to detect a real campaign is different.

Reporting rates and time to report therefore deserve more attention. Security teams should understand whether employees use the approved reporting channel, how quickly suspicious messages reach analysts and whether those reports lead to effective action. The National Cyber Security Centre’s guidance on phishing provides practical advice on recognizing and reporting suspicious messages and organizations should have this on their website or HR portals.

As I have seen in multiple simulations I have conducted, results also need careful interpretation. A test is a controlled exercise, not a guarantee of how someone will behave during a real attack, which could depend on the recipient’s state of mind. Employees may recognize familiar templates or learn the patterns used in repeated campaigns. Clicking a simulated link also does not automatically mean someone would compromise the organization in a real incident.

The objective should be to identify weaknesses and improve security, not to rank employees by how often they pass or fail, and this should reflect in the way messages about failure are passed on.

Test the response and the person

Phishing simulations should evolve alongside the threats they are intended to represent. Scenarios should reflect realistic business situations, including unexpected document sharing, supplier requests and attempts to impersonate trusted colleagues instead of clicking links or supplying credentials only. Employees should learn how to verify unusual requests and report suspected attacks without fear of embarrassment or punishment. From experience, this may have many moving parts, like custom mailboxes, a departure from the simulation norm and multiple levels of approval before exercises like this can be done but it’s worth the effort.

Security teams should also evaluate what happens after a suspicious message arrives. How quickly is it reported? Can analysts identify and contact other recipients who possibly responded to the message? Can the organization remove the message from inboxes, block malicious infrastructure and investigate potential account compromise? These questions connect awareness testing to operational readiness.

The same principle applies to incident exercises. Security, IT, finance and relevant business teams should know what to do when a real phishing attack succeeds, which it inevitably will, someday. A program that improves reporting and response can deliver value even when it cannot prevent every employee from clicking.

AI will continue to change how phishing messages are created and delivered and security awareness must change with it. The question is whether the organization can verify suspicious activity, detect an attack and limit its impact when the message looks entirely legitimate and is prone to being clicked as a result.

Yesterday’s tests can still teach useful lessons but should not define tomorrow’s readiness.

71265a1cfef2.text:
Polymarket says it is returning $3.9 million to traders following last week’s supply chain attack. Website performance monitoring firm DebugBear, meanwhile, has disclosed that its DNS records were compromised.

On October 29, the prediction market halted trading on its international platform after users reported unauthorized withdrawals. Hudson Rock researchers linked the activity to malicious JavaScript served from a DebugBear address that Polymarket’s site loaded.

The script targeted logged-in traders. It checked their portfolios, and then either dumped positions or shifted assets to a wallet chosen by the attacker. The code read credential-related data stored in the browser, but Hudson Rock saw no evidence of it sending passwords, seed phrases or private keys back to the attacker. Instead, it piggybacked on the trading permissions of the open session.

In an October 30 update, Polymarket said 726 wallets were affected. At that point, all but 37 had been made whole, and the rest were being paid once their details were checked.

Polymarket is also covering traders hurt by the trading halt or whose positions were sold or transferred by the malicious script, paying out $1.19 million across roughly 5,500 wallets. Together with the roughly $2.7 million stolen directly, that brings the payout to $3.9 million.

“The attack came through a compromised 3rd party provider which we removed within the hour. We are in active investigation with law enforcement & will share a postmortem,” Polymarket said.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

DebugBear, whose real user monitoring (RUM) script lets websites measure page load performance for visitors, initially told customers to remove the embed code and has now shared its initial findings.

“Our DNS server records were compromised through our domain registrar. We are currently unable to receive emails sent to our domain,” the company said.

According to DebugBear, the attackers appear to have gone after one customer’s website specifically, though it stressed that this is a preliminary finding. It did not name the customer, and Polymarket has not named the compromised provider.

DebugBear has not explained how the attackers obtained access at the registrar level, and its investigation is ongoing. The company said it found no indication that its internal systems were compromised.

Polymarket faced a similar incident in June, when it said a third-party vendor compromise resulted in a malicious script being injected into its frontend. The theft was reported at around $3 million.

A cyberattack on refrigeration systems has disrupted stores run by multiple supermarket chains across several European countries after hackers remotely changed temperature settings on freezers and cooling systems.

In some cases, hackers shut down refrigerators or activated defrosting systems, causing temperatures to rise, resulting in significant product losses and forcing store managers to intervene early in the morning.

Refrigeration failures were identified at dozens of supermarkets, but it is unclear whether they were hit in a coordinated attack or targeted individually.

More than 115 stores in Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Estonia have been affected. Spokespersons for multiple chains confirmed the issues in statements for BleepingComputer.

Supermarket chains that acknowledged refrigeration issues include:

ICA (Sweden) - At least 4 locations affected

Coop (Sweden) - 7 locations confirmed affected

Ahold Delhaize (Belgium and Luxembourg) - Around 40 locations affected

Carrefour (Belgium) - 15 locations affected

Spar Colruyt (Belgium) - 5 locations affected

Intermarché (Belgium) - Around 15 locations affected

SuperValu (Ireland) - 13 stores

Selver (Estonia) - 1 store

In the Netherlands, at least 17 butcher shops and neighborhood stores have been affected.

Additional stores are dealing with the same problems in Belgium, including an Ikea superstore in Mons, grocery stores, and chocoloate shops.

Spokespersons for ICA, Ahold Delhaize, and Spar Colruyt told BleepingComputer that their companies are providing support to affected stores and working to resolve the situation.

“We can confirm that we have been informed of an incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network,” stated ICA’s press officer.

“The incident impacted the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation.”

A representative of the Colruyt Group told BleepingComputer that "there is an impact on the refrigeration systems at around five Spar stores."

"These stores are operated by independent entrepreneurs who have their own refrigeration systems. We are currently doing everything we can to resolve the issue."

In a statement for BleepingComputer, Ahold Delhaize stated that refrigeration systems at several dozen stores have been impacted by an IT incident.

“We have identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen stores,” the company's communications department said, adding that the company "immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational."

A spokesperson for Coop, one of the largest grocery store chains in Sweden, said that refrigeration units at a small number of stores were impacted, and in once case the system started to generate heat.

"We can confirm that a small number of stores were affected overnight into Monday - specifically 7 out of more than 800 stores," Coop told BleepingComputer.

"The situation is currently contained and under control. The issues have ranged from completely shut-down refrigerators and freezers to partially functioning units, and in one case, the system beginning to generate heat."

In Belgium, only Carrefour stores in two regions were affected, and all hypermarkets remained completely operational.

"The impact at Carrefour is very limited: currently 15 of our 700 stores are affected, both in Flanders and Wallonia," Carrefour stated.

"Not a single hypermarket is among them. All stores remain open because it only concerns a few refrigeration units, mainly freezers. Quick action was taken so that all stores can stay open."

An ICA store manager told TV4 that temperature settings had been changed overnight to +50°C (122°F) and could not be modified, forcing the store to discard frozen food.

According to RTL media publication, Ahold Delhaize warned managers by SMS around 4 a.m. about refrigeration issues, and some stores used refrigerated trucks to try to preserve stock.

The publication also identified Sabcobel as the vendor of refrigeration systems across several of the impacted locations.

According to Sabcobel's director, Stephan Moelans, the attacker leveraged the same vulnerability used in similar attacks last month in France.

Moelans said that technicians started disconnecting affected installations since 1a.m. and attributed the disruption to remotely activated defrost functions.

Although the company tried to protect customer's systems, a simple software update is not enough, as refrigerators also require physical modifications.

"The simplest solution is to manage the refrigerators via a secure internet connection. Most of our clients have adopted this solution since the attack in France," Moelans told RTL.

BleepingComputer has contacted Sabcobel to learn more about the incident and its level of involvement, but we are still waiting for a response.

Last month's refrigerator attacks in France impacted hundreds of stores using Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC and Copeland/Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers that were compromised by remote attackers who set them to defrost mode.

8d524fc50ae6.text:
A pull request adds a helpful setup step for an AI coding assistant. No application source changes. The description calls it a developer-experience improvement, and the reviewer sees a short configuration file beside some Markdown instructions.

Before approving it, the reviewer needs to answer a different question: what will this change allow to run on a colleague’s machine?

The issue has moved beyond hypothetical repository poisoning. In an October 8 analysis of agent-skill distribution, StepSecurity revisited the June Miasma campaign, which planted AI-tool and editor configuration in a Microsoft repository without modifying application source. The configuration was intended to trigger credential harvesting through developer tooling. The October publication describes an inventory product, but the underlying campaign illustrates a wider operational problem: merging a configuration change can distribute execution instructions to the people working in that repository.

StepSecurity also reports that the commit carried a skip-CI flag and a backdated timestamp, and that it moved code execution from package install to folder open. A control that runs only in the build pipeline never sees that path. The first reliable checkpoint is the pull request, and it needs a person who knows what the file can trigger.

I recommend giving these changes a named owner and an enforceable review path. An organization should be able to identify who approved a hook, what the approval covered and where the approved version is allowed to run.

Review the behavior behind the filename

A repository file can serve several purposes. It may describe a coding convention, direct an agent toward a script, register a tool or arrange for a command to run at a lifecycle event. Those differences matter more than the extension.

A Markdown instruction is not automatically executable code. It can nevertheless influence an agent that has permission to execute commands. A JSON setting may directly register a shell command. Review should establish the mechanism, the trigger and the authority available when it fires.

Skills show why the filename is a poor guide. StepSecurity notes that a skill’s allowed-tools field can let the agent use listed tools without a permission prompt during the turn that invokes the skill, and that Claude Code’s documentation says workspace trust does not gate that field. A SKILL.md file is Markdown, so in a pull request it tends to be reviewed like a README.

Anthropic’s current hooks reference states that command hooks run with the user’s permissions. It also distinguishes interactive workspace trust from noninteractive operation: settings-file hooks in a repository can run in a noninteractive session without the trust dialog shown to an interactive user. The exact behavior depends on the configuration surface and session type. A control tested at a developer’s terminal should therefore be retested in the automated workflow that uses the same repository.

The same page names practical mitigations. Before scripting a noninteractive run over a repository nobody on the team wrote, review its .claude settings files, start the run in bare mode or turn hooks off for that run. Administrators can also use the managed-hooks-only setting so that user, project, local and plugin hooks are blocked. Which of these fits depends on the organization’s tooling, and each should be tested rather than assumed.

For a proposed setup hook, the reviewer should be able to trace the command to its script and dependencies. If the script downloads another program, determine how that program is selected and verified. If it reads credentials or accesses the network, ask why the setup step needs those capabilities.

These questions should accompany the change while its author can explain the intent. Discovering them after distribution leaves every affected developer to make an individual trust decision.

Make ownership enforceable

Engineering productivity teams are often best placed to maintain shared coding-assistant configuration. Security should define the conditions that require a second reviewer, such as adding executable hooks, broadening network access or invoking a new external tool. The application team remains responsible for whether the integration belongs in its workflow.

This need not create an approval queue for every formatting preference. Define the behavioral changes that warrant scrutiny and route those changes to people who understand the tooling.

GitHub’s code-owner documentation explains how ownership rules work with required reviews. A CODEOWNERS file alone does not make its approval mandatory; the corresponding branch protection must require it. GitHub also recommends protecting the ownership file itself.

Apply the chosen mechanism to the agent configuration and the scripts it invokes. Protecting a settings file while leaving its referenced helper script outside the review rule creates an obvious gap. Check the effective rule with a sample pull request rather than relying on the presence of a policy file.

Allow legitimate changes to move quickly through a known path. The reviewer should receive a concise explanation of the trigger, required access and expected side effects. A hook that formats changed files should not need the same justification as one that contacts an external service or modifies a user’s global configuration.

Check what the developer environment actually loads

Repository review covers only part of the environment. Developers can also install shared skills, plugins and user-level configuration outside a project. An approved repository may therefore run alongside additional instructions that its maintainers have never reviewed.

Establish a baseline for the supported tools and launch methods. Record the origins and versions of approved additions, and provide a way to inspect the effective configuration. When local copies differ, compare the content before deciding that the difference is malicious or harmless.

Microsoft’s Workspace Trust guidance for Visual Studio Code describes Restricted Mode, which limits features that can execute workspace content. It also warns that a malicious extension can ignore that boundary. Workspace trust is a useful control within its documented scope; it should be paired with a deliberate extension policy and an environment appropriate to the repository being inspected.

Use unfamiliar repositories in an isolated environment without routinely mounted production credentials. Avoid treating a container as sufficient isolation if it inherits the developer’s secrets or access to the host. Review those connections explicitly.

For approved daily work, make the safe setup practical. Publish maintained configurations, explain how to request an addition and provide a clean inspection workflow. If compliance requires developers to reconstruct their environment manually every morning, it will be difficult to sustain.

Test the approval path before trusting it

Run a benign exercise in a disposable repository and isolated environment. Add a hook that writes a harmless marker file. Check whether the pull request reaches the intended owner, whether an unapproved change can merge and whether the installed tool permits the marker action under the documented launch conditions.

Repeat the exercise through the noninteractive route if the organization uses one. Then change only the referenced helper script. That second change tests whether the review boundary covers behavior as well as configuration.

The result should identify which controls prevented execution and which merely recorded it. A scanner alert, required review and runtime restriction perform different jobs. Record the gaps without presenting one as a substitute for all the others.

Three questions make a workable first review. Who can merge a change to the files that steer our coding assistants? Does that rule also cover every script those files call? Which of our automated jobs run the assistant over code we did not write, and do they apply the same trust checks as a developer’s terminal?

For security leadership, the useful measure is whether changes capable of altering execution reach the right reviewer before distribution, and whether the working environment matches the approved scope. Start with one supported coding tool and one engineering team. Ask them to demonstrate who can change its behavior, how that change is approved and what happens when someone tries to bypass the process.

e2b1e5181aff.text:
Microsoft has resolved a known issue that prevented some users from activating the Smart App Control security feature after installing the October 2026 KB5127648 Windows 11 security update.

Smart App Control uses Microsoft's code integrity features and app intelligence services, and it works alongside SmartScreen and Microsoft Defender to block potentially harmful apps or binaries.

As the company explained when it acknowledged the issue last month, the Smart App Control option is grayed out and cannot be toggled on affected devices running Windows 11 24H2 and later.

"After installing this update, some devices might be unable to turn on Smart App Control in the Windows Security app if it has been turned off. On affected devices, the option to turn on Smart App Control might be grayed out," Microsoft said in the KB5127648 advisory. "Devices where Smart App Control is already turned on are not affected and remain protected."

On Wednesday, the company confirmed that the issue has been fixed for users who installed this month's KB5127936 preview update.

"This issue was resolved by Windows updates released October 28, 2026 [..] and later. We recommend you install the latest security update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one," it noted in a service alert sent to IT administrators.

Workaround available

Microsoft also shared a temporary fix for admins who don't want to deploy the preview update on enterprise-managed devices and want to wait for next month's Patch Tuesday cumulative updates.

This requires them to edit the registry on affected Windows 11 devices to restore the ability to turn on Smart App Control by going through the following steps:

Open a Command Prompt window by typing cmd in the Search box.

Select Run as Administrator.

At the command prompt, enter the following commands and then restart the device:

reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\Microsoft\FeatureManagement\Overrides" /v 2883193997 /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\Microsoft\FeatureManagement\Overrides" /v 2850574478 /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f

They can also work around the issue by installing the Group Policies below, which turn on Smart App Control and enable logging for troubleshooting:

Windows 11, versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 - KB5074105 261015_19222 Feature Preview

Windows 11, versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 - KB5074105 261015_19221 Feature Preview

The Group Policy settings are under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > {Group Policy name} > Windows 11, version 24H2, 25H2, and must be set to Enabled after installation. Admins must also restart affected devices to apply the Group Policy settings.

Last month's KB5127936 preview update also resolves Remote Desktop failures caused by recent Windows updates when the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled and finally fixes Always On VPN issues triggered by the September 2026 cumulative updates.

612de22e1fa1.text:
Chainalysis suffered a cyberattack exposing customer names, emails and user IDs, while investigation data and passwords remain safe.

Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis says it was the target of a cybersecurity incident. A threat actor accessed its systems and internal tools and stole some non-sensitive customer data.

“This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools.” reads the statement published by the company, which also includes the full email sent to affected customers.

Chainalysis says it discovered the attacker this month and described the methods used as offensive techniques involving AI agents. However, it did not explain how the attack was carried out. The company also warned that AI-powered attacks are becoming more common across the industry and said it is taking a company-wide approach to dealing with this growing threat.

The data the attacker reached matters most. According to Chainalysis, attackers gained access to user IDs, full names, email addresses and organization role labels for users on the platform. The company is still working out which records belong to which customer and promises a detailed breakdown when it finishes.

What the attacker didn’t reach is just as important. So far, Chainalysis has found no sign of access to investigation content such as graphs, notes or cases, or to transaction and query results. It also found no clear-text passwords, MFA secrets or user session tokens in the attacker’s hands.

“Based on the evidence available to date, we have found no indication that these incidents resulted in the unauthorized access of investigation content (such as graphs, notes, or cases), transaction or query results, passwords in clear text, MFA secrets, or user session tokens.” continues the press release.

Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users. We are in the process of determining the records for your organization that were accessed and will provide a detailed breakdown as soon as that analysis is complete.“

The company says it’s patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems around the clock. It has hired outside cybersecurity experts and is using large language models to support a wider review that goes beyond the flaws the attacker used. It has already told all its customers and will keep them updated.

Chainalysis advises customers to watch out for unexpected password reset requests or login approval prompts. The company also strongly recommends enabling two-factor authentication (2FA) for all organizations that have not already done so. Since the exposed data includes names and email addresses, attackers could use it to launch phishing campaigns.

The company also clarified that the security incident has nothing to do with the recent theft of more than $6 billion from Binance.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Chainalysis)

265299d016b4.text:
Equifax CISO Jeremy Koppen sees the same dynamics most security chiefs are facing: hackers on the one side using AI to perform more sophisticated attacks at unprecedented speed, and defenders on the other adopting AI to match that volume and velocity.

“AI is changing the pace on both sides,” he says. “Attackers are using it to operate at greater scale, and Equifax is using it to innovate more quickly.”

In the next year, Koppen will continue to evolve Equifax’s security strategy to keep with an accelerating threat environment.

“That means building on the security already embedded across our design and development process, so checks run early and automatically,” he says. “It also means expanding how we use AI in our own security operations to handle routine work, so our experts can focus on the threats and initiatives that matter most. Done well, security becomes one of the reasons a product can launch sooner.”

As for the rising tide of AI agents entering enterprise workflows, Koppen says that “identity controls are central” to his 2027 security strategy.

“Across the industry, more activity on enterprise networks now comes from AI agents, bots, and automated workflows, and most traditional security controls were designed with a human user in mind,” he explains. “That’s why we’re applying the same rigorous verification to these identities that we apply to people.”

Of course, Koppen, like other seasoned security leaders, knows his IT security strategy must evolve to address more than just AI. Geopolitics, the anticipated arrival of quantum computing, and increasingly interconnected systems, are also changing the threat landscape and attack surface — sometimes in radical ways — and should prompt strategic changes, too.

That in turn is putting pressure on CISOs to rethink their practices, policies, and approaches as we head toward a new year likely to be at least as wild of a ride as 2026 has been.

“CISOs realize they need to transform, because their current state isn’t working. And it’s going to be a pretty significant transformation over the next few years for CISOs to be successful,” says Omar Khawaja, a CISO, a faculty member at Carnegie Mellon University’s CISO program, and a board member at HITRUST and FAIR Institute.

Of course, transformation, as always, is a work in progress, Khawaja says; as a result many security execs are still working out what needs to change in 2027 and how to make those changes happen.

Still, Khawaja, Koppen, and others stress that transformation is not an option; the safety of the organization depends on strategic evolution from its cybersecurity teams.

So what exactly needs to change? Security leaders point to specific elements that won’t work as well in the year ahead and what needs to be in place instead to more adequately secure the organization in 2027 and beyond.

Static credentials need to go

Koppen believes static credentials are on their way out.

“No matter how strict the policy, passwords still end up looking like a favorite sports team or the current season with an exclamation point at the end. That makes them trivial targets for brute-force attacks,” he says, noting that his company eliminated passwords across its 22,000 employees and contractors and is now extending its passwordless standard to its B2B customers.

More manual SOC work must be automated

The new command for security teams is to move at machine speed.

“We’re not able to deal with attacks and vulnerabilities manually anymore. AI is making that impossible,” says Florida State University CISO Bill Hunkapiller.

His security strategy reflects this new reality. He has been implementing autonomous agents to replace routine security operations tasks, and his 2027 plans call for expanding the number of tasks handled by machines.

Most CISOs are on this path. The State of Incident Response Readiness from Sygnia found that 32% of organizations have extensive AI use across most or all threat detection and incident response (IR) activities, up from 25% in 2025. And 63% expect to have extensive AI use in place for threat detection and IR activities in 2027.

Generic severity scores are out, risk ratings tailored to the organization are in

Equifax’s Koppen declares that generic severity scores are no longer effective. “A vendor’s ‘critical’ rating doesn’t know if a system holds sensitive data, is externally facing, or sits behind other controls,” he says, noting that Equifax has its own quantitative risk engine that factors in that context so its teams “can focus on issues that pose real risk to the business.”

Hunkapiller, who is also chief privacy officer and an adjunct professor at FSU, also sees a need to understand how common vulnerabilities and exposures pose a risk to his organization in particular, rather than relying on ratings. To that end, he’s exploring services that could create a digital twin of his environment to simulate how hackers could exploit vulnerabilities in his organization. This service would give Hunkapiller near-real-time information on which vulnerabilities pose the most significant risks to FSU, allowing him to accurately prioritize fixing those quickly, he says.

Thus far, he’s impressed with the capability, saying it’s like “attack surface management on steroids.”

Continuous patching is now the goal

Security used to have Patch Tuesday, a moniker that reflected the regularly scheduled work of applying newly released fixes to software flaws. Although security teams today may not adhere to Tuesday specifically for the work, many still patch on a set schedule — and many still take weeks to patch. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report puts the median time to remediate known exploited vulnerabilities at 43 days, up from 32 days in 2025.

That won’t fly in 2027, says Hugh Thompson, program chair for the RSA Conference.

“We used to do patching very methodically. If a patch came out for a system, we didn’t want to roll it out right away [for fear] it could break something. So we took time and tested it out and scheduled the work. That’s not going to work now, because the speed at which these AI attackers can take advantage of vulnerabilities or discover new ones is greater than ever,” he says. “We need automation in patching.”

Jason Rader, CISO for technology solutions and systems integrator Insight, has been accelerating his company’s patching program, bringing patch windows down to seven days for its most critical components — a significant accomplishment given the size of the IT environment and the number of patches being released. Still, he wants to do better, saying he’s aiming to increase speed for patching in all areas of the IT environment in 2027 and noting that he’d like to eventually get to continuous patching.

Different treatment for agent and NHIs needs to end

With AI agents doing more work that was, until recently, performed by humans, it’s becoming increasingly clear that security can’t treat machine identities — whether agents or systems or APIs — differently than humans, Rader says.

To that end, he’s already “managing agents like people,” applying equally diligent attention to managing identity and associated permissions — and, thus, access to data and systems — to ensure that each entity can access only what is appropriate for its role.

This includes managing machine identities throughout the lifecycle of those machines, just as security should for human workers, and applying proper governance, Rader adds.

Agility and adaptability must be part of the 2027 strategy

Some CISOs still take a set-and-forget approach to policies, procedures, and standards, says Prakash Venkata, a cyber, data, and tech risk partner at PWC and the firm’s security, risk, and engineering practice leader.

That approach never worked well, as there has always been a need to improve and evolve policies, procedures, and standards as the threat landscape and the attack surface changed, Venkata explains. But the pace of change now is so fast that CISOs need to build agility and adaptability into their strategies simply to keep up and meet industry standards.

Thompson likewise preaches the need for more agility in security strategies and advises security leaders to “be prepared for agility more than we had to or could stomach in the past because problems will emerge that you can’t anticipate.”

He notes, too, that CISOs need to work with other departments, such as procurement, to bring that needed agility to security. For example, if the CISO needs to quickly buy and implement new technology to reduce a recently identified risk or defend against an emerging threat, CISOs will need procurement procedures to move as fast as security must move.

Detached AI security and governance strategies become obsolete

There has been a rise of AI governance and security strategies that are detached from the organization’s overall governance and security strategy, says James Lyne, CEO of SANS, a security training and certification organization.

Lyne believes that the attention on AI governance and security is critical. However, he thinks having fully segregated AI governance and security strategies will be increasingly detrimental in 2027 and beyond. That’s because they’re not different and separate from enterprise governance and security.

“An AI app exposed to malicious inputs is an app security problem,” he says. “AI agents accessing unauthorized things is a privilege management and operation security issue [no less than] if people had unauthorized access.”

To ensure organizations have an effective, coordinated approach to governance and security capable of protecting the entire organization, where elements work together with no siloes or redundancies, CISOs and their organizations need a unified security strategy that addresses all actors — “whether they’re human, software services, or AI agents, or automated workflows,” he says.

adda542727cc.text:
Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Synthient and Japan's National Police Agency form coordinated effort combining security research, threat intelligence and network expertise to identify and disrupt X.CPE botnet

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, a group of private and public sector partners announced a coordinated takedown of X.CPE, a global botnet hidden in more than 1.3 million set-top boxes across more than 200 countries. Hidden on devices before they were ever sold, the botnet used subscribers' devices and home internet connections without their knowledge or consent. This takedown was led by Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security and Synthient, along with Japan's National Police Agency.

"Operations like this raise the cost for criminals and show that the infrastructure they rely on isn't out of reach," said Charley Snyder, Head of Disruption Operations at Google Threat Intelligence Group. "Disrupting X.CPE took partners across industry working together. It's proof that collaboration is one of the most powerful tools we have against threats that cross borders and industries."

A familiar device hiding an unfamiliar threat

X.CPE was embedded in firmware, the software that controls a device's basic operations, before set-top boxes reached subscribers' homes. X.CPE was built to evade pre-release security checks, and Google has since updated its review process in response, as well as banned the responsible OEM and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Unlike infections that depend on a user opening a suspicious attachment or installing an application, this threat arrived as part of the device itself. Subscribers received no consent request, notification or opt-out options.

Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Synthient, working with Japan's National Police Agency, carried out a coordinated disruption campaign against X.CPE. Each organization contributed in its own way, applying its expertise in connected-device security, malware analysis, network visibility and digital fraud to analyze the botnet and disrupt its operations.

Together they dismantled a threat hiding behind seemingly routine device activity: software embedded in TV set-top boxes that gave botnet controllers remote access and allowed them to exploit home broadband connections without subscriber consent. The takedown also disrupted the command-and-control domains that operate the criminal affiliates' malware modules. Because these affiliates distribute their modules through channels beyond X.CPE, Google assesses that taking down these domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

The effort demonstrates the importance of connecting intelligence across organizations to confront threats that cross technology and network boundaries. By bringing together distinct perspectives on compromised devices, malicious software and internet traffic, the partners supported a coordinated takedown aimed at disrupting unauthorized access and monetization and addressing risks to subscriber privacy, broadband resources and trust in connected devices.

Turning home broadband into a business without permission

The botnet generated revenue from compromised devices in a variety of ways, including: reselling bandwidth, delivering video content, ad fraud, loading additional backdoors and, in earlier versions, installing apps for payment.

Residential proxy software allowed third-party traffic to pass through subscribers' internet connections, using their home internet addresses and bandwidth without permission. Researchers also found collection of device, network and account information, alongside persistent remote access capabilities.

For service providers, the findings highlight a supply chain risk that may not be apparent from a device's everyday performance. A functioning streaming box can still generate unexplained traffic and undermine trust in the broadband service.

"Protecting the connected home requires visibility into threats that subscribers cannot see and should not be expected to detect," said Chris Griffiths, Chief Technology Officer at Plume. "By contributing broadband intelligence to this joint effort, we helped expose hidden supply chain risks and support coordinated action to make networks safer for service providers and their subscribers."

Complementary expertise, coordinated action

The partners contributed to the Google-led effort to disrupt X.CPE:

TrendAI™ Robert McArdle, Director of Cybercrime Research at TrendAI™ "We applaud Google's decisive action in removing this threat. Our research identified over 1.3 million devices affected by this campaign. That's millions of households and businesses completely unaware that their equipment was being used as an accessory in active criminality - whether defrauding advertisers or piggybacking on their connections to carry out other attacks via residential proxies - which would commonly include identity theft impersonating people in their region. This action by Google and research partners significantly sets back these attackers, and TrendAI research will be watching them closely if they attempt to rebuild."

HUMAN Gavin Reid, CISO at HUMAN "Compromised-device networks are sustained by profit: operators take control of devices and household connections without consent, then monetise that access through proxy services and various fraud activities. Group action, as exemplified in this operation, interrupts the infrastructure needed for monetisation, raising the cost of operating these networks and weakening the incentives that sustain them. "

SYNTHIENT Benjamin Brundage, CEO at Synthient. "Illicit pay-per-install networks provide a significant backbone to the larger fraud ecosystem, powering everything from direct ad fraud to unregulated proxy networks that push credential stuffing and DDoS botnets. The takedown of X.Cpe helps protect this space as a whole, as well as the unsuspecting consumers victimized by this scheme." - Benjamin Brundage

Research and resources:

Google: https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shutting-the-door-on-the-xcpe-botnet Plume: http://www.plume.com/xcpe-botnet-whitepaper-pdf TrendAI™: https://www.trendaisecurity.com/en-us/resources-insights/trendai-security-blog/trendaitm-research-helps-disrupt-android-tv-botnet-of-more-than-13-million-pre-infected-devices

About Plume

Plume provides an AI-powered platform that enables internet service providers improve connectivity, security and the subscriber experience. Combining cloud-managed Wi-Fi, network intelligence and customer care orchestration, Plume helps service providers across more than 60 countries build subscriber confidence and operate more efficiently. More details about Plume.

About TrendAI™

Introduction

As part of proactive threat monitoring, Kaspersky’s Cyber Threat Intelligence team identified a malicious campaign involving C2 agents controlled by artificial intelligence. Confirmed victims of the campaign included organizations in the education sector in several countries across Africa and Latin America. CyberStrikeAI played a key role in the post-exploitation phase. This is an open-source framework in which an LLM orchestrator on the command-and-control server plans actions, selects tools, and generates commands, while an implant executes them on compromised hosts. Using CyberStrikeAI, the attackers progressed from reconnaissance to full domain compromise.

According to our data, this is one of the first public descriptions of a compromise involving an LLM in the wild. The campaign we discovered clearly illustrates how the role of AI in attackers’ arsenals is evolving: until recently, language models were used primarily during preparatory stages – for writing phishing emails, debugging code, or searching for vulnerabilities. Now, however, they are being embedded into the very core of the attack, automating actions at every stage: payload execution, persistence on the host, discovery, lateral movement, and, finally, data collection and exfiltration. Post-exploitation – the stage that traditionally required manual work by an experienced operator – plays a particularly significant role here.

A key feature of the scheme using the CyberStrikeAI framework is that the implant ceases to be a simple tool for executing the operator’s commands. Decisions are distributed across two levels: the operator defines the task in general terms, while the model determines how to execute it – specifically, which commands to send to the host and in what sequence. Thus, the strategic planning remains with the human, while the choice of technical steps is delegated to the model, and the implant executes the model’s decisions.

To understand how this scheme works in practice, let’s examine the chain of actions taken by the attackers, as reconstructed by our analysts during the incident investigation.

Timeline of the attack

Let’s examine the timeline of the attack using an example from one incident within the detected campaign.

The first phase follows a standard approach: a human operator gains access to the victim’s infrastructure via a compromised SQL Server (version 16.0.1000), then collects basic information about the host, deploys tools, and conducts network reconnaissance. All of this activity takes nearly a day, followed by a two-week pause.

The second phase is fundamentally different. The first step involves deploying the CyberStrikeAI C2 agent, which receives commands from a server-based LLM orchestrator. During the second phase, the agent performs the following:

establishing persistence and conducting local reconnaissance within 2 minutes;

conducting domain reconnaissance over the next 5 hours;

after a brief pause of several days, moving on to the final stage – lateral movement via SMB and WMI, mass credential dumping on hosts, and database export – with the entire operation taking no more than one hour.

We’ll discuss these stages in more detail in the next section.

Technical details

CyberStrikeAI overview

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source, modular platform written in Go for automating penetration testing. Its key feature is combining LLM-based attack orchestration and a built-in C2 server with agents (beacons) within a single server process.

The entire “intelligent” layer is isolated on the control server. C2 functions (calling reconnaissance and exploitation utilities, managing webshell connections, assigning tasks to agents, and reading results) are available to the model as MCP tools. The implant is a classic C2 agent with no AI functionality – no API keys, no calls to AI service APIs, and no autonomous logic. It periodically polls the listener server via HTTP/S, TCP, or WebSocket, executes shell commands, and interacts with the file system. To the victim, this activity looks like a typical remote-control session, where a server-side LLM orchestrator queues tasks instead of a live operator. The LLM influences how decisions are made, but not how the corresponding commands are delivered to the host.

Although CyberStrikeAI is publicly available, specific instances of the framework can be linked to specific attackers or campaigns. Detection and attribution are possible based on the following artifacts:

Control panel: Upon launch, a self-signed TLS certificate is generated, with the framework’s name appearing in the issuer and subject fields. The certificate is created in memory at each startup, so the not_before field effectively records the time the process was launched. Accordingly, as with Cobalt Strike, the chronology of restarts can be reconstructed from the scan history.

CyberStrikeAI control panel’s self-signed TLS certificate

Implant: The build metadata (go version -m) contains a path to the main package, which includes data pointing to the built-in CyberStrikeAI generator – a temporary directory with the build identifier. This path is identical for all payloads, making it a reliable signature. Additionally, the build info field contains version control system metadata, which can be used to compare samples against one another.

Authentication: When communicating with the server, the implant sends an X-Implant-Token header with a fixed value in the HTTP request. The token is unique to each C2 server and is embedded into the malicious payload during the build phase; therefore, it serves as both a network indicator and a sign that the samples belong to the same server.

HTTP header parameters sent by the implant to the server

It should be noted that the implant version does not reflect the server version. The implant can operate for months while the operator updates the server-side components: listener configurations and keys are preserved during updates. In the incidents we detected, we observed the use of a single agent version throughout the entire incident. In such cases, the sample’s build date may indicate the earliest possible deployment date of the CyberStrikeAI infrastructure, but it still does not provide an estimate of the compromise duration.

Execution & Privilege Escalation

The first malicious commands on the victims’ systems in the campaign under investigation originated from the sqlservr.exe process, indicating the likely initial access vector and the context in which the attackers gained the ability to execute code. It is important to note that the commands marked as having been executed prior to agent installation were executed manually by the attacker specifically within the context of this process. At this stage, we are not yet dealing with automated implant activity, but rather with manual actions by the operator.

Before launching the agent on the machines, the attackers checked for its presence using a PowerShell script, from which we can deduce its default deployment paths: C:\Windows\Temp\, C:\Windows\, C:\ProgramData\, C:\Temp. At the same time, the attacker can disguise the agent’s name as that of a legitimate system process. In the example below, it mimics svchost.exe (svchosts.exe)

Checking for the presence of the CyberStrikeAI agent on the system

Delivery and execution of the CyberStrikeAI agent

Like most C2 agents for Windows, CyberStrikeAI uses PowerShell to execute its payload. When a request is received from the operator, the commands to be executed are additionally encoded in Base64 to bypass keyword-based detection.

Decoded form of the command:

When administrative privileges were available (for example, a domain administrator account), instead of executing commands directly, the agent on remote hosts often created scheduled tasks so that the malicious payload would run with SYSTEM privileges:

An alternative method that does not use schtasks utility is to create a task via the Schedule.Service COM object:

The payload (p1.ps1) from the example above is a reverse shell that connects to the server at 185.186.245[.]144:5501:

The p1.ps1 payload and similar scripts were distributed across the network using shared network administrative folders and the WMI protocol, which we will describe in more detail in the Lateral Movement section.

Stealth

In addition to encoding commands in Base64 and obfuscating SQL/LDAP queries – which we will describe in the Collection & Exfiltration and Discovery sections, respectively – the attackers split the malicious payload into multiple files. It is noteworthy that the scripts were transmitted in this manner even before the agent was installed – that is, at a stage where human intervention is typically required – yet they clearly bear the hallmarks of being generated by an LLM.

Below is a sequential record of several script fragments written to the file d3.b64.

Subsequently, the attackers used the certutil utility to decode the resulting file and executed it with the following command:

Once assembled and decoded, the script’s contents looked like this:

The script is a tool for decrypting DPAPI secrets from the file C:\ProgramData\dsn_line.txt. This file, in turn, is populated by the following command, which searches for a DSN string containing connection settings in the SQL Server Reporting Services configuration file rsreportserver.config and copies its contents to dsn_line.txt.

It is worth noting that some of the scripts delivered and executed as described above contain comments in Chinese (## – researcher’s comments).

Persistence

If the CyberStrikeAI implant was successfully delivered, the first step was to establish persistence on the target system. To do this, the agent created a scheduled task named SystemUpdate, which specified the path to the implant as the action to be performed:

Analysis of the framework’s source code revealed an alternative method of persistence: by adding a value to the registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, where the name of the created value matches the task name (SystemUpdate).

Agent persistence on Linux systems is also implemented in two ways – by adding the entry @reboot <path_to_beacon> & to the user’s crontab (in which case the process runs at system startup), or by adding the line (nohup <path_to_beacon> &>/dev/null &) to ~/.bashrc (in which case the agent starts when an interactive bash shell is opened).

It is worth noting that the choice of a specific persistence method is delegated to the LLM connected to CyberStrikeAI. However, thanks to the human-in-the-loop (HITL) mechanism, the operator retains full control over the process: commands generated by the model may require manual approval or correction before they are executed.

Discovery

Local Discovery

Before installing the agent on a compromised host, the attackers manually gathered basic system information using a fairly trivial set of commands:

The attackers also manually checked for internet access and obtained the external IP addresses of the compromised machines using the Chinese service dnslog[.]cn. The service generates a random third-level domain, after which the attackers attempt to resolve it on the compromised machine.

If the machine has internet access, the request succeeds, and the attackers obtain the external IP address of the compromised device on the service’s page.

For reconnaissance purposes, the agent generates a more complex script designed to map out a path for further privilege escalation by compromising SCCM or exploiting msiexec (the AlwaysInstallElevated key):

Additionally, to find ways to elevate privileges locally, the agent executed scripts to inventory services running under domain accounts and tasks running under the SYSTEM account:

During their activity, the attackers periodically checked for Microsoft Defender detections:

Remote Discovery

After gathering information about the compromised host, the attackers proceeded to conduct reconnaissance within the network. During the preparatory phase of the attack, they manually collected additional information about remote hosts using the net.exe utility.

During the main phase, the agent used PowerShell’s built-in functionality to detect accessible hosts without relying on additional utilities (such as nmap or fscan):

Additionally, relevant LDAP queries to Active Directory objects helped build a network map:

Furthermore, the presence of the installed agent on remote hosts was verified using WMI:

Domain Discovery

The next step was to gather information about the victims’ domains. To this end, before installing the agent, the attackers used standard OS utilities:

However, later on, using the CyberStrikeAI implant, reconnaissance was carried out via generated PowerShell scripts:

In addition to basic domain information, the agent performed LDAP queries to gather information for Kerberoasting and AS-REP Roasting attacks:

Finally, the agent was used to check the domain for the presence of LAPS and Microsoft Azure:

To detect signs of Microsoft Azure usage within the infrastructure, the attackers also searched for the .azcopy directory – created by the AzCopy (Microsoft Azure Storage Copy) utility – in users’ home directories:

Credential Access

After successfully conducting reconnaissance and mapping the network, the attackers moved on to the next stage – dumping credentials. For this purpose, the agent used a classic set of LOLBINs and well-known third-party tools.

The agent dumped registry hives containing credentials using the reg.exe utility:

The agent dumped the lsass.exe process using the MiniDump function of the comsvcs.dll library. In doing so, the target process’s PID was used instead of its name to make static detection based on the command line more difficult:

After successfully compromising privileged domain accounts (specifically, the built-in domain administrator), the attackers also carried out DCSync and Golden Ticket attacks via the agent using a renamed version of the mimikatz utility:

Lateral Movement

To spread across the network using compromised accounts, the attackers employed utilities from the Impacket toolkit, specifically WMIExec, as indicated by the utility’s characteristic command line:

Once installed, the agent prefers to use standard OS mechanisms, such as shared network folders.

Another method the agent uses to remotely execute commands is the WMI protocol. In particular, the agent used it to distribute the aforementioned p1.ps1 reverse shell script. This involved using compromised user accounts with local administrator privileges on the target hosts:

A second method of lateral movement via WMI uses the Invoke-CimMethod cmdlet:

Command & Control

To deliver the aforementioned tools (malicious scripts, mimikatz, and the agent itself) to the initial nodes in the infection chain, the attackers used standard OS utilities:

After the agent is installed, it checks the availability of the C2 server’s ports. The implementation mechanisms here are virtually unlimited and depend on the “creativity” of the respective LLM agents connected to the server:

To download additional utilities, the CyberStrikeAI implant also used built-in utilities (LOLBINs). The tools could be hosted on the attackers’ own servers or downloaded directly from GitHub:

Collection & Exfiltration

The data collection phase deserves special attention. It demonstrates yet another capability of LLM orchestration – the automatic generation of SQL and LDAP queries tailored to a specific task.

In one incident during the campaign, the attackers deployed the CyberStrikeAI implant on an educational organization’s SQL server and collected information from the database via PowerShell. Here is an example of a command executed by the agent:

Normalized view of the executed script with comments:

Before accessing the data, the agent checked the privileges of the account under which it connected to the database:

In decoded form, the check looks as follows:

On network resources, file collection was preceded by a recursive directory scan to identify files of interest.

To interact with the file system, the implant provides a built-in interface that supports direct uploading and downloading of files. Files are transferred directly via the main encrypted communication channel with the C2 server (HTTP or TCP), and the data itself is encoded in Base64 and packaged into the agent’s standard JSON responses.

Another built-in capability of the implant is taking screenshots of the infected machine. As with other actions, the implant does not initiate this on its own: the command to capture the screen is issued by the LLM orchestrator, and the agent merely executes it and returns the result via the same control channel.

On Windows, the command for taking screenshots looks like this:

The Linux version looks like this:

In the incidents we detected, data collection was the final stage of the attack: the chain ended there, and we observed no further activity.

Attribution

The key artifact for attribution in this campaign is the implant’s build metadata. The attackers built the malicious payload inside a Git clone of the project, so the Go compiler embedded version control system information into the binary files – the hash and commit time, as well as the vcs.modified=true flag (analogous to the +dirty suffix) – indicating uncommitted local changes in the working copy. The combination of these fields forms a unique fingerprint for a specific build.

Based on this fingerprint, the samples are divided into two independent groups, in each of which the Windows implant and the Linux implant have completely identical build metadata. A match indicates that, within each group, both payloads were built from the same project working copy.

Identical build metadata for the Windows and Linux implant samples, indicating a shared build environment

However, these groups do not overlap with one another. They do not share a common C2 infrastructure, and different versions of CyberStrikeAI are deployed on the command-and-control servers. In other words, the build metadata reliably links the samples within each group but does not provide grounds for linking the two groups together.

Differences in CyberStrikeAI versions on the command-and-control servers

The available data does not allow us to link the activity to any known group of attackers, nor to state with certainty that the same operator is behind both campaigns. Two factors prevent this. First, the tool’s openness: CyberStrikeAI is publicly available, so different operators could have independently deployed it and assembled malicious payloads under similar conditions. Second, command generation by the model: the “signature” characteristic of a specific operator is largely shaped not by a human but by an LLM. On the one hand, this increases the diversity of commands: the same command, when generated multiple times, can look different. On the other hand, it strips them of their individual characteristics, which reduces the value of behavioral metrics for attribution.

However, the Chinese-language comments found in the attackers’ scripts and the use of Chinese services still suggest a connection between the activity and a Chinese-speaking operator. In addition, analysts noted the timing of the control servers’ restarts: since the self-signed TLS certificate is regenerated each time the process starts, its not_before field records the restart time, and most of these restarts occurred during business hours in the UTC+8 time zone.

The origin of the tool itself also indirectly points in the same direction: CyberStrikeAI was developed within the Chinese cybersecurity community and is well known there.

In summary

CyberStrikeAI is a telling – though not unique – example of a shift occurring within the class of C2 frameworks: the LLM orchestrator is no longer merely an add-on to reconnaissance but has become a control layer over post-exploitation. If HexStrike AI and similar tools cover the “find and break” phase, and Sliver/Mythic/Havoc cover the “establish a foothold and control” phase, CyberStrikeAI completes the kill chain: a single server-side process written in Go executes utilities via MCP, handles webshell connections, and assigns tasks to the implant, while the model analyzes the results and decides what to do next.

The key takeaway is that the introduction of AI into the attack chain does not yet present fundamentally new challenges for detection. All the “intelligent” work remains on the attacker’s side, while the compromised host is subjected to familiar actions: from reconnaissance via Kerberoasting and AS-REP Roasting to LSASS dumps, DCSync, and the Golden Ticket attacks. This is a typical, well-documented set of domain compromise techniques. The novelty of the attack lies not in the methods themselves, but in the speed and ease with which they were executed: AI orchestration has lowered the skill requirements for the operator, but has not taken the attack beyond what defenders already know and are capable of detecting. The timing is also telling: individual key phases of the activity (such as establishing a foothold, lateral movement, and obtaining credentials) took only a few hours, and the entire attack – from agent deployment to the compromise of domain administrators – was completed within 3–4 days.

However, the CyberStrikeAI architecture does not limit users to the scenario described. The same mechanisms allow for the on-demand assembly of more complex chains – including DPAPI secret extraction and attacks on SCCM and Azure IMDS – all of which are within reach of the same group of actors, with a relatively low skill barrier. As the models evolve, the gap between the complexity of orchestration and the level of techniques used will narrow, and the operator’s role will gradually shift from setting tasks to monitoring the model’s actions.

Detection by Kaspersky solutions

It may seem that attacks using AI agents require the creation of fundamentally new detection rules. Indeed, to detect the activity of an LLM agent installed on a host within the infrastructure, it is necessary to create detection logic based on the specific characteristics of the agents. Detection rules for this activity can be found using Hunt Hub with the following filter.

However, in the case of the attack described, a different logic applies. The main difference lies in the architecture of the attack itself: the LLM agent was not located within the corporate network perimeter. It operated remotely via a C2 agent, orchestrating actions, and left no traces of its presence in the infrastructure (such as specific API requests to local LLMs or anomalous patterns of resource consumption by hosts).

The key difference between this activity and an attack by an experienced human operator lies largely in speed. Tactically, technically, and methodologically, AI, for the most part, uses exactly the same tools, utilities, and techniques as a human penetration tester. It does not write unique exploits from scratch, but rather combines known methods and dynamically adapts them to the situation, handling the tools’ errors on its own.

Since the actions performed by an AI agent on the network are indistinguishable from those of a human, classic, well-tuned correlation and behavioral analysis rules are sufficient to detect it. Here are a few examples of how Kaspersky Next EDR Expert successfully detects the attack described:

To detect the execution of a malicious script via a remote scheduled task, you need to monitor the creation of the schtasks.exe process with the /s argument. EDR Expert detects this activity using the rules create_task_on_remote_host_using_standard_tool, scheduled_task_creation_as_system_via_schtasks, and scheduled_task_with_powershell_execution.

During the attack, the adversary will need access to the victim’s credentials; in the described case, one way to obtain them was through a well-known technique that uses legitimate tools to dump LSASS, specifically by calling the MiniDump function from comsvcs.dll. The EDR Expert solution detects this activity using the rules dumping_memory_with_com_services_dll and suspicious_lsass_memory_access.

A significant part of the attack chain is lateral movement, which helps the attacker navigate within the infrastructure and achieve their desired objectives. In the described case, the WinRM protocol is used to initiate connections directly from PowerShell. This is a standard technique that allows the attacker to execute commands on remote machines without using additional network tunnels. The EDR Expert solution detects this activity using the rules using_powershell_for_remote_execution_via_wmi and winrm_send_command.

Kaspersky Anti Targeted Attack (KATA) is used to detect malicious activity in network traffic. Communication between CyberStrikeAI agents and the command-and-control server occurs without accessing AI platforms such as ChatGPT or Claude. Instead, the agent’s C2 server is an infrastructure pre-configured by the attackers, just as in attacks that do not use AI agents. Analysis of decrypted network traffic using NDR-class solutions reveals characteristic communication patterns of CyberStrikeAI agent activity. When these patterns are detected, KATA generates an alert with the verdict Backdoor.CyberStrikeAI.HTTP.C&C.

Alert regarding the detection of CyberStrikeAI communication with a C2 server

To detect post-exploitation activity, you can use not only IDS technology but also NAD (Network Anomaly Detection). It analyzes all traffic for suspicious indicators that do not correspond to a node’s typical network activity.

For example, actions performed by CyberStrikeAI during the Domain Discovery phase are detected by an NDR:NAD rule named “Scanning domain records via LDAP queries.”

NDR:NAD alert: reconnaissance via LDAP queries detected

You can learn more about NDR:NAD technology in our article on Securelist.

You can also visualize the connections between C2 addresses and files used by attackers in the Research Graph section of the Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal. This includes tracking the emergence of new CyberStrikeAI implants that communicate with malicious addresses.

Visualization via the Research Graph on the Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal

In addition, the Threat Lookup service available on the portal allows you to determine whether malicious files belong to CyberStrikeAI using attribution mechanisms based on the executable file’s code.

Demonstration of attributing a malicious implant to the CyberStrikeAI framework

Kaspersky SIEM detects all stages of an attack by the CyberStrikeAI agent. The product repository contains over 100 rules for detecting the techniques discussed in this article; we will list the most critical ones below.

Execution of various commands from the sqlservr.exe process:

R300_04_Windows shell started by a web application

Downloading and executing a payload via PowerShell:

R110_03_PowerShell code downloaded and executed

Creating Windows scheduled tasks:

R099_04_Suspicious arguments when running schtasks.exe

R300_03_Windows shell started by the scheduler

Persisting via crontab or bashrc:

R099_06_Suspicious cron job activity

R405_02_UNIX shell configuration modification

Rules located at the KUMA Packages/SOC package/Configuration discovery path detect the collection of information about hosts, network settings, and domains using various reconnaissance tools. Rules that aggregate detections by reconnaissance tools:

R224_14_Windows reconnaissance activity

R224_09_System information discovery by running multiple utilities within a short period

R224_04_System information discovery via standard Linux tools

Data collection for Kerberoasting and AS-REP Roasting:

R034_01_Multiple TGS ticket requests (Kerberoasting)

R452_18_AS-REP Roasting

Dumping registry hives containing credentials using the reg.exe utility:

R230_02_Copying data containing credentials from the Windows registry

Dumping the lsass.exe process using the MiniDump function of the comsvcs.dll library:

R233_04_Process memory dump via comsvcs.dll

R262_Suspicious access to the LSASS process

DCSync and Golden Ticket attacks using the renamed mimikatz utility:

R073_DC Sync attack

R450_41_Golden Ticket Attack

R100_03_Traces of Mimikatz use via cmd

Lateral movement using WMIExec:

R460_08_Lateral movement using WMIexec Impacket

R460_09_Lateral movement using WMIExec and Impacket

For the rules to work, you must configure the SIEM system to receive the relevant events:

Process launches (Windows security log – 4688, auditd – execve) and PowerShell commands (4104)

User logins to the system (Windows security log – 4624, 4768, 4769)

Various object manipulations (Windows security log – 4662, 4663, 4656; auditd – openat)

Interaction with shared resources (Windows security log – 5145)
