Over 1,000 Internet-exposed GitLab servers are still unpatched against a maximum-severity flaw actively exploited in remote code execution attacks.

Tracked as CVE-2026-97229, this vulnerability stems from an integer overflow weakness and was discovered in the CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler, which parses and evaluates regular expressions in pipeline configuration files.

"GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation," the company explained on October 12 when it released security patches to address the security issue in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8.

"These versions contain important bug and security fixes, and we strongly recommend that all self-managed GitLab installations be upgraded to one of these versions immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version. GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action," it added.

On Friday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed that attackers have begun exploiting the flaw in the wild and added CVE-2026-97229 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, ordering federal agencies to secure their servers by Sunday.

Although GitLab released patches three weeks ago, threat watchdog Shadowserver revealed over the weekend that it tracks more than 1,000 unpatched GitLab servers exposed to ongoing attacks.

​​CVE-2026-97229 is the latest in a series of GitLab security issues addressed since the start of the year. In January, GitLab fixed a high-severity flaw (CVE-2026-0723) that lets attackers bypass two-factor authentication, and in September, a maximum-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-85706) in the repository commits API that can be exploited to steal credentials and other secrets.

CISA also flagged CVE-2026-85706 as actively abused in the wild after cybersecurity firm watchTowr reported that attackers had already begun scanning for vulnerable GitLab servers.

Last month, it addressed another maximum-severity Regular Expression Compiler bug (CVE-2026-110264) that lets threat actors run arbitrary code on targeted instances.

"We are currently tracking over 1000 GitLab instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-97229 (on @CISACyber KEV) and over 11300 instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-110264 (out of around 39K GitLab instances we see daily)," Shadowserver said on Sunday.

Since November 2021, CISA has added six GitLab flaws to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, one of which has also been used in ransomware attacks.

GitLab says its DevSecOps platform has over 70 million registered users and is used by more than 50% of Fortune 100 companies worldwide.

Deepseek released a research prototype of dsh-superagent, a coding agent that does work on a GitHub repository for you.

Who can ask for work

The agent gets to work in two situations: an allowed user asks for something, or a rule your team wrote covers it. You can also open up a chat or GitHub scope, and then anyone in it can request work just by mentioning the agent. A message, comment or quoted document can’t expand what the agent is allowed to do, since the host is the one enforcing the lists and rules.

By default, requests that aren’t explicit, such as an unaddressed message, a bot’s message or an unlisted person’s follow-up, are assessed and recorded as ones the agent would have accepted, but none is accepted. Explicit requests, such as an allowed user mentioning the agent, work in every mode. The advice is to switch to auto after you’ve reviewed those records.

Merging

A prompt called Delivery requirements controls auto-merge, and the host adds no merge logic of its own. By default the agent doesn’t turn on auto-merge under its own account, because GitHub credits the merge to whoever enabled it. Unless the prompt names another account for merging, people merge.

dsh-superagent is available for free on GitHub.

In this Help Net Security interview, Vinay Thakker, CTO of KloudStax, explains how to set identity, credentials, and network limits for AI agents. He argues that agents should run under their own identity, with the person’s identity attached when acting on someone’s behalf. He covers where credential proxies go wrong, what the first ten lines of a command policy for a coding agent should say, and how to stop data from leaving through package installs or URL parameters. He also describes how red teams should test agent deployments.

Should an agent get its own identity, borrow the identity of the human who launched it, or something in between? Walk me through how you’d decide for two cases: an agent that triages support tickets and one that pushes infrastructure changes.

Neither extreme. The deciding question is whether the agent is doing a job for the business or a task for one person.

If it’s doing a job for the business, it gets its own identity, with permissions scoped to that job. If it’s doing a task for one person, it still gets its own identity, but each request also carries the identity of the person who asked. The agent can then only do what both are allowed to do, and the logs show both names. Borrowing the person’s login outright is the option I’d rule out, because the agent’s actions become indistinguishable from the person’s, and it inherits everything that person can reach.

A ticket-triage agent is doing a job for the business. It works across every customer’s tickets and doesn’t belong to any one rep, so it runs as itself, with read access to the queue and write access only to routing and labels.

An infrastructure agent is usually doing a task for an engineer, so it carries that engineer’s identity alongside its own. But proposing a change and applying it should be separate permissions. The agent can open the change and run the plan. Applying it goes through the same review and pipeline a human’s change would.

Should agents hold secrets directly, or should they go through a vault or proxy that injects credentials at call time? Where have you seen the proxy approach go wrong?

Never hand an agent a long-lived secret. Past that, the question bundles two decisions worth separating: how long a credential lives, and whether the agent ever holds it.

Short-lived credentials limit how long a leaked one stays useful. A proxy that attaches the credential at call time limits whether it can leak at all, since the agent never sees it. The two work together, and the strongest setups do both: the proxy verifies the agent’s identity, obtains a short-lived credential scoped to that call, and attaches it on the way out.

For services that only accept static API keys, a proxy is the only way to keep the key out of the agent. If an agent does hold a short-lived token directly, check what sits next to it. A refresh token in the same environment is a long-lived secret by another name. Better still, tie the token to the machine or container that requested it, so a copy that leaks is useless anywhere else.

Neither control stops a hijacked agent from misusing access it legitimately has, and that’s where proxies go wrong. A proxy that attaches credentials to any request the agent makes is a confused deputy waiting for instructions. One that forwards the caller’s token downstream turns every hop into a place to steal it. One shared credential behind the proxy makes every agent look identical in the logs. And a vault on the same host as the agent hasn’t protected the secret, only moved it. A proxy doesn’t remove an agent’s authority. It concentrates it, so it needs per-agent identity, least privilege and a destination allowlist like anything else.

If you had to write the first ten lines of a command policy for a coding agent with terminal access, what would they say?

A short list of hard denies is a reasonable first step for a team just getting started. For an agent with a terminal, though, I’d write the policy as an allowlist, because a coding agent will always find the command you didn’t think to forbid. I’d also make sure every line is enforced by the harness rather than by asking the model to behave. Roughly:

1. The agent works inside one checked-out repository in a disposable environment and can’t read or write anything outside it. 2. It runs only approved commands: the project’s build, test, lint and format tools, read-only git, and file edits inside the repo. Anything else asks first. 3. No credentials live in its environment. Anything that needs one goes through a broker the agent can’t read. 4. It can’t open files that carry secrets, such as .env files, SSH keys or cloud credential files, even if one turns up in the workspace. 5. Network access is off except for the internal package mirror and the specific hosts this project needs. 6. Packages come only from the internal artifact repository, and adding a new dependency needs a human. 7. It can commit to its own branch and open a pull request. It can’t push to protected branches, force-push or merge. 8. Anything that changes shared infrastructure or data, such as an apply, a deploy, a migration or a delete, stops and asks. 9. It can’t escalate privileges or change its own policy, hooks or configuration. 10. Every command is logged with the agent’s identity and the task that triggered it, and a spend or runtime cap ends the session when it’s hit.

Several of these lines shouldn’t depend on the command policy at all. Branch protection belongs in version control, network rules in the firewall and credential access in the identity system, so they hold even if the agent finds a way around its own policy. None of this is new.

It’s the discipline we already apply to CI pipelines, applied to something that writes its own commands.

What should an agent be allowed to reach on the network by default? How do you stop data from leaving through an innocent-looking request, like a package install or a URL parameter?

I’d start every agent with no network access and work forward from what it holds. The test I use is whether a single agent combines private data, content from people you don’t control, and a way to send data out. With all three, one poisoned email or ticket is enough to move data out of the company. A research agent that reads the open web but can’t see anything internal can have fairly broad reach. A support agent reading customer email next to customer records shouldn’t have an open outbound path at all, and its replies should go through a channel someone controls.

When an agent does need the network, I’d deny by default, list exact hosts rather than wildcards, and enforce it somewhere the agent can’t edit. Package installs are where most allowlists quietly fall apart, because the public registries end up on the list. We’ve had internal artifact repositories for years for exactly this reason. Pointing agents at yours instead of the public registry closes most of that gap and gives you one place to hold back new releases or packages nobody has reviewed.

The URL parameter is the harder case, and I don’t think the network solves it. A plain GET to an approved host can carry data in its query string, and approving a host means trusting the platform, not everything people can write on it. Inspection is worth having for visibility, but I wouldn’t rely on it to catch injected instructions, since an attacker only needs the one variant the filter misses. What I trust more is design: once an agent has read untrusted content, it shouldn’t be able to send data out or take a consequential action without someone approving it.

How should a red team test an agent deployment? What does a good tabletop exercise for a hijacked agent look like?

I’d have a red team test the system around the model rather than the model itself. Assume an injection will eventually work, and measure what a hijacked agent can do from there: how far it got, which controls held, and how long it took anyone to notice. The known paths, such as reading its own credentials, reaching a host off the allowlist or editing its own configuration, should run as automated tests every time someone adds a tool or connector, because that’s when the exposure changes. That leaves the human red team free to hunt for the paths nobody has written a test for yet.

For the tabletop, I’d be careful about which incident you rehearse. The costliest agent incident I’ve seen this year was agents on one engineer’s account spending roughly $500,000 on cloud infrastructure in about 36 hours. That one was loud, and the bill eventually gave it away. A hijacked agent is built to stay quiet, reading the data it always reads and calling the systems it’s allowed to call, so rehearsing the loud case teaches the wrong instincts.

I’d run it in stages instead. A support agent processes a ticket carrying hidden instructions, and over the following week other customers’ records leave a few at a time inside its replies to the attacker. Reveal one clue at a time: a customer complaint, then an odd pattern in the agent’s logs, then the poisoned ticket itself. At each stage, ask the room what they’d do with only what they know. Can they tie the activity to one agent? Can they stop it without taking down support? Who decides, and how fast?

Then ask the question most teams can’t answer: after you end the session, how do you know it’s gone? If the attacker had the agent write an instruction into its memory, a shared configuration file or a reply template, the next session picks it up and starts again. Recovery means cleaning everything the agent could write to, not just revoking its credentials.

Taiwanese network-attached storage (NAS) appliance maker Synology warned customers to update their devices immediately due to a surge in C3RB3r ransomware attacks.

The company urged users to enable automatic updates and upgrade the DiskStation Manager (DSM) software running on their NAS devices to the latest version to protect their data.

"Synology has identified threat actors exploiting a vulnerability patched in December 2024 to target devices running outdated versions of DSM. These attacks aim to encrypt data and extort ransom," it said in a Thursday advisory.

"Synology strongly urges all users running vulnerable versions to update DSM immediately to protect their systems. Synology also recommends enabling automatic updates to keep DSM up to date at all times."

A Synology spokesperson was not immediately available when BleepingComputer reached out for more information on these C3RB3r ransomware attacks.

While Synology has yet to share which vulnerability is being exploited in these ongoing attacks, it linked to a November 2024 security advisory with information about patches released for vulnerabilities allowing attackers to execute arbitrary code (CVE-2024-10441), read files (CVE-2024-50629), and write files (CVE-2024-10445) on unpatched devices.

Synology users are advised to immediately block access to the management web interface from the Internet and update their DSM software to block attackers' attempts to hack and encrypt their devices.

Synology rarely issues security advisories warning of attacks targeting its customers' devices, with the last such alert published in August 2019 following large-scale brute-force attacks that led to eCh0raix ransomware infections.

Last week's advisory follows a massive wave of reports from Synology customers whose data was encrypted and who were prompted to buy "C3rb3r Decryptor" tool from a dark web portal for thousands of dollars.

The first reports surfaced more than two weeks ago, with affected users saying the ransomware dropped a ransom note (read-me3.txt) and added a .L0CK3D extension to encrypted files.

"All your important files have been encrypted. Any attempts to restore your files with thrid-party software will be fatal for your files! The only way to decrypt your files safely is to buy the special decryption software 'C3rb3r Decryptor'," the ransom note warns.

"At this page you will receive the complete instructions how to buy the decryption software for restoring all your files. Also at this page you will be able to restore any one file for free to be sure 'C3rb3r Decryptor' will help you."

The Cerber ransomware (also known as C3RB3R and CerberImposter), now deployed in attacks targeting Synology NAS devices, borrowed its name from a notorious Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) with the same name that emerged in 2016.

Before disappearing at the end of 2019, the old Cerber ransomware operation accounted for more than 80% of all ransomware attacks and a quarter of all ransomware infections on enterprise endpoints.

Starting in December 2021, when it was first spotted, C3RB3R was also deployed on Atlassian Confluence and GitLab servers as part of several attack waves exploiting remote code execution (CVE-2021-26084 and CVE-2021-22205) and authentication bypass (CVE-2023-22518) flaws.

Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 380,000 Internet-exposed Synology NAS devices, but doesn't provide information on how many have already been secured against these attacks or are honeypots.

Byoky is an open-source wallet for AI API keys, available as a Chrome and Firefox extension and as iOS and Android apps.

Users store their keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini and other providers in it, encrypted on their own device. Apps that want those keys ask the wallet for access, and the wallet sends each request to the provider itself. The app gets a session token. The key stays in the wallet.

Byoky goes after the habit of pasting a key into a web app’s settings page to try a new tool. “A key pasted into a settings page is a key you no longer control,” the project’s homepage says. Byoky copies the model of MetaMask, the crypto wallet that decentralized apps connect to: the app asks, the user approves, and one click revokes access.

Users set a master password and add their keys. Byoky encrypts them with AES-256-GCM, a standard cipher that also detects tampering, using a key derived from the password through 600,000 rounds of PBKDF2. That iteration count makes each guess slow for anyone who steals the encrypted vault and tries to crack the password. Byoky requires a password of at least 12 characters.

Developers keep the official Anthropic or OpenAI library and hand it a session key and a fetch function from Byoky’s SDK. Streaming, tool calls and image inputs pass through, according to the documentation. Users can cap spending per app, and the wallet logs every request locally with the app’s origin, the provider and the status.

The wallet supports 13 cloud providers plus local Ollama and LM Studio servers. It can also translate between Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and Cohere request formats, so a user can drag an app written for Claude onto a GPT key without the developer touching code.

Command-line agents such as OpenClaw, Claude Code and Hermes connect through a local proxy called the bridge. The bridge rejects requests that lack a bridge token, a check meant to stop other programs on the same machine from spending the keys. It also does something less advertised. When a third-party agent runs on a Claude Pro or Max subscription token, the bridge renames the agent’s tools and moves its system prompt so that Anthropic’s first-party detection accepts the request.

Byoky is available for free on GitHub.

On Saturday, October 24, 2026 we conducted a successful exercise demonstrating that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate without depending on any infrastructure outside the European Union (EU). This was the first public technical exercise demonstrating the independence of a sovereign cloud Region.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is a new, independent cloud partition for Europe that became generally available in January 2026, with its first AWS Region in Brandenburg, Germany. It is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions, with no critical dependencies on non-EU infrastructure, and all customer content and customer-created metadata remains in the EU.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is managed through dedicated European legal entities established under German law and operated entirely within Europe. My fellow Managing Director, Stefan Hoechbauer, and I called for the exercise. We are EU citizens residing in the EU, responsible for its management and operations, including its infrastructure, technology, and services. Only EU residents located in the EU control its operations and support, and AWS is gradually transitioning the AWS European Sovereign Cloud to be operated exclusively by EU citizens located in the EU.

What we did

In standard operations, the AWS European Sovereign Cloud uses two global systems: the AWS Global Network backbone, and a dedicated system operated by the local EU team to manage limited, controlled transfers of operational AWS data. As we explained ahead of the exercise, neither is critical to running the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. During the exercise, the team switched off both systems, and traffic that normally travels across the AWS Global Network backbone rerouted securely over the public internet.

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud can operate independently at any time, and for several hours on October 24 the team showed exactly that, running it on only its own software and hardware resources, operated by EU-resident staff within the EU.

Workloads continued running, and customers could still access their data. The exercise did not affect service availability within the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, other AWS Regions, or private connectivity through AWS Direct Connect. When the exercise finished, traffic returned to its normal path.

Why we ran it

Transparency is at the core of our digital sovereignty commitment, so we ran the AWS European Sovereign Cloud exercise openly and reported back on the outcome. The exercise produced verifiable technical and operational evidence that the AWS European Sovereign Cloud can continue to operate independently within the EU. It turns a design claim into a verified result. Organizations in regulated industries and the public sector can take this result to regulators and their boards as evidence for their compliance and assurance documents.

What customers and partners are saying

“Digital sovereignty is ultimately about trust and safeguarding business continuity. The successful demonstration of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud’s operational independence is an important proof point for European organizations with the most stringent sovereignty requirements. Combined with Capgemini’s European heritage, presence and AWS capabilities, we can deliver a sovereign proposition in Europe, for Europe, by Europeans, enabling clients to accelerate secure and resilient cloud and AI transformation at scale whilst assuring business continuity.” – Fernando Alvarez, Chief Strategy and Development Officer and Group Executive Board Member, Capgemini

“Autonomy, resilience and operational control are foundations driving digital sovereignty concerns across the public sector and regulated industries. Achieving sovereignty requires more than a sound and consistent architecture; it demands operational evidence to build trust. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud team has provided evidence, supporting organizations on the transformation of their critical data and digital assets toward greater sovereign control. Having engaged with this team since the inception of the project, and as a Launch Partner of the AWS Digital Sovereignty Competency, Atos helps customers define their sovereignty roadmaps, adopt the appropriate graduated solutions, and confidently operate and govern their target sovereignty posture.” – Michael Kollar, Digital Sovereignty Leader and Head of Cloud & Modern Infrastructure and Digital Workplace, Atos Group

“For organizations in regulated industries, meeting strict data and operational requirements cannot come at the cost of a great customer experience. Running on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, Genesys can help European organizations deliver exactly that, with their data and operations kept in the EU. Seeing the AWS European Sovereign Cloud operate independently under real conditions helps give our shared customers added confidence to move their most sensitive workloads to the cloud.” – Daniel Karadza, Senior Director, Partners and Alliances, EMEA Central and Benelux, Genesys

“Operational independence is a defining pillar of digital sovereignty, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud has shown what that means in practice. It runs without reliance on any infrastructure outside the EU and is operated entirely by EU residents, which makes it a strong fit for Europe’s regulated industries and public sector. As an early collaborator with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud team before its launch, Accenture is uniquely positioned to help clients navigate sovereignty requirements and scale with greater confidence and control.” – Emanuele Baldassarre, Managing Director, Accenture

Learn more

To learn more about the design and digital sovereignty controls of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, visit aws.eu. If you have questions about this exercise or want to discuss your workloads, reach out to AWS Support or contact your AWS Account team.

Stéphane Israël

Stéphane is the leader and Managing Director of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. He is responsible for the management and operations of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, including infrastructure, technology, and services, in addition to broader digital sovereignty efforts at AWS. Prior to AWS, he was the CEO of Arianespace, where he oversaw numerous successful space missions, including the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope.

192be2127550.text: Hello and welcome to the Monday, November 2nd, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. OneNote is one of those tools that you probably can't escape if you have to work in an enterprise environment. And Didier had all along a neat tool that allowed you to extract attachments from OneNote file. The problem with the tool was it was one file at a time, which of course gets tedious after a while. So now Didier has added a new feature to his OneNote extraction tool. And this feature will save all of the attachments into a JSON formatted file. It can even be applied to multiple files at the same time and makes your data extraction with that quite a bit more efficient. So if you have to do that, well, definitely take a look at this updated tool by Didier. 19d0eed47fbf.text:
Every security team is being told to adopt AI. Far fewer have been shown what "good" looks like in practice. Turnkey agents handle common, well-defined security tasks, but no two security teams operate the same way. Each has its own data, playbooks, escalation paths, and risk tolerances; unique context that no vendor can anticipate in a packaged solution. That’s why we built CrowdStrike® Charlotte AI™ AgentWorks: a no-code workspace that lets every security team build the exact agents they need, on the Falcon platform.

The power of the crowd is one of the most enduring advantages we have as an industry against the adversary. What one analyst learns on the front lines, the whole community inherits. Now, adversaries are rapidly gaining AI fluency, and defenders need to transform the SOC the way we always have: together. When one team turns a hard problem into a working agent, it raises the bar for all of us. Every team can learn from that agent, adapt it, and build on it.

So, we summoned the ingenuity of the crowd like never before. Working with NVIDIA, we launched the first AgentWorks Hackathon and invited security teams to nominate agents they’ve built. The brief was wide open: each team picked its own problem and defined its build. Nearly a hundred nominations poured in from more than 50 countries, each aimed at a persistent bottleneck its builders knew firsthand and forged to earn its place as a trusted extension of the team.

The standouts went further. They were intentionally designed, governed by clear guardrails, and deliver real impact. Here are the winning agents and five lessons every security team can apply today.

Winner Spotlights

“Agent Smith”: Finding the MCP Servers Nobody Knew Were Running

AI coding tools can launch an MCP server on a developer laptop with a single command. Most security teams have no inventory of them. In one day, one company discovered 1,710 hosts running unapproved MCP servers, including a revoked server, unapproved mailbox readers, and one with TLS verification turned off. Nobody had been watching.

Agent Smith hunts these cases down. It finds MCP servers running on endpoints, checks each against the organization's approved list, and reads redacted command lines for risky settings. In doing so, it turns a blind spot into a daily inventory with a clear next step for every server.

The sophistication here wasn't just in the prompt. It was in the architecture: a deliberate division of labor between the model and deterministic tools like queries and workflows. That split sharpened accuracy and controlled cost.

Before the agent runs, an upstream query in CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM does the heavy lifting, carrying the company's own context: signature rules encoding the approved tool list, noise filters tuned during testing, and host lookups mapping each server to a business unit. It also redacts sensitive data before handing the agent a command-line sample and package names.

The agent then gets to work: explaining what each server is, flagging risky settings (TLS off, unpinned versions, credentials on the command line), and recommending a next step based on the team's existing approval process (switch to an approved server, request a review, or register a custom build). Charlotte Agentic SOAR then passes that context into a new case for the governance team to review.

“Help Desk Takeover Defender” Agent: Catching MFA Reset Abuse in 70 Seconds

Multifactor authentication (MFA) exploitation is one of the most effective plays in the modern attacker's playbook: Call the service desk, impersonate an employee, get their MFA reset, register your own device, and walk into the account. The challenge for defenders is that a malicious reset can look almost exactly like a legitimate one.

The Help Desk Takeover Defender agent ensures every MFA reset is investigated for abuse within moments of a new reset. Manual investigations that previously took 20 to 30 minutes now run in about 70 seconds against live data, and containment drops from hours to minutes. It pulls Entra ID logs and the supporting Falcon telemetry behind a reset, then scores the likelihood of a social engineering attack. If the signs point to a takeover, it can revoke sessions, disable the user, or contain the host.

What earned this agent its recognition was how it balanced trust and speed. The scoring is deterministic, computed upstream by a CrowdStrike Falcon® Foundry function rather than the model, so the same evidence produces the same verdict. The model compares each reset against that user's 30-day history, then draws on knowledge files that encode the team's playbook: what's considered normal, how to verify a user with a callback, and which containment paths are warranted and when. No action happens without a human in the loop: Every containment step requires explicit approval and the approver's name on record.

“Exclusion Adversary” Agent: The Agent that Attacks its Own Work

Every security team manages exclusions: rules that tell security tools to stop alerting on recurring, harmless activity. But left unattended, exclusions can become blind spots of their own. A rule written too loosely doesn't just quiet the noise; it hides any real attack that happens to share the same pattern. A good exclusion has to thread the needle: wide enough to catch the noise, but tight enough that an attacker can't hide behind it.

The Exclusion Adversary agent turns that balancing act into a repeatable, evidence-backed step. It gathers live detection counts and drafts the narrowest exclusion that would safely apply. Then it does what analysts rarely have time for: It attacks its own draft. It lists every field the rule leaves wide open and writes bypass strings an adversary might use to slip through, such as a same-named binary dropped in a writable folder. It ends with a verdict and an approval checklist for an analyst to review.

What sets this agent apart is its adversarial mindset turned inward. Most agents try to be right. This one assumes it might be wrong and goes looking for proof. Its discipline caught a real defect in testing: The agent's first draft used a common wildcard pattern that matched a program by name in any folder. That meant an attacker could plant a lookalike elsewhere and the exclusion would silence it too. The agent flagged the gap and tightened the rule to the exact file path.

Notable Runners-Up

This is CQL Agent: Security queries can run without errors but still fail. AI-drafted detections are especially prone to this. This agent checks whether queries and detection rules work as intended. It takes output from CrowdStrike’s LogScale query assistant or the Falcon Next-Gen SIEM Correlation Rule Generation Agent and runs it through a fixed series of gates, including a check against a 196-function CrowdStrike Query Language (CQL) catalog, 23 silent-failure rules, and a reproducible unit test. Each one ends with a verdict: validated, validated with limits, or inconclusive. Judges singled out its reproducible tests and its willingness to return an inconclusive result. An agent that admits what it can't prove is one you can trust when it returns a "validated” verdict.

TaHiTI Threat Hunting Agent: Structured threat hunting can take a senior analyst hours; most of it spent on research, schema lookups, query debugging, and write-ups rather than hunting. This agent runs the full Targeted Hunting integrating Threat Intelligence (TaHiTI) methodology end-to-end. It scopes queries to keep costs under control and produces a standardized, ServiceNow-ready hunt record. The result: junior analysts can now run hunts that once waited on senior staff. The method stops living in one person's head and can be run by the whole team.

HOPSCOTCH Agent (Lateral Movement Flight Recorder): Tracing an identity or process across entry, internal hops, and exit points can be a time-consuming process. Given an account name, HOPSCOTCH reconstructs that entity’s path as a chronological, confidence-rated chain, corroborating source activity, authentication, destination execution, and post-arrival behavior at each hop. At each link, the agent provides supporting evidence and a confidence level, so analysts can see what it knows and what it’s inferring.

EASM Heartbeat Agent: An organization's external attack surface changes constantly. Each morning, the EASM Heartbeat agent emails the security team a short report on what changed across its external attack surface in the last 24 hours: new findings, new IPs, new “Critical” and “High” CVE misconfigurations, and which way the risk score is moving. One weekend, its findings more than doubled, tracing the spike to newly attributed assets carrying critical, actively used exploits. Its report revealed to the team that much of the inventory had never been reviewed, which led to a recurring asset review.

Dysfunctional Family-Tree Agent: Most attacks today are malware-free. To catch them, this agent proactively audits two- and three-generation process lineage (grandparent, parent, child) against a lookup table of patterns common to LOLBin attacks, decodes obfuscated command lines, and opens a case for medium-or-worse findings.

Hall Pass Agent: Security exemptions rarely expire on their own. One organization found more than 25,000 hosts carrying a USB exemption, with no active approval on record for over two years. The Hall Pass agent reconciles the exemptions the Falcon platform enforces against internal approval records, measures whether each is still used, and opens a renew-or-revoke case for the owner, so exceptions stay current and reviewed.

SneakerNet Agent: The Falcon sensor records every file written to USB, far too many for any team to review by hand. In a 30 day window, one team found merger documents, litigation holds, and pay statements copied to removable drives without triggering a single alert. Blocking USB would break legitimate work, so every hour a detection query flags sensitive files written to or opened from USB drives and SD cards. The agent scores each device, checking the machine’s role and whether the same drive has been on other hosts. It then opens a case for the data owner showing what left, how, and why it scored the way it did, without blocking anything or naming the user.

What Makes a Good Security Agent?

Five traits set apart the best agents:

They solve real problems: The best agents target the work that drains analyst time, or worse, the work that always loses to urgent tasks and never gets done. These problems aren't always glamorous, but they're often low-risk and high-return cases for automation. Moreover, the best builds didn't just move a bottleneck downstream or create new ones. They closed the gap, doing work that otherwise wouldn't happen.

They connect data, reasoning, and action, and plug into processes that teams already run: A good agent is defined by an architecture that applies AI reasoning exactly where judgment is needed and leans on other technologies for everything else. The strongest builds didn't make the model do everything. They made it do the one thing only a model can, then handed the rest to tools that are faster, cheaper, and deterministic, such as for routing, loops, query searches, and fixed calculations. They also structured outputs to hand off cleanly to the workflows, cases, and agents downstream.

They have built-in guardrails: The best builders treated trust as a design problem. They capped tool calls, retry limits, and per-run credits. They redacted sensitive data before the model ever saw it. They refused to let the model invent facts, or required a named human to approve any consequential action. The best of them made the dangerous action structurally impossible, such as instructing agents to disclose when information is incomplete or routing containment through workflows that require analyst approval. As one judge noted, “For a cyberdefense team, an agent’s ability to disclose missing evidence, avoid unsupported conclusions, and preserve human control matters as much as its speed.”

They drive measurable outcomes and improve over time: The top builds were designed around tasks that could be evaluated, then refined across versions and benchmarked against real or synthetic datasets until they met the required bar for accuracy. This is what separates a demo from a production-ready agent: one that can be measured and continuously optimized, earning the trust to graduate to more autonomous work.

They're creative: Some of the most memorable submissions weren't faster versions of existing work. They approached problems from entirely new angles: an agent that attacks detection exclusions to expose the blind spot, an agent that hunts down unauthorized agents. Some of the most forward-looking builds pointed at questions the industry is only beginning to ask, like whether an agent's activity isn’t just internally authorized but legal under local regulations.

Agent Traces: How the Best Agents Got Even Better

One last habit set the standout agents apart: They used AgentWorks agent traces to understand how their agent worked and to optimize its design.

Every time an AgentWorks agent runs, it leaves an execution trace, a step-by-step record of what the agent did: which tools it called, the exact query it sent, what came back, how long each step took, and how many credits each step consumed. The trace view is a powerful resource for troubleshooting and optimizing agent design. Builders noted how this helped them troubleshoot four common issues:

Errors the agent ignores: A tool errors out, and the agent either moves on or quietly substitutes different results, building a confident conclusion on missing data. The fix: Include explicit prompt instructions for how to handle errors, including never filling gaps with substitute data.

Zero rows misread as "none": No error appears, just an empty result. The agent reports "nothing found" when the real cause was a timeout or a query that never ran. The fix: Have the agent confirm the query completed before reporting "none," and report "not retrieved" if it can't. Then redesign the query, for example by narrowing the time window, rather than retrying it unchanged.

Over-chaining and wasted turns: Timeouts and excessive agent-to-agent chaining inflate latency and cost without improving accuracy. The fix: Trim the chain to the steps that actually improve the answer, and remove tools the agent doesn't need.

Knowledge bases that never got used: An agent is only as good as its context. Traces can also reveal when agents don’t open their attached knowledge base. The fix: Force a knowledge lookup on every run or encode knowledge as an agent skill.

48c551b9fc64.text:
The disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 placed immediate pressure on organizations running PHP. Both vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated remote code execution, including in products and appliances where PHP is embedded, and updates depend on third-party vendors [1].

Early guidance focused on patching internet-facing systems and monitoring for behavior associated with successful exploitation, including unexpected command execution, Webroot changes and outbound connections from PHP servers.

Darktrace observed widespread scanning across monitored environments involving hundreds of distinct source IP addresses that public reporting has associated with activity targeting the PHP vulnerabilities. The volume of scanning was significantly greater than the evidence available for successful exploitation. For analysts, that distinction is important. Scanning demonstrates interest in exposed infrastructure; establishing compromise requires evidence of subsequent behavior on the targeted system, including command execution, file modification or unexpected outbound communication.

PHP is not an isolated example. Imperva subsequently demonstrated remote code execution against a vulnerable Node.js build through malicious Brotli data, reproducing execution through compressed HTTP responses and configured request parsers. The same inputs were rejected by the patched runtime. Imperva linked its Node2Shell and PHP2Shell research to the increasing speed of vulnerability discovery and exploit development. [2]

While Darktrace has not observed direct evidence of CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 exploitation, on October 21st we observed a six-month high in detections consistent with zero-day exploitation activity, representing a 64% increase compared to historic data. This increase has not been confirmed as related to the PHP vulnerabilities. Darktrace’s behavioral approach is designed to detect anomalous activity without relying solely on rules written for a specific exploit. Comparable increases were observed around the Log4j disclosure and other globally significant vulnerability disclosures.

AI-assisted vulnerability research

The PHP disclosure arrives as AI systems have become more capable at vulnerability research [3]. OpenAI launched Daybreak in June 2026, combining GPT-5.5-Cyber, Codex Security and partnerships with security researchers and software maintainers. OpenAI says its models have been applied to discovering and generating patches for vulnerabilities in browsers, network infrastructure, FreeBSD and the Linux kernel. Darktrace joined the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program in June to explore how OpenAI's cyber capabilities could be integrated within Darktrace products and services [4][10].

OpenAI reported in August that Codex Security Cloud had analyzed more than 30 million commits across more than 30,000 codebases. According to OpenAI, Cloudflare uses models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code and combines findings with live traffic and security signals to assess whether affected routes are active or receiving suspicious traffic, with proposed mitigations and patches remaining subject to customer review [5][6].

Faster discovery still leaves defenders with the work of locating affected software, testing fixes and completing remediation. The PHP case shows that gap clearly, particularly when vulnerable runtimes are embedded inside other products.

Enterprise agents as an attack surface

Darktrace Signal Labs has also examined how a trusted enterprise agent could be abused after an attacker has already obtained access to an environment. In a controlled simulation, researchers demonstrated that, in that post-compromise scenario, the Claude platform’s memory stores feature could be abused to establish a live C2 channel between an external operator and internal Claude Code agents. The external operator was able to dynamically assign network discovery, credential access, and data exfiltration tasks to the agents via this C2 channel. Detection of the agents’ activities relied on the correlation of process creation and network traffic activity from agent harness processes, alongside behavioral analysis to identify deviations from expected behavior. Darktrace has not claimed it observed this memory-store command-and-control technique in operational attacks [7].

AI-assisted attacks in Japan

Evidence from Japan indicates AI being used for vulnerability scanning and attacks outside controlled research. On 21 October, JPCERT/CC published findings from an investigation into recent unauthorized access incidents affecting organizations in Japan. JPCERT/CC states that it confirmed attackers had used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and conduct attacks through APIs. According to JPCERT/CC, its examination of attack infrastructure found evidence of Android application analysis, API discovery and testing for weaknesses including server-side request forgery, and the infrastructure also targeted services intended for users outside Japan [8].

JPCERT/CC does not identify ARTEX by name in that publication. The named ARTEX attribution comes from separate investigations, including Microsoft's analysis of Storm-0940.

AI in offensive operations

Microsoft describes ARTEX as an open-source, multi-agent penetration-testing system capable of automating activity with limited human interaction. Microsoft reported that Storm-0940, which it assesses to be a China state-aligned actor active since 2021, used ARTEX against hundreds of organizations, and Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise [9].

Microsoft observed ARTEX accelerating scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying and OAuth application abuse. Several ARTEX-driven operations reached privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting. Following the ConnectWise compromise, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate to more than 2,250 tenants at rates of up to 2,900 attempts per minute [9].

Darktrace Threat Research found activity in its own telemetry involving infrastructure later associated with the campaign. On 13 October, Darktrace recorded failed authentication activity involving 144.172.64[.]128, one of the addresses Microsoft later identified as performing sign-ins and Microsoft Graph activity in ConnectWise customer environments. Darktrace analysis identified 65 failed authentication attempts in around 20 minutes.

The telemetry establishes repeated failed authentication from infrastructure later associated with the campaign. It does not establish ARTEX execution or successful compromise. At the time of observation, Microsoft's later attribution was unavailable. Analysts therefore had the behavior itself: repeated failed authentication from the same source over a short period, together with any related identity, application or network activity inside the environment.

Microsoft documented a wider password-spray campaign against 327 accounts across eight organizations between 10 and 14 October. It recorded more than 151,000 failed logons, including more than 111,000 on 11 October, but no successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call or directory change from that campaign. Microsoft also reported that most Storm-0940 targeting was unsuccessful [9].

Where the actor progressed beyond authentication, Microsoft observed service-principal sign-ins followed by Graph and directory operations. Activity included reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to modify privileges. Microsoft recommends correlating service-principal sign-ins with Graph activity, directory changes and resource access [9].

Behavior before attribution

The PHP and ARTEX cases begin with different information. PHP defenders knew which software required urgent remediation but initially had limited information about exploitation. Process execution, file modification and outbound communication could still provide evidence of compromise.

The PHP and ARTEX observations also illustrate the difference between volume and impact. Darktrace observed broad scanning around the PHP disclosure, while the ARTEX-associated infrastructure produced concentrated authentication activity. Neither observation independently demonstrates compromise and in each case examining the behavior that follows the initial interaction is the investigative clue.

The Darktrace ARTEX-related observation began with authentication behavior. Microsoft publicly attributed the source infrastructure eight days later. That attribution added context, but it did not change what had originally been recorded in the environment.

AI is now present at several points in this cycle. Daybreak applies models to vulnerability discovery and remediation. Darktrace Signal Labs demonstrated how a trusted enterprise agent could be co-opted in a controlled environment. JPCERT/CC confirmed AI-assisted vulnerability scanning and API attacks in recent incidents. Microsoft documented ARTEX being used by Storm-0940 in active operations [4][7][8][9].

Microsoft's findings also show why scale and impact must be assessed separately. One ARTEX-associated campaign produced more than 151,000 failed logons without successful access, while other operations reached privileged cloud access in less than three hours. Security teams have to distinguish high-volume attempts from activity that progresses through authentication, privilege changes and resource access.

The evidence required to assess these cases remains familiar: authentication records, process execution, application and directory changes, file activity and network communication. AI can increase the rate at which those behaviors occur. Defenders still need to establish their sequence and impact.

Credit to Emma Foulger, Sam Lister, Dylan Evans, Moishe Tajtelbaum

[3] Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2026-151/

[4] OpenAI, Daybreak: Tools for securing every organization in the world, 22 June 2026. https://openai.com/index/daybreak-securing-the-world/

[5] OpenAI Developers, Scaling cyber defenders with Daybreak, 21 August 2026. https://developers.openai.com/blog/scaling-cyber-defenders-with-daybreak

[6] OpenAI, Cloudflare links vulnerability discovery to defense with OpenAI, 21 October 2026. https://openai.com/index/cloudflare-cyber/
