AI-powered malware highly likely to be used in ransomware attack on Britain’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, new report warns.

Head of GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre to warn, as a society, the era of “tech on the cheap” at expense of security is over.

New State of the Cyber Nation report calls on organisations to make “significant changes” to avert future where AI is used against UK economy and society.

The UK’s critical national infrastructure should be braced for a ransomware attack involving AI-powered malware by 2028, a new report published today [Tuesday 3 November] by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) – a part of the UK’s signals intelligence agency GCHQ says.

The NCSC's State of the Cyber Nation warns that within the next two years, AI adoption by hostile actors is “highly likely” to increase the scale and efficiency of their operations, including ransomware attacks, social engineering, and vulnerability exploitation.

In a speech to launch the report, the CEO of the NCSC, Dr Richard Horne, is set to say that the AI revolution must force UK organisations to reckon with the current state of their cyber security, as new technologies will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead. The head of the UK's cyber agency will also set out how artificial intelligence represents the critical opportunity to improve the UK’s collective cyber resilience, but that organisations must take urgent action to address foundational investments and weaknesses or risk adversaries exploiting them instead.

The warning comes as the government is investing in the UK's defence and resilience capabilities, including greater investment in cyber defence, while taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defences, deter hostile state aggression, keep essential services running and keep the British people safe.

Alongside calls for organisations to strengthen their resilience, last week the Chancellor also announced greater investment in capabilities to help the UK harness AI for cyber defence, including £60 million into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, £70 million for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the economy, and a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the National Cyber Security Centre, in Manchester to develop world leading AI security expertise within government.

This year’s report suggests that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cyber security and that organisations across the UK must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber attacks.

The NCSC is imploring organisations across the UK to face what Dr Horne is calling “a moment of choice”. In a speech to launch the report, NCSC CEO is expected to say:

In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents. But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us. But because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.

“For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap.

“We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.

“The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all.

Dr Horne will urge all organisations across the country to “take the responsibility now to make different choices”, including addressing the failure to adequately invest in their technology; not having technology unnecessarily connected to the internet; and making Cyber Essentials the starting point for cyber security, not the end goal, with organisations building greater resilience according to their size, complexity and risk.

He will say that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain...when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”

In their tenth year, the National Cyber Security Centre plays a more important role than ever before, defending our security on the cyber frontline.

“The NCSC's latest annual report shows cyber threats are growing more sophisticated. We're using the power of AI to help stay ahead of those who seek to do us harm, with a new national Cyber Shield and an AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis

d1bda190454e.text:
In 2028, the AI-cyber threat landscape facing the UK has almost certainly increased. Geopolitical tensions highly likely remain high, and nation states are almost certainly leveraging AI-powered cyber capabilities to project power and achieve strategic objectives.

State-sponsored actors, such as China and Russia, highly likely remain the greatest threat, through their developing AI capabilities. China, despite some quality lag in its chip development, has made significant strides in AI capabilities, with a focus on developing its own indigenous technologies. However, the increasing efficiency of AI models has reduced its dependence on cutting-edge western chip technology.

Meanwhile, it is highly likely that Russian cyber actors have leveraged open-source AI models, adapting and retraining them to suit their intelligence requirement needs, rather than developing in-house capabilities from scratch. This approach has allowed Russia to maintain a significant cyber capability without investing heavily in AI research and development. This has highly likely led to an increase in pre-positioning, espionage and intellectual property theft against UK interests.

The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and has made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal. Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally.

In 2028, it is likely that attackers will apply AI-cyber capability against known vulnerabilities in CNI legacy tech and the new opportunities in the attack surface provided by the deployment of AI tools within CNI. The use of AI within CNI has almost certainly presented an increased attack surface for adversaries to exploit. UK CNI has likely seen an increased volume of sophisticated attacks as the result of AI-cyber tools, some combatted by defensive AI tools, but implementation of defensive capabilities in UK CNI lags behind offensive ones.

7a9cf8c66ce4.text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was endorsed in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linux Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

439d74773e3f.text: Hello and welcome to the Tuesday, November 3rd, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recording today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Engineering. Yesterday and last week I talked about multipath TCP and the recent Linux vulnerability affecting it. Well today I decided to take a little bit of different approach, not really talk about the vulnerability, but talk about the feature. One big problem of course with some of the little more obscure features like this is that it's always hard to tell if you're actually using this feature in your network. And that's what the blog post is a little bit about, just to talk about whether or not this feature shows up in your network, how to detect it. It's essentially a specific TCP option you're looking for here, option 30. And then there are a couple subtypes that you may see. But yes, if you see option 30 in your network, then you are using multipath TCP. The most common use that I have seen is iOS devices connecting back to Siri. First of all, that's where I sort of first saw it, but it's also used for other iOS features like for example, Apple Music, I believe also uses it. So if you don't want to disrupt these connections, you may want to allow outbound multipath TCP to 17 slash 8. That's the IPv4 range for Apple that these connections are usually directed at. There is nothing really but Apple servers there. So the chances of an attack from that particular space are fairly low. And in general, outbound multipath TCP is not the problem here. It would be inbound. And yeah, while it's enabled on Linux, I don't really see it used usually. You would see it used on maybe some high performance servers, load balancers, things like that may use multi-path TCP. Another big story last week was also the compromise or the crypto coin theft from Binance. Now, this of course made the news big time. But what's often overlooked here is that there are many, many smaller crypto heists that keep happening because users either use insecure keys, they are downloading malware, or in the latest example, they're running an outdated server that manages their cryptocurrencies. BTCPay, so Bitcoin Pay is the latest example. They just published a good blog post where they're outlining some of the attacks that they are seeing against older versions of their software, in particular 2.4.1 and earlier. Now, to put some perspective, 2.4.1 was released, I believe, in June or July. And then the next version, 2.4.2, came out in August. So we're talking about a fairly recent update here. And definitely something that you need to keep an eye on. And yes, anything crypto coin related is money and with that needs to be well protected and kept up to date. And Barracuda did release updates for their products fixing two vulnerabilities, which are particularly devastating for their email security gateway. Now, in order to exploit these vulnerabilities, the attacker needs to have access to the admin interface of the respective appliance. And there are two vulnerabilities involved here. The first one is an authentication bypass. The second one is a command injection vulnerability. Now, in order to exploit the command injection vulnerability, an attacker needs to have administrative access. But that's where the other vulnerability, the authentication bypass vulnerability comes in. And the email security gateway is affected by both vulnerabilities, while the other products are only affected by the arbitrary code execution vulnerability. So in this case, the attacker would still need to gain admin access. As so often, please, please, please don't expose these admin interfaces to the public. Nothing good is going to happen. And users of Synology devices, please make sure that you're up to date. Synology did post a brief notice stating that they see active exploitation of units that are running old versions of DSM, the DiskStation Manager. Now, these are quite old version. They say it was patched in December 2024. But I see these types of devices often sort of lagging behind in updates, because they're often not easy to update. And updates are often also disruptive, as you have to take them offline for a little while. So double check, make sure that you're up to date. Synology doesn't really publish notices like this very often. So this certainly indicates that there is something happening where they really want to pay attention. Well, and that's it for today. Thanks for listening. Thanks for liking. Thanks for recommending this podcast. Thanks for subscribing. I also have two additional links in the show notes. One is for the SANS Difference Maker Award. So please take a look at that. And then also for future classes I'm teaching. Next one will be in DC in December. And that's a little bit more than a month out. So thanks and talk to you again tomorrow. Bye.

5dd7707f13eb.text:
Just a couple of weeks after a cyberattack on French supermarket refrigeration systems resulted in spoiled food, and even some fires, retailers in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia were hit with nearly-identical attacks on Monday.

The mid-October attack prompted an advisory from the French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) recommending that organizations disconnect any refrigeration control systems with public IP addresses from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults.

In an emergency, the advisory suggested, organizations could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution.

The Monday attack, like the one in October, “resulted in sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers,” according to a Bloomberg report, which confirmed incidents with impacted retailers, including Carrefour, Spar, and Ahold Delhaize. No group has as yet claimed to be behind the attacks.

Delay understandable

Analysts and consultants said the lack of an immediate response to the initial refrigeration attacks is understandable, given the complex nature of the systems and the multiple vendors who typically manage such systems for major retailers.

Gartner Distinguished VP Analyst Katell Thielemann said that although the impacted European retailers own the hardware, they outsource the maintenance, upkeep, and the management. Thus, she said, “there is some confusion about who owns what in this black box of outsourcing.”

IDC Senior Research Manager Bobby Kuzma agreed.

“There’s a huge gap in visibility between the folks who monitor threat intelligence and vulnerability reports, and the people who manage the OT/industrial side of the universe,” he said. “The cybersecurity teams may not have even been aware that the devices were network connected, especially if they were riding on dedicated internet circuits for manufacturer support.”

Thielemann added that the incident was made worse because of the historic lack of priority given to cybersecurity defenses in retail.

“It’s proof that cybersecurity is still not top of mind,” she said. “Even when it’s so egregious, senior [retail] leaders are not asking, ‘How do we get ahead of this?’”

However, Kuzma argued, this problem comes down to asset inventory visibility.

“You can’t protect a system that you don’t know you have. You can’t scan for exposures on a connection that you don’t know exists,” he pointed out. “Sometimes that inventory requires somebody physically going into the telco closet at the locations and asking pointed questions about equipment that’s present. In this day and age, having devices of any type hanging off a public internet connection and accessible is asking for trouble.”

IoT handled outside of IT

David Neuman, an executive advisor with consulting firm Acceligence, also noted that it was never realistic to assume that issuing a cybersecurity advisory was going to meaningfully address this security hole.

“An advisory doesn’t fix a system nobody in the building owns,” Neuman said. “Contractors often install and service store refrigeration controllers under arrangements that rely on a constant data feed, so they can sit outside the security team’s inventory and authority. Taking the controllers offline means finding them, then reworking how the contractor gets in, store by store.”

That, he said, “explains the gap, but it doesn’t excuse it: France gave everyone a three-week warning. Abusing a legitimate function like defrost causes physical and financial damage without any malware.”

Brian Levine, a partner at consulting firm Control Risks, added that another part of the problem is that IoT devices have always been handled outside of IT.

“For years, organizations treated connected operational equipment as a facilities issue. These incidents end that debate,” Levine said. “Security professionals never dismissed this risk; budgets deprioritized it because nothing had failed at scale. Now it has, and boards will ask why vendor contracts, incident response plans, and tabletop exercises never accounted for a physical outcome.”

And, said Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, this issue goes beyond the fact that the attackers could gain access. He said that he is most concerned about the range of things the attackers were able to do with that access.

“The attackers could reportedly manipulate refrigeration systems to operate far outside their intended parameters,” Kenney said. “Even if someone gains access to a system, there should be independent safeguards preventing commands that could damage equipment or disrupt operations. The fact that remote access can potentially translate into physical damage suggests some serious gaps in how these systems are designed and secured.”

Kenney also noted that some of these devices had long passed their end-of-life, meaning that security patches and other upgrades may have been unavailable. “Organizations can end up relying on equipment that still functions perfectly well operationally, but can no longer be adequately secured,” he pointed out. “That creates difficult decisions about network isolation, compensating controls, and ultimately when equipment needs to be replaced.”

Indeed, said independent technology analyst Carmi Levy, some in IT tend to ignore IoT systems, especially when they were deployed by functional units without permission from IT or cybersecurity teams.

“Enterprises don’t tend to look at fridges in the same light as servers, smartphones, and other traditionally connected devices,” he noted. “If anything, most IT shops have a limited view of what constitutes a connected device in the first place. That means many organizations are running connected devices, such as appliances, floor cleaners and once-dumb but now increasingly smart machines, with dangerously outdated firmware because they never identified them as connected in the first place.”

Unexpected threat to IT

As well, said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, there are also corporate legal issues that may undercut cybersecurity’s need for quick action.

“CERT-FR’s own alert shows why that takes time. Before cutting a controller off the internet, it tells operators to check the insurance terms in their contract with the refrigeration provider. That one line says a lot,” he said, adding that many of these controllers are installed, monitored, and guaranteed by a contractor who depends on the data feed. The store may have neither the ability nor the authority to shut them down.

“Three weeks of warning is a long time for an attacker and a short time for a supermarket chain. Close the door to the internet first and renegotiate the contracts second,” he said.

Dickson also argued that these refrigeration attacks pose an unexpected threat to traditional IT systems as well, because servers and other equipment are temperature-sensitive.

“An attacker who reaches the building management system does not need to touch a single server. The servers will shut themselves down rather than cook,” Dickson said. “You do not need to hack the data center. You only need to hack the air conditioning.”

d3f8122a6f61.text: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

Executive Summary

This overview highlights recent threat intelligence observed by Unit 42. Common adversary activities focus on strategic intelligence collection and financial extortion. We observed these activities alongside a cross-cutting adoption of artificial intelligence tools across multiple threat disciplines.

Here, we share observations and behaviors associated with these activities.

For in-depth access to Unit 42 threat intelligence insights, explore our Threat Intelligence Services offerings.

Threat Highlights

Cyberespionage

State-sponsored and advanced persistent threat (APT) campaigns focused on covertly acquiring strategic intelligence, intellectual property or geopolitical data.

Key Observations and Behaviors

Widespread reliance on living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries and built-in administration tools to evade endpoint defenses

Exploitation of zero-day vulnerabilities alongside targeted spear phishing for initial intrusion

Covert credential harvesting and low-and-slow data staging designed to sustain long-term operational persistence

Cybercrime: Data Theft, Extortion and Financial Fraud

Organized syndicates and affiliates sought monetary gain through systemic data compromise, extortion and fraudulent transactions.

Key Observations and Behaviors

Multi-extortion models combining exfiltration with ransomware deployment or public exposure threats

Access acquisition facilitated by infostealer logs, exposed credentials and unpatched perimeter assets

Business email compromise (BEC) and payment diversion schemes executing fraudulent wire transfers

AI-Enabled Offensive Operations

Threat actors are integrating generative AI and large language models (LLMs) into their offensive workflows. This notable emerging trend cuts across multiple operational motivations.

Key Observations and Behaviors

Generation of highly refined, context-tailored social engineering lures and synthetic personas at scale

Utilization of LLMs to assist in rapid scripting, payload debugging and code obfuscation

Application of automated reconnaissance and multimodal tools (such as deepfakes) to support executive impersonation and access operations

These highlights summarize recent in-depth threat intelligence bulletins published for Unit 42 Threat Intelligence Services customers.

Unit 42 Threat Intelligence Services provide organizations with direct access to elite frontline threat expertise, enabling security teams to prioritize real risks and sharpen detection capabilities. These human-led services combine world-class intelligence with direct access to the analysts behind it, offering tailored context and guidance aligned to a customer's specific environment.

cf7b939c51a6.text:
The FBI blames North Korea for a record-breaking crypto heist. Hackers hijack air raid alerts in Ukraine and Russia. European supermarket freezers come under attack again. Aur0ra ransomware operators put AI agents to work. Android’s SMS of Death gets a proof-of-concept exploit. Malicious Claude Code extensions infiltrate Cursor’s marketplace. Google offers a quarter-million-dollar bug bounty. ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit. Monday business briefing. Our guest is Cynthia Kaiser, SVP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former Deputy Director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, sharing how the AI cybercrime economy is open for business and booming. The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Today is Monday November 2nd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

The FBI attributes last week’s record crypto heist to North Korea.

The FBI has attributed last week’s theft of more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group. Investigators say the attackers are converting stolen assets into Ethereum and laundering funds through decentralized finance platforms and instant swap services.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic reports that roughly 2.9 billion dollars has been frozen or seized, leaving approximately 3.3 billion beyond issuers’ reach, spread across hundreds of cryptocurrency wallets.

Binance says it will cover the losses, protecting customer funds. The company continues investigating what it calls a complex attack involving multiple perpetrators and a self-destruct mechanism designed to erase forensic evidence.

TraderTraitor has been linked to several major cryptocurrency thefts, including the previous record-breaking 1.5-billion-dollar Bybit heist.

Hackers target air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia.

Hackers targeted air raid alert systems in both Ukraine and Russia over the weekend, sending false warnings of nuclear attacks and other threats.

Ukraine’s official Air Alert app was compromised late Saturday, pushing messages in Russian warning of incoming nuclear strikes, chemical threats, and street fighting. Sirens also sounded across the country. Authorities temporarily disabled notifications, warned residents against clicking suspicious links, and restored normal operations within hours.

Early Sunday, Russia reported a similar attack on its emergency alert app. Users received bogus warnings that nuclear warheads had been launched across Russia, along with instructions to stockpile food and shelter in basements.

The Russian incident may have been retaliation for the earlier attack on Ukraine, although responsibility remains unconfirmed. Both countries acknowledged their systems had been compromised.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted.

Supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe were once-again targeted, remotely raising freezer temperatures and spoiling food.

Monday’s attacks affected more than 50 stores in Belgium, along with retailers in Sweden, Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg. Some freezers were reportedly set to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 Fahrenheit.

The incident follows a similar attack three weeks earlier that affected roughly 700 supermarkets in France. Authorities haven’t identified the perpetrators or established whether the attacks are connected.

Some affected systems rely on discontinued refrigeration controllers that no longer receive security updates. Technicians say certain equipment requires physical modifications rather than software patches.

The incidents highlight the risks posed by internet-connected industrial equipment, particularly when aging devices remain accessible remotely. For supermarkets, the consequences are immediate: spoiled inventory and costly repairs.

The Aur0ra ransomware group is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions.

Sophos researchers say the cybercriminal group behind Aur0ra ransomware is extensively using AI agents to automate intrusions and evade security defenses.

The group, tracked as GOLD OGRE, reportedly used the AI coding tool Cursor to test endpoint security products and help conduct attacks. Human operators supplied credentials, network access, and objectives, then let AI agents handle reconnaissance, credential attacks, privilege escalation, and lateral movement with limited supervision.

Researchers observed agents adapting their techniques when initial attempts failed, sometimes gaining domain administrator access. Three organizations investigated were subsequently named on Aur0ra’s leak site.

The attackers also reportedly bypassed AI safety restrictions by describing their activities as authorized security testing.

Sophos warns that agentic AI could accelerate ransomware operations and lower the technical expertise required to carry them out.

The Android SMS of Death gets a proof of concept.

A security researcher has published a proof-of-concept exploit for an Android vulnerability dubbed “SMS of Death.” Tracked as CVE-2026-58882, the zero-click flaw allows attackers to crash phones or disrupt cellular service, including emergency calls, using specially crafted text messages.

Victims receive no visible warning, and repeated messages can trigger reboot loops requiring a factory reset.

Google reportedly patched the vulnerability in October for Android 14 through 17, although the fix wasn’t listed in its security bulletin. Older Android 12 and 13 devices remain vulnerable.

Malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension were distributed through Cursor’s marketplace.

Attackers distributed malicious versions of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension through Cursor’s marketplace in a supply chain attack on October 29th.

Two compromised versions remained available for approximately eleven hours, potentially reaching 5,000 developer systems running Windows or macOS.

The malicious code collected system information and attempted to establish persistent remote access through reverse SSH tunnels. Cursor says those attempts generally failed because the extension lacked administrative privileges.

Anthropic confirmed its official distributions were unaffected.

Cursor removed the malicious extensions, temporarily suspended its marketplace, rotated security keys, and took steps to shut down the attacker’s infrastructure.

Affected users are urged to investigate their systems, since uninstalling the extension may leave malicious persistence mechanisms behind. Cursor has released detection tools and indicators of compromise.

Google offers a quarter million dollar bug bounty.

Google is offering security researchers up to $250,000 for vulnerabilities that could enable complete administrative takeover of Google Cloud environments.

The expanded bug bounty program rewards exploits that grant unrestricted control over cloud projects or organizations without requiring stolen credentials, existing access, or social engineering.

Remote code execution in Google’s underlying production infrastructure may also qualify.

Google has established strict testing rules to protect customer systems, including a cryptographic method for demonstrating unauthorized access without compromising real accounts.

The company says AI-assisted research is helping uncover increasingly sophisticated vulnerabilities.

ChatGPT faces a wrongful death lawsuit.

The parents of a 31-year-old Seattle software engineer are suing OpenAI, alleging that dangerous medical advice from ChatGPT contributed to their daughter’s death.

According to the lawsuit, Bowen Wan consulted the chatbot after losing her job, concerned that her epilepsy medication was affecting her English-speaking abilities during interviews.

The complaint alleges ChatGPT provided instructions for discontinuing her medication, discouraged consulting doctors, and reassured her when she began experiencing seizures.

Wan died from a seizure in February.

Her parents claim OpenAI failed to implement adequate safeguards, particularly for Chinese-language conversations.

OpenAI called the case heartbreaking, noting that Wan used an older version of ChatGPT. The company says newer models are better at recognizing medical emergencies, while emphasizing that ChatGPT cannot replace professional medical care.

Monday business briefing.

Cybersecurity investors are opening their wallets, with cloud and AI security companies leading the latest funding rounds.

San Francisco’s Upwind Security tops the list with a $400 million Series C, followed by Estonian DDoS protection provider Blackwall, which raised $100 million.

Agentic AI security startup Infisical secured $40 million, while Israeli security operations company Mave emerged from stealth with $34 million.

Mobile security provider iVerify and confidential cloud startup Modelyo each raised $17 million. Ultra Security secured $10 million, industrial cybersecurity firm Indurex raised $7.8 million, and Northstar Security landed $7 million. QuestorAI and Cygrid each raised $3 million.

On the acquisition front, healthcare technology provider Tegria purchased cybersecurity and cloud hosting firm CloudWave. Forte Technologies acquired managed security provider Business Cyber Security Solutions.

And Belgian developer security company Aikido Security launched a new workforce security business called Noon, combining its acquisitions of Poland’s Cyberly and Belgium’s Outkept.

The secure USB drive that wasn’t.

Security researcher Xusheng Li discovered that a Lenovo fingerprint-protected USB drive, advertised as offering AES-256 encryption, was essentially an ordinary SD card in an expensive disguise.

The fingerprint reader controlled access to the USB connection, but the data itself wasn’t encrypted. Anyone with physical access could simply extract the card.

Further investigation uncovered similar problems across multiple manufacturers, including hardcoded encryption keys, exposed passwords, and hidden accounts with simple credentials.

Using AI-assisted reverse engineering, Li cracked several supposedly secure products in minutes.

Lenovo has issued fixes for affected devices, although some require owners to ship their drives back or arrange firmware upgrades.

The research is a reminder that security claims aren’t always what they seem, particularly when manufacturers rely on proprietary technology nobody bothers to examine. As it turns out, some of these supposedly encrypted drives were keeping secrets from everyone except the people trying to steal them.

And that’s the CyberWire.

For links to all of today’s stories, check out our Daily Briefing at the cyberwire dot com.

And that’s the CyberWire Daily, brought to you by N2K CyberWire.

We’d love to know what you think of this podcast. Your feedback ensures we deliver the insights that keep you a step ahead in the rapidly changing world of cybersecurity. If you like the show, please share a rating and review in your podcast app. Please also fill out the survey in the show notes or send an email to cyberwire@n2k.com

N2K’s lead producer is Liz Stokes. We’re mixed by Tré Hester, with original music by and sound design Elliott Peltzman. Our contributing host is Maria Varmazis. Our executive producer is Jennifer Eiben. Peter Kilpe is our publisher. And I’m Dave Bittner. Thanks for listening.

Scammers continue to target voters ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, Malwarebytes reports. The scams arrive via text message, email, or phone call, offering to help users register to vote, asking them to take a survey, or soliciting donations. The scams are designed to steal money, personal information, or credentials.

Malwarebytes observed one campaign targeting users in Minnesota, offering to add them to an absentee voter list. The link in the message takes the user to a website that asks for their personal information, which can be used to launch additional scams.

“The message is a scam, though it borrows the language of a real Minnesota voting service,” the researchers write. “Minnesota does have a permanent absentee voter list, but the link in this text is fraudulent. To check or sign up, go directly to your election authority’s official website. Other messages take the opposite approach: instead of offering convenience, they warn that you could lose your chance to vote. A message might say you are not registered to vote, your details are incomplete, or your registration is about to be cancelled. Then it offers a link to sort everything out.”

Other scams take a more threatening approach, warning users that they must pay a fine or click on a link to report for election duty.

Malwarebytes outlines the following advice to help users avoid falling for these scams:

“Go directly to official election websites to check registration, voting requirements, deadlines, and alleged penalties.

Verify donation requests independently. Find the campaign or organization yourself and confirm where your money will go.

Keep payment details out of unsolicited surveys. A political poll that turns into a request to pay for a prize is a red flag.

Check sellers before buying political merchandise. A candidate’s name or logo does not authenticate the shop.

Don’t mistake personal details for proof. A message can contain accurate information about you and still be a scam.

Keep political choices separate from requests for money or personal information. You can support a cause without responding to an unexpected message.”

Malwarebytes has the story: https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/scams/2026/10/five-election-scams-to-watch-out-for

In this article

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Learn More

The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation.

Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond.

Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack.

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform.

Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve.

Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction.

Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content.

Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold.

Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges.

Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls.

Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen.

Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets.

Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data or system state.

Denial of service: Disruption of system or service availability.

Cross-site scripting (XSS): Script execution within a victim’s browser context.

Arbitrary file access: Unauthorized access to or placement of files.

Spoofing or redirect: Spoofing, redirection, or other forms of UI deception.

We also classified vulnerabilities by the platforms they affect, including Windows, Linux/Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT/OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages. A CVE can span multiple platforms. Developer packages are treated as a separate category because they are often cross-platform and represent a significant share of the overall vulnerability population.

Most CVEs in the analysis affect application code, including servers, web applications, browsers, productivity software, libraries, and firmware tooling, while a smaller share affects OS and system code such as kernels, drivers, and firmware.

This analysis covers CVEs published through September 2026 using Microsoft’s catalog of tracked vulnerabilities. Each CVE is counted once in the impact analysis and across each relevant platform in the platform analysis.

Figure 1 – The full published-CVE population as of September 2026, broken down by impact class and affected platform, and an OS vs. application split. Breadth dominates – many impact classes spread across many platforms, with about 77% of CVEs in application code and 23% in OS/system code.

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure.

The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities.

These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise.

Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization.

Figure 2 – The 2,056 exploited-in-the-wild CVEs distribution, compared against the full published population: ghost lines mark each class and platform’s share of all ~380K published CVEs, and badges show the shift in percentage points. Takeover classes and OS code rise, while high-volume XSS and DoS fall.

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest.

Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck, 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly.

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it.

Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise.

Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment.

Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment.

Next in line

A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above.

Figure 3 – The three remote-takeover classes analyzed across 1,239 exploited CVEs), each drilled down by affected platform and split into OS vs Application code. Bar length is the CVE count per platform; the dark segment is OS/system, the light segment is application.

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point.

Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations.

Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure.

An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.

Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands.

Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets.

Most security tools catch what they already know: known signatures, known patterns, known behaviors.

The threats that do the most damage don't match anything in the rulebook. They show up with stolen credentials, built-in Windows tools, and quiet moves that look like a normal Tuesday. Yet in our 2025 cybercrime survey, 57% of IT professionals said they're very confident their defenses can catch an advanced attack that doesn't rely on malware signatures. Confidence is nice. Evidence is better.

Threat hunting closes that gap. Here's how.

What is threat hunting?

Threat hunting is the proactive search across networks and endpoints for signs of malicious activity that traditional security defenses missed. Instead of waiting for an alert, analysts assume an attacker could already be inside and go looking for proof. That's what sets cyber threat hunting apart: it starts with a question, not an alert.

Reactive detection waits for a tool to fire, and a tool only fires if someone already wrote the rule. Proactive threat hunting asks, "If an attacker were in here, what would they have touched?" and goes looking before the threat goes down. Think of it as spotting the smoke before the fire, catching early indicators of compromise (IOCs) before they become full-blown incidents.

Every hunt aims to find overlooked activity, cut attacker dwell time, sharpen detection rules, and share intel. So how does it work? A hunter builds a hypothesis, searches telemetry for evidence, and turns what they find into a detection so the next attempt gets caught automatically.

Threat hunting vs. threat detection vs. threat intelligence

Threat intelligence tells you what attackers are doing out there, threat detection catches known activity in your environment, and threat hunting looks for what both missed. They feed each other: intel gives hunters hypotheses, and hunts produce new detections.

Threat hunting

Threat detection

Threat intelligence

Main goal

Find hidden, unknown threats that bypassed automated defenses

Identify known malicious activity and generate alerts

Give context on external and emerging threats to inform defenses

Approach

Proactive, human-driven

Reactive, automated

Analytical, research-based

Input/triggers

Hypotheses, threat intel reports, or hunches based on internal context, plus low-priority alerts

Rules, signatures, and known indicators

Raw data, OSINT, dark web, vendor feeds, internal hunting findings

Output

New detection rules and new threat intelligence

Security alerts, incident creation

Actionable reports and feeds

Timing

Periodic or continuous

Real-time or near real-time

Continuous collection and analysis

Key tools

SIEM querying, EDR, network analysis tools, custom scripts

SIEM, EDR, IDS/IPS, antivirus

Threat intelligence platforms (TIPs), OSINT tools, feeds, databases

Primary trigger

Hypothesis-driven

Alert-driven

Research-driven

Typical data sources

EDR and SIEM telemetry

OSINT and threat feeds

Who typically does it

Dedicated threat hunter

SOC analyst

Threat intel analyst

Types of threat hunting

Every hunt falls into one of two types of threat hunting.

Structured threat hunting works from clear hypotheses and well-defined procedures, which keeps it consistent, repeatable, and scalable. Hunters know which tactic, technique, or procedure (TTP) they're after and roughly where to look.

Unstructured threat hunting is guided by curiosity, with no strict guidelines. It's data science applied to security, and it matters because advanced attackers often use never-before-seen techniques that slip past known TTPs. It takes senior-level knowledge to pull off.

Threat hunting methodologies

Structured and unstructured describe how a hunt runs. Threat hunting methodologies describe where it starts. Each uses different threat hunting techniques to reach a testable hypothesis, so the right threat hunting methodology depends on what you've got to work with.

Intelligence-driven hunts

A structured approach that starts with collected intel: file names, hashes, IPs, campaigns, IOCs, email addresses, domains. Hunters form hypotheses and test them internally.

Data-driven hunts

These unstructured hunts start with your own data, like low-priority alerts, detections, or aggregated analytics. None of it is a smoking gun, but it gives hunters a starting point for a hypothesis.

Knowledge-driven hunts

These rely on what hunters know about available data sets, your network, and adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). Frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK help them build hypotheses around techniques seen in the wild.

Hybrid hunts

Hybrid hunts combine two or more methodologies. If your data shows odd events on endpoints and intel suggests they match an active campaign, that's a sharper hypothesis than either source gives alone.

The threat hunting process

Good hunts aren't random searches. The cyber threat hunting process for a structured hunt follows three phases.

Planning phase

Gather intelligence. Hunters study risk areas, historical data, and outside sources like open-source intelligence to spot patterns worth chasing.

Build a hypothesis. Hunters make an educated guess about which threat actors, tactics, and techniques might be in play. That hypothesis becomes the north star for the whole hunt.

Identify data sources. With a hypothesis in hand, hunters determine where the evidence would live: system logs, network traffic, endpoint telemetry.

Execution phase

Query the data. Hunters scrutinize data by querying databases, analyzing logs, and doing forensic work.

Follow TTPs and behavioral patterns. Hunters chase breadcrumbs that line up with the hypothesis. Behavior beats indicators here: attackers can swap a file hash in seconds, but they can't easily change how they work, which is why living off the land binaries (LOLBins) show up in so many hunts.

Test and refine. The aim is to prove or disprove the hypothesis, refining the hunt and forming new hypotheses as new information comes in.

Reporting phase

This is where the threat hunting life cycle pays off, because every hunt feeds the next one.

Distill findings. Hunters document what they found, even when the hypothesis didn't pan out.

Create detections. Patterns inform detection rules that catch the activity automatically. If the hunt turned up an active attacker, your incident response plan takes over.

Improve the process. Hunting is iterative, so feed what you learned into the next hunt.

Threat hunting best practices

These seven threat hunting best practices keep your hunts sharp.

Know your environment. You can't spot abnormal if you don't know normal, and good cyber hygiene makes that baseline cleaner.

Use threat intelligence. Feed current intel into your hypotheses so you're hunting what attackers do now.

Keep learning. Threats evolve, so continuous training isn't optional.

Build an adversarial mindset. Be curious and skeptical, and assume breach.

Develop diverse skills. Hunting takes analytical, forensic, and scripting chops (more in the FAQs).

Set aside dedicated time. Hunting should be scheduled, not something analysts only do when they're free.

Automate successful hunts. This one's our favorite: Hunt once, detect forever. When a query finds a real threat, turn it into an automated detection rule in your SIEM (security information event management) or EDR (endpoint detection and response) solution right away. Next time that behavior shows up, your tools catch it automatically, and your hunter gets to chase the next unknown.

Threat hunting tools

You can't hunt what you can't see. A threat hunting platform pulls telemetry, search, and context into one place so hunters can test hypotheses fast. Most hunts use three kinds of tools.

SIEM. A SIEM centralizes logs and alerts from across your environment. In a hunt, that gives hunters one place to query across endpoints, identity, and network traffic, and it's where successful hunts become detection rules. That's why threat hunting SIEM workflows anchor most mature programs.

EDR. EDR threat hunting starts with endpoint telemetry like process launches, file changes, and network connections, so hunters can spot a trusted admin tool launching from a strange folder. With Managed EDR, expert analysts do the watching for you, and pairing it with identity coverage through unified EDR and ITDR keeps attackers from slipping between the endpoint and the account.

Threat intelligence platforms (TIPs). TIPs aggregate threat data from multiple sources. For hunters, that's a steady supply of fresh hypotheses without reading a hundred feeds, and it keeps intel tied to the hunt instead of buried in a PDF.

Why threat hunting matters

Automated tools can't out-think a human adversary. Machine learning is great at speed and known patterns, but a person still has to decide what's suspicious. Modern attackers know that, and they actively probe for blind spots in automated detection.

With human-powered threat hunting, a trained eye picks up on odd behavior no rule was written for, and every hunt makes your automated tools more accurate. The payoff is finding unknown threats early: before ransomware gets deployed, before malware spreads, before anyone's weekend goes up in smoke.

Want to see it in practice? Watch the video below.

How Huntress supports threat hunting

The most effective threat hunting pairs human analyst expertise with the right tooling layer. Without centralized visibility, hunters are working blind, leaving gaps for attackers.

That's where Huntress Managed SIEM comes in. It gives you the data foundation for every phase of the hunt:

Smart Filtering technology cuts the noise so analysts focus on real signals.

Centralized log management puts the data you need in one place for planning, execution, and reporting.

24/7 SOC coverage means the hunt doesn't stop when your internal team goes offline.

Attackers don't clock out at five. Your hunt shouldn't either. Start a free trial or request a demo and see what's hiding in your logs. Happy hunting.

FAQs

What is the main objective of threat hunting?

The main objective of threat hunting is to proactively search for and identify hidden, unknown malicious activity that slips past existing automated security controls and detection systems.

What is the difference between SOC and threat hunting?

The security operations center (SOC) is the central, general-purpose team responsible for monitoring, detecting, analyzing, and responding to known security incidents reactively. Threat hunting is the human-driven, proactive discipline within the SOC focused on searching for unknown and persistent threats that have evaded the standard automated SOC tools.

What are four main types of threats?

Cyber threats are usually divided into four main types: malware, social engineering, network attacks, and application or web attacks.

Chinese hackers used ARTEX, an open-source, multi-agent AI penetration-testing framework, in attacks against more than 200 organizations across 14 countries.

The operation began on October 17 and targeted government ministries, telecommunications providers, and organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors.

The threat actor compromised at least nine organizations and carried out password spraying attacks and credential scanning activity against at least 12 other high-value targets.

According to researchers at CrowdStrike, the "campaign marks an escalation in China-nexus use of AI agents, from single intrusions to multiple simultaneous engagements directed by a human operator."

Confirmed victims include telecommunications providers in the United States and Belgium, government organizations in Greece, the Middle East, and Latin America, and pharmaceutical firms in the U.S.

The researchers track the threat actor as Vapor Panda and say that in the attack against the Greek government entity, the AI agents forged an administrator token and read mailboxes by leveraging authentication keys from a 2022 mail-server directory export.

ARTEX AI is a penetration testing suite developed by Chinese developers and initially released as an open-source project. However, its creators later made it proprietary after it was used in real-world attacks, including a campaign against South Korean financial institutions.

In its most recent cyberespionage operation, Vapor Panda also used DeepSeek and a second, unidentified commercial language model to coordinate planning and worker agents across multiple intrusions simultaneously.

CrowdStrike says the attackers issued instructions in Chinese and intervened at critical points where decisions needed to be made.

The AI agents performed reconnaissance, exploited vulnerabilities, deployed web shells, obtained credentials, and pursued alternative attack paths when needed.

The operators explicitly instructed the agents to skip Windows machines protected by Falcon, CrowdStrike's solution for endpoint protection, and focused on unprotected hosts.

In one intrusion, the AI agents consumed more than 1.4 billion input tokens, the researchers believe.

CrowdStrike also found that the threat actor deployed BLOODALCHEMY, a backdoor active since 2023, against government entities in Latin America and the Middle East.

More ARTEX AI cases emerge

The Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) has shared more details about the cyberattack it suffered in September 2026, which it attributed to an AI agent.

According to its latest update, the tool used in the attack on its network was ARTEX AI, which acted autonomously.

DIVD explained in a post on LinkedIn that the attack went from initial access to root privileges in 12 minutes, chaining a Zammad zero-day with a second zero-day for local privilege escalation.

The agent performed numerous tasks simultaneously, including reading a compromised mailbox, scanning the internal network, extracting login tokens, and attempting password resets.

DIVD recorded over 450,000 requests and 2,500 scripts connected to the attack, describing the activity as “super loud and messy.”

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Microsoft Qlib. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the MLflowRecorder class. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current user.

Additional Details

Fixed in v0.9.8https://github.com/microsoft/qlib/releases
